title: Replica Module (RPM)
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS Replica Module (RPM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Category: AI and Interpretation Subcategory: Representation and Copy Module: Replica Module (RPM) Type: Classification Module Standard: Representation & Copy Standard (RCS™) Status: Canonical Module Version: 1.0 Effective Date: 19 March 2026 Canonical Definition A Replica is a deliberately created asset that imitates, reconstructs, or reinterprets an original asset with the intention of resembling it. A replica is not the original and is not a direct reproduction. It is a constructed representation based on the original. Why This Matters Without clear classification of replicas: replicas may be confused with originals value may be misrepresented authorship may become unclear intentional imitation may be mistaken for reproduction Replicas must be distinguished from both copies and originals. Minimum Implementation Framework (MIF) Step 1 — Identify Reference Original Define the original asset being imitated or reconstructed. Step 2 — Confirm Constructed Nature Ensure the asset is intentionally created to resemble the original, not directly reproduced from it. Step 3 — Define Intent Establish that the purpose is imitation, reconstruction, or reinterpretation. Step 4 — Declare Replica Status The asset must be clearly identified as a replica. Step 5 — Define Relationship The connection to the original must remain identifiable but must not imply identity. Use Case 1 — Museum Reconstruction Scenario A museum creates a physical reconstruction of a historical object (e.g. dinosaur, artifact). Application The object is classified as a replica. Result original remains protected accurate representation is accessible no confusion with the original asset Use Case 2 — Artistic Interpretation Scenario An artist creates a painting inspired by a known artwork (e.g. reinterpretation of Mona Lisa). Application The work is classified as a replica or reinterpretation. Result clear distinction from the original new authorship is preserved creative freedom remains intact Structural Principle A replica is defined by intent, not by duplication. Closing Statement Resemblance does not create identity. A replica reflects the original but does not become it.

title: Representation & Copy Standard (RCS™)
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS Representation & Copy Standard (RCS™) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Category: AI and Interpretation Subcategory: Representation and Copy Type: Representation and Classification Standard OriginID: OOF-OID-AI-INT-RCS-2026-03-17-0001 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 17 March 2026 Compatibility: OOF™ Methodology OS · Origin Declaration Standard (ODS™) · Audit in Real Time™ Authority: OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Protection: MIP™ — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) A. Standard Abstract The Representation & Copy Standard (RCS™) defines the structural distinction between an original asset, its copies, and its representations across physical, digital, and virtual environments. The standard establishes a clear framework for identifying what a work is, how it exists, and under what conditions it may be reproduced, represented, exhibited, or referenced. RCS™ does not replace ownership law, copyright law, or institutional policy. RCS™ defines structural classification. B. Canonical Definition Representation & Copy Standard (RCS™) is a methodology for classifying original assets, copies, and representations according to their origin, form, relationship to the source, and declared mode of existence. RCS™ distinguishes between: what constitutes an original what constitutes a copy what constitutes a representation how each form may exist without confusion of status Origin defines what it is. Representation defines how it exists. C. Base An asset may exist in more than one form, but not in more than one origin state. A copy is not an origin. A representation is not the original. A digital form does not automatically invalidate authenticity. A physical form does not automatically guarantee originality. Clear classification is necessary whenever value, authorship, exhibition, insurance, licensing, or public trust depends on the declared status of a work. D. Core Principle A work must be classified according to its true structural state. No copy may be presented as an original. No representation may be treated as identical to source unless explicitly defined. No asset may derive legitimacy from ambiguity. Core Structural Categories RCS™ recognizes the following core states: Original Asset Physical Copy Digital Copy Digital Original Virtual Representation Replica Additional rights, authorization, and exhibition conditions may apply, but they do not alter the underlying state of the asset. Scope This standard applies to: artworks museum objects gallery editions digital cultural assets archival reproductions virtual exhibitions scanned or photographed works digitally originated works licensed reproductions Structural Rule Every asset must be classified according to: origin state form of existence relationship to the source declared representation status If these elements are not clearly declared, the asset remains structurally ambiguous. Methodology identify the source asset determine whether the asset is original, copy, or representation determine whether the form is physical, digital, or virtual define the relationship between the asset and the source declare the status of the asset assign any additional rights or exhibition conditions separately Use Context museums and collections galleries and edition structures insurance and valuation contexts virtual exhibitions cultural archiving licensed display systems digital heritage systems Positioning Not every visible form is an original. Not every copy is illegitimate. Not every digital form is secondary. Classification creates clarity. Canonical Closing Statement When the status of a work is unclear, trust collapses. Representation requires classification before value can be protected. title: Responsibility Assignment Standard - (RAS-A)
text: Responsibility Assignment Standard - (RAS-A) OriginID: OOF-OID-AGA-RASA-2026-06-17-0012 Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: Accountability Governance Architecture (AGA™) Operational Layer: Responsibility Assignment Governance Layer Governed Space: Responsibility Assignment Governance Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Accountability Governance Architecture Type: Parent Standard Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Origin Date: 17 June 2026 Compatibility: OOF Methodology OS · Accountability Governance Architecture (AGA™) · Responsibility Governance Standard (RGS) · Authority Governance Standard (AGS) · Authority Delegation Standard (ADS) · Evidence Accountability Standard (EAS) · INTEGROS® — Integrity Standard AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF Protection: MIP — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL) Canonical Definition System Canonical Definition Responsibility Assignment Standard (RAS-A) defines the structural conditions under which responsibilities may be assigned, allocated, transferred, accepted, recorded, governed, reconstructed, and enforced while preserving legitimacy, traceability, accountability, clarity, and operational validity throughout the responsibility-assignment lifecycle. RAS-A governs responsibility assignment. The standard establishes the foundational conditions required to determine who assigned responsibility, to whom responsibility was assigned, what responsibility was assigned, whether the assignment was valid, and whether the assigned responsibility remained governable. Responsibility does not become operationally valid merely because a task exists. Responsibility becomes governable when it is properly assigned. RAS-A governs that assignment. A. Standard Abstract Every governance system assigns responsibility. Organizations assign responsibility. Contractors assign responsibility. Supervisors assign responsibility. Institutions assign responsibility. AI orchestration systems increasingly assign responsibility. Human-AI environments require responsibility assignment governance. Without responsibility-assignment governance: duties become unclear task ownership becomes fragmented responsibility gaps emerge responsibility conflicts increase accountability becomes weakened operational failures become harder to reconstruct RAS-A exists to govern these conditions. B. Core Principle Responsibility assignment becomes valid only when assigned responsibilities remain identifiable, legitimate, accepted, traceable, reconstructable, accountable, and operationally valid throughout the responsibility- assignment lifecycle. C. Scope This standard may apply to: organizations institutions governments contractor networks subcontractor chains temporary workforce environments supervisory systems operational task assignment compliance environments AI systems autonomous agents orchestrated agent systems Human-AI operational environments robotics ecosystems future intelligent governance systems RAS-A applies wherever responsibility is assigned to an actor, system, role, organization, agent, or operational entity. D. Why This Standard Exists Responsibility governance requires more than identifying responsibility. Governance must also determine how responsibility was assigned. Common failures include: unclear task assignment undocumented responsibility allocation assignment to the wrong actor assignment without authority assignment without acceptance assignment without capability overlapping assignments abandoned assignments hidden responsibility transfers The challenge is not only determining who was responsible. The challenge is determining whether responsibility was validly assigned. RAS-A exists because responsibility assignment is a distinct governance space. E. Responsibility Assignment Integrity Logic Responsibility assignment integrity exists only when the following remain materially preservable: 1. Assignment Origin Integrity The assignment remains attributable to a legitimate assignment source. 2. Assignment Scope Integrity The assigned responsibility remains connected to clearly defined duties and boundaries. 3. Assignment Validity Integrity The assignment remains legitimate, accepted, recognized, and operationally valid. 4. Assignment Traceability Integrity The assignment remains reconstructable throughout the assignment lifecycle. 5. Assignment Accountability Integrity The assignment remains connected to accountable governance structures and consequence-bearing relationships. F. Operational Architecture Space RAS-A defines the operational architecture space for: responsibility assignment governance task allocation governance duty assignment governance responsibility allocation assignment traceability assignment validity assignment accountability contractor responsibility assignment Human-AI responsibility assignment agent responsibility assignment operational duty governance This space exists because responsibility must be assigned before it can be fulfilled, traced, enforced, or connected to accountability. RAS-A governs whether responsibility assignment remains valid. G. Difference Between Responsibility and Responsibility Assignment Responsibility defines the duty to act. Responsibility assignment defines how that duty is allocated to a specific actor. Responsibility may exist as an obligation. Assignment determines who carries that obligation. RGS governs responsibility. RAS-A governs responsibility assignment. Both are required. H. Runtime Position RAS-A operates within the Responsibility Layer of AGA™. It follows: Relationship Accountability Standard (RAS) Authority Governance Standard (AGS) Authority Delegation Standard (ADS) Authority Validation Standard (AVS) Authority Escalation Standard (AES) Responsibility Governance Standard (RGS) and supports: Responsibility Continuity Standard (RCS) Responsibility Traceability Standard (RTS) Capability Readiness Governance Standard (CRGS) Chain of Control Standard (CCS) Accountability Governance Standard (AGS-A) RAS-A governs how responsibility becomes assigned before governance evaluates continuity, traceability, capability, control, oversight, evidence, or accountability. I. Responsibility Assignment Failure Rule Responsibility assignment failure occurs when responsibility assignments cannot be reliably identified, validated, accepted, reconstructed, governed, enforced, or connected to accountable governance structures. Examples include: undocumented assignment unclear assignment assignment without authority assignment to an incapable actor assignment without acceptance overlapping responsibility assignment hidden responsibility transfer responsibility-assignment gaps RAS-A exists to expose and govern these conditions. J. Validity Logic A responsibility-assignment environment is valid under RAS-A when: assignment sources remain identifiable assigned duties remain clearly defined assignment legitimacy remains demonstrable assignment acceptance remains reviewable assignment history remains reconstructable assignment accountability remains preservable assigned responsibilities remain operationally valid A responsibility-assignment environment becomes invalid when: assignment origin is unknown assigned duties are unclear assignment authority cannot be demonstrated assignment acceptance is absent or unverifiable assignment history cannot be reconstructed assignment accountability is lost K. Relationship to Other OOF Standards RAS-A derives from: Responsibility Governance Standard (RGS) Authority Governance Standard (AGS) Relationship Accountability Standard (RAS) and supports: Responsibility Continuity Standard (RCS) Responsibility Traceability Standard (RTS) Capability Readiness Governance Standard (CRGS) Chain of Control Standard (CCS) Evidence Accountability Standard (EAS) Accountability Governance Standard (AGS-A) RGS governs responsibility. RAS-A governs assignment of responsibility. RCS governs whether responsibility remains preserved. RTS governs whether responsibility can be reconstructed. L. Foundational Principle Responsibility cannot be enforced if responsibility was never validly assigned. Canonical Closing Statement Responsibility Assignment Standard (RAS-A) defines the structural conditions under which responsibilities may be assigned, allocated, transferred, accepted, recorded, governed, reconstructed, and enforced while preserving legitimacy, traceability, accountability, clarity, and operational validity throughout the responsibility-assignment lifecycle. Responsibility becomes governable only when assignment is clear. If responsibility assignment cannot be identified, validated, accepted, or reconstructed, accountability becomes unreliable. title: Responsibility Continuity Standard - (RCS)
text: Responsibility Continuity Standard - (RCS) OriginID: OOF-OID-AGA-RCS-2026-06-17-0013 Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: Accountability Governance Architecture (AGA™) Operational Layer: Responsibility Continuity Governance Layer Governed Space: Responsibility Continuity Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Responsibility Governance Type: Parent Standard Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Origin Date: 17 June 2026 Compatibility: OOF Methodology OS · Accountability Governance Architecture (AGA™) · Responsibility Governance Standard (RGS) · Responsibility Assignment Standard (RAS-A) · Chain of Control Standard (CCS) · Accountability Governance Standard (AGS-A) · INTEGROS® — Integrity Standard AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF Protection: MIP — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL) Canonical Definition System Canonical Definition Responsibility Continuity Standard (RCS) defines the structural conditions under which responsibilities remain preserved, connected, governable, traceable, transferable, reconstructable, enforceable, and operationally valid throughout the responsibility lifecycle despite organizational, operational, contractual, technological, supervisory, or governance changes. RCS governs responsibility continuity. The standard establishes the foundational conditions required to determine whether responsibility remained continuously preserved from assignment to outcome and whether responsibility survived transitions, transfers, escalations, reorganizations, substitutions, automation events, and governance changes. Responsibility may be assigned. Responsibility may be transferred. Responsibility may be shared. Responsibility may evolve. RCS governs whether responsibility remains continuous. A. Standard Abstract Many governance failures occur because responsibility disappears between events. Responsibilities often pass through: managers supervisors contractors subcontractors temporary workers organizations departments AI systems autonomous agents Without continuity governance: responsibility gaps emerge ownership becomes fragmented accountability weakens investigations become difficult governance reliability deteriorates RCS exists to govern these conditions. B. Core Principle Responsibility remains governance-valid only when responsibility continuity remains preservable, reconstructable, traceable, and enforceable throughout the responsibility lifecycle. C. Scope This standard may apply to: organizations institutions governments contractor networks subcontractor chains temporary workforce environments certification systems operational governance systems AI governance systems autonomous-agent environments Human-AI operational systems future intelligent governance systems RCS applies wherever responsibility must survive change. D. Why This Standard Exists Many systems successfully assign responsibility. Many systems fail to preserve responsibility. Examples include: responsibility transferred without records responsibility abandoned during transitions responsibility fragmentation responsibility gaps between organizations contractor continuity failures governance handover failures Human-AI responsibility discontinuity automation-related responsibility loss The challenge is not assigning responsibility. The challenge is preserving responsibility. RCS exists because responsibility continuity is a distinct governance space. E. Responsibility Continuity Integrity Logic Responsibility continuity integrity exists only when the following remain materially preservable: 1. Continuity Origin Integrity The continuity relationship remains attributable to legitimate responsibility sources. 2. Continuity Scope Integrity The preserved responsibility remains connected to clearly defined governance boundaries. 3. Continuity Validity Integrity Responsibility continuity remains legitimate and operationally valid. 4. Continuity Traceability Integrity Responsibility continuity remains reconstructable throughout the responsibility lifecycle. 5. Continuity Accountability Integrity Responsibility continuity remains connected to accountable governance structures. F. Operational Architecture Space RCS defines the operational architecture space for: responsibility continuity responsibility preservation responsibility transfers responsibility succession governance handovers contractor continuity governance Human-AI responsibility continuity AI responsibility continuity responsibility lifecycle governance continuity traceability This space exists because governance requires responsibility to remain preserved despite operational change. RCS governs whether responsibility remains continuous. G. Difference Between Assignment and Continuity Responsibility Assignment asks: Who received the responsibility? Responsibility Continuity asks: Did responsibility remain preserved afterward? RAS-A governs assignment. RCS governs preservation. Both are required. H. Runtime Position RCS operates within the Responsibility Layer of AGA™. It follows: Responsibility Governance Standard (RGS) Responsibility Assignment Standard (RAS-A) and supports: Responsibility Traceability Standard (RTS) Capability Readiness Governance Standard (CRGS) Chain of Control Standard (CCS) Governance Oversight Standard (GOS) Accountability Governance Standard (AGS-A) RCS governs whether responsibility survives operational reality. I. Responsibility Continuity Failure Rule Responsibility continuity failure occurs when responsibility cannot be reliably preserved, reconstructed, transferred, reviewed, governed, or connected to accountable governance structures. Examples include: responsibility gaps abandoned responsibility undocumented transfers continuity failures contractor responsibility discontinuity governance handover failures Human-AI continuity breakdowns fragmented responsibility chains RCS exists to expose and govern these conditions. J. Validity Logic A responsibility-continuity environment is valid under RCS when: responsibility remains continuously identifiable responsibility transitions remain visible continuity relationships remain reconstructable continuity accountability remains preservable continuity governance remains reviewable responsibility remains operationally valid A responsibility-continuity environment becomes invalid when: responsibility disappears continuity relationships become unverifiable transitions cannot be reconstructed responsibility ownership becomes fragmented governance continuity is lost K. Relationship to Other OOF Standards RCS derives from: Responsibility Governance Standard (RGS) Responsibility Assignment Standard (RAS-A) and supports: Responsibility Traceability Standard (RTS) Accountability Governance Standard (AGS-A) Accountability Continuity Standard (ACS) RGS governs responsibility. RAS-A governs assignment. RCS governs continuity. L. Foundational Principle Responsibility cannot remain governable if responsibility continuity cannot be preserved. Canonical Closing Statement Responsibility Continuity Standard (RCS) defines the structural conditions under which responsibilities remain preserved, connected, governable, traceable, transferable, reconstructable, enforceable, and operationally valid throughout the responsibility lifecycle despite organizational, operational, contractual, technological, supervisory, or governance changes. Governance may assign responsibility, but trustworthy governance requires responsibility to remain continuous. Responsibility Continuity therefore becomes a foundational condition of trustworthy governance systems. text: Responsibility Governance Standard - (RGS) OriginID: OOF-OID-AGA-RGS-2026-06-14-0006 Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: Accountability Governance Architecture (AGA™) Operational Layer: Responsibility Governance Layer Governed Space: Responsibility Governance Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Accountability Governance Architecture Type: Parent Standard Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Origin Date: 14 June 2026 Compatibility: OOF Methodology OS · Accountability Governance Architecture (AGA™) · Relationship Accountability Standard (RAS) · Authority Governance Standard (AGS) · Authority Delegation Standard (ADS) · Authority Validation Standard (AVS) · Authority Escalation Standard (AES) · INTEGROS® — Integrity Standard AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF Protection: MIP — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL) Canonical Definition System Canonical Definition Responsibility Governance Standard (RGS) defines the structural conditions under which responsibilities remain assignable, identifiable, traceable, governable, accountable, reconstructable, enforceable, and operationally valid throughout the responsibility lifecycle. RGS governs responsibility. The standard establishes the foundational conditions required to determine who was responsible, what they were responsible for, when responsibility existed, how responsibility was assigned, whether responsibility remained valid, and whether responsibility was fulfilled. Authority grants the right to act. Responsibility creates the obligation to act. RGS governs whether responsibility remains valid. A. Standard Abstract Every governance system depends on responsibility. Organizations assign responsibility. Institutions assign responsibility. Governments assign responsibility. Contractor networks assign responsibility. AI systems increasingly assign responsibility. Autonomous agents require responsibility governance. Human-AI operational environments require responsibility governance. Without responsibility governance: obligations become unclear responsibility gaps emerge accountability becomes difficult ownership disappears governance failures increase operational reliability decreases RGS exists to govern these conditions. B. Core Principle Responsibility becomes valid only when responsibility assignments remain identifiable, traceable, governable, accountable, reconstructable, enforceable, and operationally valid throughout the responsibility lifecycle. C. Scope This standard may apply to: organizations institutions governments regulatory environments contractor networks subcontractor chains temporary workforce environments supervisory systems operational environments AI systems autonomous agents orchestrated agent systems Human-AI governance environments robotics ecosystems future intelligent governance systems RGS applies wherever responsibility exists. D. Why This Standard Exists Many governance failures originate from responsibility ambiguity. Common examples include: unclear ownership responsibility conflicts responsibility gaps overlapping responsibilities abandoned responsibilities delegated responsibilities without oversight contractor-chain ambiguity Human-AI responsibility uncertainty The challenge is not assigning responsibility. The challenge is preserving responsibility integrity. RGS exists because responsibility governance has become a distinct governance space. E. Responsibility Integrity Logic Responsibility integrity exists only when the following remain materially preservable: 1. Responsibility Assignment Origin Integrity Responsibility remains attributable to a legitimate assignment source. 2. Responsibility Scope Integrity Responsibility remains connected to clearly defined obligations and boundaries. 3. Responsibility Validity Integrity Responsibility remains legitimate, recognized, and operationally valid. 4. Responsibility Traceability Integrity Responsibility remains reconstructable throughout the responsibility lifecycle. 5. Responsibility Accountability Integrity Responsibility remains connected to accountable governance structures and consequences. F. Operational Architecture Space RGS defines the operational architecture space for: responsibility governance responsibility assignment responsibility ownership responsibility boundaries responsibility traceability responsibility accountability responsibility fulfillment responsibility continuity contractor responsibility governance Human-AI responsibility governance agent responsibility governance This space exists because governance requires clarity regarding who was obligated to act. RGS governs whether responsibility remains valid. G. Difference Between Authority and Responsibility Authority defines what an actor may do. Responsibility defines what an actor must do. Authority grants rights. Responsibility creates obligations. Authority may exist without responsibility. Responsibility may exist without authority. Both must remain governable. AGS governs authority. RGS governs responsibility. H. Runtime Position RGS operates as the sixth foundational layer of AGA™. It follows: Relationship Accountability Standard (RAS) Authority Governance Standard (AGS) Authority Delegation Standard (ADS) Authority Validation Standard (AVS) Authority Escalation Standard (AES) and supports: Capability Readiness Governance Standard (CRGS) Chain of Control Standard (CCS) Governance Oversight Standard (GOS) Evidence Accountability Standard (EAS) Accountability Governance Standard (AGS-A) RGS governs who was obligated to act. I. Responsibility Failure Rule Responsibility failure occurs when responsibility assignments cannot be reliably identified, reconstructed, governed, fulfilled, enforced, or connected to accountable governance structures. Examples include: responsibility gaps unclear ownership abandoned responsibilities undocumented responsibility transfers responsibility conflicts contractor-chain ambiguity Human-AI responsibility failures unfulfilled obligations RGS exists to expose and govern these conditions. J. Validity Logic A responsibility-governance environment is valid under RGS when: responsibility assignments remain identifiable responsibility scope remains visible responsibility legitimacy remains demonstrable responsibility history remains reconstructable responsibility accountability remains preservable responsibility fulfillment remains reviewable responsibility governance remains operationally valid A responsibility-governance environment becomes invalid when: responsibility cannot be identified responsibility scope is unclear responsibility legitimacy disappears responsibility history cannot be reconstructed responsibility accountability is lost responsibility obligations become unverifiable K. Responsibility determines who must act. RGS governs that obligation. L. Foundational Principle Governance cannot function if responsibility cannot be identified. Canonical Closing Statement Responsibility Governance Standard (RGS) defines the structural conditions under which responsibilities remain assignable, identifiable, traceable, governable, accountable, reconstructable, enforceable, and operationally valid throughout the responsibility lifecycle. Authority may define what actors are allowed to do, but responsibility defines what actors are obligated to do. Governance therefore depends not only on authority, but on the ability to identify, govern, trace, and enforce responsibility throughout operational reality. title: Responsibility Mapping Analysis™
text: OOF® — Use is Open. Validity is Conditional. Responsibility Mapping Analysis™ Identifying Who Is Responsible Across Organizations, AI Systems, Supply Chains, Projects, and Multi-Layer Operational Environments What Is Responsibility Mapping Analysis™? Responsibility Mapping Analysis™ is a professional assessment and intelligence service focused on identifying, tracing, documenting, validating, and analyzing responsibility relationships across organizational, operational, contractual, governance, AI, and multi-party environments. Many organizations experience recurring conflicts because responsibility is assumed rather than mapped. As a result: responsibility becomes fragmented responsibility becomes transferred informally responsibility gaps emerge operational failures occur accountability becomes unclear Responsibility Mapping Analysis3™ exists to identify responsibility before responsibility becomes disputed. Why This Service Exists Organizations frequently ask: Who should do the work? However, the more important question is often: Who is actually responsible? In complex environments involving: contractors subcontractors staffing agencies AI systems autonomous systems external providers multiple departments responsibility often becomes difficult to identify. Responsibility Mapping Analysis™ was created to address this challenge. What We Do We help organizations identify: Responsibility Chains™ Responsibility Ownership™ Responsibility Continuity™ Responsibility Transfers™ Responsibility Dependencies™ Responsibility Gaps™ Responsibility Conflicts™ Multi-Layer Responsibility Structures™ The objective is creating responsibility clarity. Typical Starting Points Clients may approach us with: Organizational Conflicts™ "We do not know who is responsible." AI Deployment Projects™ "We need to understand responsibility surrounding AI decisions." Supply Chain Environments™ "We need to understand responsibility across multiple contractors." Outsourcing Arrangements™ "We need to understand responsibility transfer and control." Governance Challenges™ "We need responsibility visibility before implementation." Operational Failures™ "We need to reconstruct responsibility relationships." Architecture Foundations Responsibility Mapping Analysis™ utilizes relevant OOF® governance frameworks depending on the environment being analyzed. Responsibility Governance Architecture™ Primary framework used for: responsibility mapping, responsibility continuity, responsibility transfer analysis, responsibility ownership identification. Core Question: Who is responsible? Accountability Governance Architecture™ Used for: accountability alignment, consequence ownership analysis. Core Question: Who bears the consequences? OBIDENITY™ — Origin-Bound Identity™ Used for: actor identification, traceability, responsibility attribution. Core Question: Which actor holds responsibility? IGA™ — Intelligence Governance Architecture™ Used when responsibility involves: AI systems, intelligent systems, autonomous systems, governance architectures. Core Question: Which governance space contains the responsibility relationship? GIE™ — Governance Intelligence Engine™ Used for: responsibility dependency analysis, governance intelligence generation, responsibility conflict identification. Core Question: How does responsibility flow? Operational Reality™ Used for: reality verification, operational condition analysis. Core Question: What responsibility existed in reality? ART™ — Audit in Real Time™ Used for: evidence validation, responsibility reconstruction, traceability. Core Question: Can responsibility be verified through evidence? Responsibility Mapping Activities Depending on scope, services may include: Responsibility Chain Mapping™ Responsibility Ownership Analysis™ Responsibility Transfer Analysis™ Responsibility Continuity Analysis™ Multi-Layer Responsibility Analysis™ Responsibility Gap Identification™ Responsibility Conflict Analysis™ Responsibility Dependency Mapping™ Operational Responsibility Reconstruction™ Typical Outputs Clients may receive: Responsibility Map™ Responsibility Chain Report™ Responsibility Gap Analysis™ Responsibility Conflict Report™ Responsibility Continuity Assessment™ Multi-Layer Responsibility Assessment™ Responsibility Intelligence Report™ Governance Recommendations™ AI and Autonomous Systems Responsibility Mapping Analysis™ is particularly valuable within AI environments. Typical questions include: Who authorized deployment? Who configured the system? Who approved system behavior? Who supervises the system? Who may override decisions? Who bears responsibility for outcomes? What responsibility remains with humans? What responsibility remains with organizations? The service helps establish responsibility visibility before disputes occur. Who May Benefit Organizations Understanding responsibility structures. Startups Designing responsibility architectures. AI Companies Understanding responsibility around AI deployment and operation. Supply Chain Operators Understanding responsibility across contractor networks. Compliance Teams Understanding responsibility exposure. Investors Understanding governance and operational risks. Public Institutions Understanding responsibility within complex governance environments. Typical Questions We Help Answer Who is responsible? Where does responsibility begin? Where does responsibility end? Has responsibility been transferred? Has responsibility been fragmented? Do responsibility gaps exist? Can responsibility be verified? What responsibility risks exist? Why It Matters As organizations become more complex, responsibility becomes increasingly difficult to identify. AI systems, autonomous environments, outsourcing models, supply chains, and multi-party governance structures all increase responsibility complexity. Responsibility Mapping Analysis™ exists to help organizations understand responsibility before responsibility becomes disputed. Canonical Closing Statement Responsibility Mapping Analysis™ helps organizations, startups, AI companies, supply chain operators, investors, compliance teams, governance leaders, and public institutions identify, trace, verify, and understand responsibility across complex operational environments. By utilizing Responsibility Governance Architecture™, Accountability Governance Architecture™, OBIDENITY™, IGA™, GIE™, Operational Reality™, and ART™, the service transforms fragmented responsibility structures into structured responsibility intelligence capable of supporting stronger governance, clearer ownership, reduced risk, and more effective operational decision-making.

title: Responsibility Mapping Analysis™ Question Index
text: Responsibility Mapping Analysis™ Question Index OOF Problem Space Intelligence Index™ (PSII™) Mapping Responsibility, Accountability, Authority, Delegation, and Ownership Relationships Organizations frequently experience failures not because work was not performed, but because responsibility was unclear. People assume others are responsible. Authority exists without accountability. Accountability exists without authority. Responsibilities are delegated without oversight. Ownership remains undefined. Responsibility Mapping Analysis™ exists to identify, analyze, document, and understand responsibility relationships across organizations, governance systems, supply chains, projects, AI systems, autonomous agents, contractors, and operational environments. This Question Index™ provides a structured collection of questions designed to support responsibility analysis, accountability mapping, authority assessment, delegation review, and ownership clarification. The objective is not merely to assign responsibility. The objective is to understand how responsibility operates. Responsibility Identification Who is responsible? What responsibilities exist? Are responsibilities clearly defined? Are responsibilities documented? Are responsibilities understood consistently? Can responsibilities be demonstrated? Are responsibilities accepted? Are responsibilities measurable? Are responsibilities operational? Can responsibilities be audited? Accountability Analysis Who is accountable? Is accountability clearly assigned? Are ownership conflicts present? Can ownership be demonstrated? Is ownership traceable? Does ownership support accountability? Responsibility Continuity Does responsibility remain continuous? Can responsibility gaps occur? Does responsibility transfer during delegation? Is responsibility maintained during organizational changes? Is responsibility maintained across projects? Is responsibility maintained across supply chains? Can continuity failures be identified? Is responsibility traceable over time? Does continuity support governance? Is responsibility continuity protected? Multi-Layer Responsibility Are multiple organizations involved? Are subcontractors involved? Are external partners involved? Are responsibility chains visible? Are responsibility transfers documented? Can responsibility be traced across layers? Are responsibility gaps present between layers? Are accountability conditions preserved? Can multi-layer relationships be audited? Is responsibility clear throughout the chain? Responsibility Risk What responsibility risks exist? Are responsibility gaps creating risk? Are accountability failures creating risk? Are authority conflicts creating risk? Are ownership disputes creating risk? Can responsibility failures be anticipated? Are responsibility controls effective? Are risks documented? Can responsibility risks be mitigated? Is responsibility resilience sufficient? AI and Autonomous Systems Responsibility Who is responsible for AI actions? Who is accountable for AI decisions? Can responsibility be assigned to an AI system? Who authorizes AI operations? Who oversees AI behavior? Can AI responsibility be audited? Are escalation pathways defined? Are human oversight requirements clear? Are autonomous decision boundaries established? Is responsibility preserved throughout AI operations? Responsibility Intelligence Are responsibility relationships visible? Can responsibility complexity be managed? Does responsibility support governance objectives? Does responsibility support trust? Does responsibility support operational stability? Can responsibility improve decision-making? Are responsibility dependencies understood? Are responsibility conflicts resolved effectively? Does responsibility architecture support organizational goals? Is the responsibility environment fit for purpose? Related OOF® Service Responsibility Mapping Analysis™ Responsibility Mapping Analysis™ helps organizations identify, document, analyze, and improve responsibility, accountability, authority, delegation, ownership, and responsibility continuity relationships across operational, organizational, contractual, governmental, AI, and multi-layer environments. About the OOF Problem Space Intelligence Index™ The OOF Problem Space Intelligence Index™ (PSII™) is a growing collection of structured questions designed to help identify, understand, classify, and investigate problems before searching for solutions. Questions are organized into categories, clusters, and problem environments to improve clarity, analysis, governance, and decision-making. The objective is not merely to provide answers. The objective is to ensure that the right questions are being asked.

title: Responsibility Traceability Standard - (RTS)
text: Responsibility Traceability Standard - (RTS) OriginID: OOF-OID-AGA-RTS-2026-06-17-0014 Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: Accountability Governance Architecture (AGA™) Operational Layer: Responsibility Traceability Governance Layer Governed Space: Responsibility Traceability Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Responsibility Governance Type: Parent Standard Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Origin Date: 17 June 2026 Compatibility: OOF Methodology OS · Accountability Governance Architecture (AGA™) · Responsibility Governance Standard (RGS) · Responsibility Assignment Standard (RAS-A) · Responsibility Continuity Standard (RCS) · Evidence Accountability Standard (EAS) · Accountability Governance Standard (AGS-A) · INTEGROS® — Integrity Standard AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF Protection: MIP — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL) Canonical Definition System Canonical Definition Responsibility Traceability Standard (RTS) defines the structural conditions under which responsibility relationships, responsibility assignments, responsibility transfers, responsibility decisions, responsibility actions, responsibility transitions, responsibility outcomes, and responsibility-governance activities remain traceable, reconstructable, reviewable, auditable, governable, enforceable, and operationally valid throughout the responsibility lifecycle. RTS governs responsibility traceability. The standard establishes the foundational conditions required to determine how responsibility moved throughout operational reality, who carried responsibility at specific points in time, how responsibility changed, and whether the complete responsibility chain can be reconstructed. Responsibility may exist. Responsibility may be assigned. Responsibility may remain continuous. RTS governs whether responsibility can be reconstructed. A. Standard Abstract Many governance systems know that responsibility existed. Many governance systems cannot reconstruct responsibility afterward. Investigations often fail because responsibility history is lost. Governance often fails because responsibility pathways cannot be reconstructed. Without traceability governance: responsibility chains become invisible investigations become difficult accountability weakens evidence loses context governance transparency deteriorates RTS exists to govern these conditions. B. Core Principle Responsibility remains governance-valid only when responsibility history remains traceable, reconstructable, reviewable, and auditable throughout the responsibility lifecycle. C. Scope This standard may apply to: organizations institutions governments contractor networks subcontractor chains temporary workforce environments project environments compliance environments AI governance systems autonomous-agent environments Human-AI operational systems future intelligent governance systems RTS applies wherever responsibility must be reconstructed. D. Why This Standard Exists Many governance failures occur because responsibility cannot be traced. Examples include: undocumented responsibility transfers missing responsibility records fragmented responsibility chains contractor traceability failures responsibility ambiguity governance handover failures Human-AI traceability failures accountability reconstruction failures The challenge is not identifying responsibility. The challenge is reconstructing responsibility. RTS exists because responsibility traceability is a distinct governance space. E. Responsibility Traceability Integrity Logic Responsibility traceability integrity exists only when the following remain materially preservable: 1. Traceability Origin Integrity Responsibility history remains connected to legitimate responsibility sources. 2. Traceability Scope Integrity Traceable responsibility relationships remain connected to clearly defined governance boundaries. 3. Traceability Validity Integrity Responsibility traceability remains legitimate and operationally valid. 4. Traceability Reconstruction Integrity Responsibility history remains reconstructable throughout the responsibility lifecycle. 5. Traceability Accountability Integrity Responsibility traceability remains connected to accountable governance structures. F. Operational Architecture Space RTS defines the operational architecture space for: responsibility traceability responsibility reconstruction responsibility-chain governance responsibility-history governance responsibility auditability contractor responsibility traceability Human-AI responsibility traceability AI responsibility traceability governance transparency responsibility lifecycle reconstruction This space exists because governance requires responsibility history to remain visible. RTS governs whether responsibility can be reconstructed. G. Difference Between Continuity and Traceability Responsibility Continuity asks: Did responsibility remain preserved? Responsibility Traceability asks: Can responsibility be reconstructed? Responsibility may remain continuous. Yet continuity may not be reconstructable. RCS governs preservation. RTS governs reconstruction. Both are required. H. Runtime Position RTS operates within the Responsibility Layer of AGA™. It follows: Responsibility Governance Standard (RGS) Responsibility Assignment Standard (RAS-A) Responsibility Continuity Standard (RCS) and supports: Evidence Accountability Standard (EAS) Accountability Governance Standard (AGS-A) Decision Accountability Standard (DAS) RTS governs whether responsibility history remains visible. I. Responsibility Traceability Failure Rule Responsibility traceability failure occurs when responsibility history cannot be reliably reconstructed, reviewed, audited, governed, validated, or connected to accountable governance structures. Examples include: missing records undocumented transitions invisible responsibility chains contractor traceability failures governance transparency failures Human-AI traceability breakdowns responsibility reconstruction failures RTS exists to expose and govern these conditions. J. Validity Logic A responsibility-traceability environment is valid under RTS when: responsibility history remains visible responsibility transitions remain reconstructable responsibility-chain relationships remain reviewable responsibility records remain auditable traceability accountability remains preservable responsibility governance remains transparent A responsibility-traceability environment becomes invalid when: responsibility history disappears transitions cannot be reconstructed responsibility-chain visibility is lost governance transparency collapses accountability reconstruction becomes impossible K. Relationship to Other OOF Standards RTS derives from: Responsibility Governance Standard (RGS) Responsibility Assignment Standard (RAS-A) Responsibility Continuity Standard (RCS) and supports: Evidence Accountability Standard (EAS) Accountability Governance Standard (AGS-A) Decision Accountability Standard (DAS) RGS governs responsibility. RAS-A governs assignment. RCS governs preservation. RTS governs reconstruction. L. Foundational Principle Responsibility cannot be governed if responsibility history cannot be reconstructed. Canonical Closing Statement Responsibility Traceability Standard (RTS) defines the structural conditions under which responsibility relationships, responsibility assignments, responsibility transfers, responsibility decisions, responsibility actions, responsibility transitions, responsibility outcomes, and responsibility-governance activities remain traceable, reconstructable, reviewable, auditable, governable, enforceable, and operationally valid throughout the responsibility lifecycle. Governance may preserve responsibility, but trustworthy governance also requires responsibility to remain reconstructable. Responsibility Traceability therefore becomes a foundational condition of trustworthy governance systems. title: Reusable Methodologies
text: Reusable Methodologies OOF® — Methodology Authority™ Core Statement One of the greatest inefficiencies in modern society is the repeated creation of solutions for problems that have already been solved. Organizations repeatedly rebuild: processes, frameworks, governance models, operational systems, implementation structures. Reusable Methodologies™ exist to transform methodologies from one-time solutions into reusable operational assets. The objective is not repetition. The objective is structured reuse. Why Reusability Matters Most organizations focus on building solutions. Few focus on building reusable methodologies. As a result: knowledge remains isolated, resources are wasted, implementation costs increase, innovation slows, organizations repeatedly solve identical problems. A reusable methodology allows one solution to create value many times. What Is a Reusable Methodology? A reusable methodology is a methodology that can be applied across multiple environments without requiring complete redesign. It preserves its core logic while adapting to different operational contexts. Reusable methodologies are not tied to: a single company, a single technology, a single industry, a single country. They operate at the methodological level rather than the implementation level. Methodology vs Implementation This distinction is critical. An implementation is specific. A methodology is transferable. For example: A hospital information system is an implementation. The methodology governing patient information flow may be reusable across healthcare systems worldwide. Similarly: A software application is an implementation. The methodology behind its governance model may be reusable across industries. OOF® focuses on methodologies rather than implementations. Reusability as Infrastructure Reusable methodologies function as operational infrastructure. Just as physical infrastructure can support many users, reusable methodologies can support many implementations. One methodology may later support: governments, enterprises, AI systems, robotics platforms, educational institutions, healthcare environments, future technologies. The methodology becomes more valuable with each successful reuse. The Reuse Before Reinvention Principle OOF® promotes a simple principle: Reuse before reinvention. Before creating a new methodology, organizations should ask: Does a methodology already exist? Can it be adapted? Can it be extended? Can it be combined with another methodology? Innovation should occur where necessary. Reinvention should occur only where unavoidable. Modular Methodologies Reusable methodologies are often modular. A methodology may contain: core components, optional modules, extension layers, domain-specific adaptations. This allows organizations to reuse proven components without adopting an entire framework. Modularity increases flexibility while preserving consistency. Reusable Methodologies and AI Artificial intelligence creates a new demand for reusable methodologies. AI systems increasingly require: governance methodologies, memory methodologies, decision methodologies, validation methodologies, safety methodologies. Without reusable methodologies, every AI project begins from zero. Reusable methodological assets dramatically accelerate development while reducing risk. Reusable Methodologies and Origin Open Registry™ Origin Open Registry™ serves as the discovery layer for reusable methodologies. Organizations can identify: existing methodologies, compatible methodologies, related methodologies, reusable modules. The registry transforms methodological reuse from accident into strategy. Reusable Methodologies and Governance Architecture™ Governance Architecture™ depends heavily on methodological reuse. When organizations encounter similar problems, reusable methodologies provide: faster deployment, lower risk, improved consistency, reduced implementation cost. Architecture becomes scalable because methodologies become reusable. Reusability and Long-Term Value Many assets lose value over time. Reusable methodologies often gain value over time. Every successful implementation: improves understanding, strengthens evidence, reveals optimization opportunities, increases confidence. A mature reusable methodology becomes a form of accumulated operational intelligence. The OOF® Perspective OOF® views reusable methodologies as one of the highest forms of methodological capital. A methodology that can be applied repeatedly across different environments possesses significantly greater value than a methodology limited to a single implementation. The future belongs not only to those who create methodologies. It belongs to those who create methodologies that others can successfully reuse. Why This Matters Modern organizations cannot afford to continuously rebuild knowledge from the beginning. As complexity increases, the ability to reuse validated methodologies becomes a strategic advantage. Reusable methodologies reduce waste, accelerate innovation, and improve operational consistency across systems. Final Statement Solutions solve problems once. Reusable methodologies solve problems repeatedly. The true value of a methodology is not measured by a single implementation, but by its ability to create value across many implementations, environments, and generations. title: RICM — Runtime Interaction Consent Module
text: RICM — Runtime Interaction Consent Module Parent Standard: Continuous Interaction Layer Category: AI & Interpretation Subcategory: Runtime Interaction Consent Type: Continuous Interaction Module Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 12 May 2026 Compatibility: OOF Methodology OS · Continuous Interaction Layer · CLIA · RIS · OGL · EVIP · AIL · Autonomous Runtime Systems · Realtime AI Architectures Authority: OOF Protection: MIP — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Runtime Interaction Consent Module defines the structural conditions under which continuous listening, monitoring, interpretation, presence, proactive participation, and live interaction behavior remain valid only while consent conditions remain explicit, active, bounded, reviewable, and runtime-compatible. A system satisfies RICM only if: interaction consent states are explicitly defined continuous participation does not remain active under vague or assumed permission passive listening, monitoring, and interpretation require governable consent logic consent remains reviewable during runtime, not only at onboarding or first activation changes in presence, scope, or behavior can affect consent validity in real time A system that remains continuously active through inherited, hidden, or structurally unbounded consent does not satisfy RICM. Module Function RICM defines the consent layer of continuous interaction governance. It ensures that continuous participation by an intelligent system does not operate under symbolic, outdated, or overly broad permission, but remains tied to explicit runtime-valid consent conditions. The module applies wherever a system may: listen continuously monitor continuously interpret continuously remain ambiently present enter interaction proactively observe environments in real time preserve passive awareness states escalate from passive presence to active participation Its function is not merely to collect initial permission. Its function is to govern whether continuous interaction remains valid while it is happening. Step 1 — Define the Consent Object The organization must define what exactly requires runtime-valid consent. Minimum requirement: the consent object is explicit the scope of consent-governed interaction is structurally bounded undefined consent targets are excluded from valid governance logic The consent object may include: passive listening continuous monitoring active interpretation multimodal observation proactive intervention attention persistence contextual memory continuation environmental sensing linked to interaction behavior Step 2 — Define Consent States The system must define which consent states may exist during continuous interaction. Minimum requirement: consent states are explicit the system can distinguish active consent from absent, expired, restricted, suspended, or invalid consent continuous participation does not rely on one unbounded consent condition Consent states may include: active restricted suspended expired withdrawn environment-limited scope-limited structurally invalid Step 3 — Define Consent Scope Boundaries The system must define what consent covers and what remains outside consent. Minimum requirement: consent scope is explicit permission to one form of presence is not silently extended to another form listening, monitoring, interpretation, intervention, and escalation are not treated as automatically equivalent This prevents a system from converting narrow consent into broad behavioral permission. Step 4 — Define Runtime Consent Validity Conditions The system must define which runtime conditions must remain satisfied for consent to remain valid. Minimum requirement: runtime consent conditions are explicit changes in context, presence intensity, modality, or behavior can affect consent validity consent does not silently remain active when governing conditions have changed Such conditions may include: environment interaction mode presence state time escalation level monitoring intensity active participation state operational context change Step 5 — Define Consent Transition Logic The system must define how consent changes during continuous interaction. Minimum requirement: consent transition logic is explicit consent can move between valid states in governed ways the system can recognize when consent must be refreshed, restricted, paused, or treated as invalid This means the system must know not only whether consent was once given, but whether it still remains justified now. Step 6 — Preserve Consent Traceability The system must preserve traceability of consent states, consent changes, and consent-relevant runtime events. Minimum requirement: consent-state changes are reviewable active consent conditions remain reconstructable later audit can determine what consent existed, what changed, and under which interaction conditions the system remained active If runtime consent cannot be reconstructed, then continuous participation becomes structurally unverifiable. Step 7 — Restrict Invalid Consent Design The system must not be treated as valid if continuous interaction remains active through broad assumption, hidden inheritance, or structurally undefined consent logic. Minimum requirement: invalid consent conditions are identifiable symbolic consent is excluded continuous participation without runtime-valid consent logic is blocked, bounded, or invalidated where required Scenario A realtime assistant remains continuously available through passive listening and may shift into active interpretation or proactive interaction during live use. Application RICM is used to ensure: passive listening and active interpretation are not treated as the same consent state changes in interaction mode can trigger different consent validity requirements consent remains reviewable during ongoing use continuous presence does not silently outgrow the consent that originally enabled it Result The system gains a stronger interaction architecture in which continuous presence remains governed by explicit runtimevalid consent rather than inherited permission. Scenario A multimodal system remains present through audio, visual, and contextual streams and continuously interprets a live environment while interacting with humans and systems. Application RICM is used to ensure: monitoring and interpretation states remain consent-bounded runtime changes in modality or behavior affect consent validity where required broad environment presence does not silently authorize deeper intervention later review can reconstruct what continuous interaction remained validly consented to Result The environment gains a stronger realtime governance structure in which consent remains active, bounded, and traceable throughout continuous participation. Canonical Closing Statement If continuous interaction remains active without runtime-valid consent, presence becomes structurally enabled behavior rather than governed participation. title: Rights & Authorization Module (RAM™)
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS Rights & Authorization Module (RAM™) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Category: AI and Interpretation Subcategory: Representation and Copy Module: Rights & Authorization Module (RAM™) Type: Governance Module Standard: Representation & Copy Standard (RCS™) Status: Canonical Module Version: 1.0 Effective Date: 19 March 2026 Canonical Definition The Rights & Authorization Module (RAM™) defines who is permitted to create, reproduce, represent, exhibit, or monetize an asset. Authorization determines whether an action is valid, independent of the asset form. Why This Matters Without clear authorization: copies may be created without permission representations may be misused ownership may be violated monetization becomes illegitimate Authorization separates existence from permission. Minimum Implementation Framework (MIF) Step 1 — Identify the Asset Define the asset to which rights are applied. Step 2 — Identify the Authority Determine the individual or entity that holds control over the asset. Step 3 — Define Permissions Specify what is allowed: create copy represent exhibit monetize Step 4 — Assign Authorization Status Declare whether the action is: authorized partially authorized not authorized Step 5 — Maintain Traceability Authorization must remain linked to the asset and its origin. Use Case 1 — Licensed Exhibition Scenario A gallery receives permission to exhibit copies of an artwork. Application Authorization is defined under RAM™. Result clear exhibition rights controlled usage legal and structural clarity Use Case 2 — Unauthorized Reproduction Scenario A copy of an artwork is created and distributed without permission. Application The asset is classified as not authorized. Result clear identification of misuse separation from legitimate copies protection of original ownership Structural Principle Ownership defines control. Authorization defines permission. Closing Statement An asset may exist without permission. It cannot be used without it.

title: RIIM — Relationship Identification Integrity Module
text: RIIM — Relationship Identification Integrity Module OriginID: OOF-OID-AGA-RIIM-2026-06-14-0001 Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: Accountability Governance Architecture (AGA™) Operational Layer: Relationship Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Accountability Governance Architecture Type: Relationship Accountability Standard Module Parent Standard: Relationship Accountability Standard (RAS) Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Origin Date: 14 June 2026 Compatibility: Accountability Governance Architecture (AGA™) · Relationship Accountability Standard (RAS) · Authority Governance Standard (AGS) · Responsibility Governance Standard (RGS) AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF Protection: MIP — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL) Canonical Definition Relationship Identification Integrity Module (RIIM) defines the structural conditions under which operational relationships between actors remain identifiable, distinguishable, traceable, reconstructable, and operationally valid throughout governance analysis. RIIM governs relationship identification. The module establishes the conditions required to determine who is connected to whom before authority, responsibility, control, oversight, evidence, accountability, and consequence can be evaluated. Module Operational Role RIIM serves as the identification layer of the Relationship Accountability Standard. Its role is to establish visibility of relationships before governance analysis proceeds to subsequent accountability layers. RIIM answers the first operational question: Which actors are actually connected within the operational environment? Module Operational Space RIIM governs: relationship identification actor identification relationship visibility relationship discovery relationship reconstruction relationship traceability governance relationship mapping The module applies wherever governance requires identification of participating actors and their relationships. Module Function The module ensures that governance can identify: direct relationships indirect relationships contractual relationships supervisory relationships delegated relationships organizational relationships Human-AI relationships AI-agent relationships multi-party relationships before accountability analysis begins. Its function is to prevent invisible actors from remaining hidden within governance structures. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Define the Relationship Environment Identify the operational environment being analyzed. Examples: organizations contractor networks manufacturing chains supply chains AI systems multi-agent systems Human-AI environments robotics ecosystems 2. Identify Participating Actors Identify all actors participating in the environment. Examples: individuals organizations departments contractors subcontractors staffing agencies AI agents autonomous systems robots 3. Identify Existing Relationships Determine which actors maintain operational relationships. Examples: direct reporting relationships contractual relationships supervisory relationships delegated relationships collaborative relationships execution relationships 4. Validate Relationship Existence Determine whether identified relationships actually exist in operational reality. Governance must distinguish: formal relationships operational relationships assumed relationships undocumented relationships 5. Preserve Relationship Traceability Maintain sufficient evidence to reconstruct identified relationships throughout governance analysis. Use Case 1 — Multi-Layer Contractor Network Scenario A manufacturing company operates through multiple contractors and subcontractors. Application RIIM identifies every participating actor and maps operational relationships between organizations. Result Governance gains visibility into the complete relationship structure before responsibility and accountability analysis begins. Use Case 2 — Orchestrated Agent Environment Scenario A Human-AI environment contains human supervisors, AI agents, orchestration systems, external tools, and robotic execution systems. Application RIIM identifies participating actors and maps operational relationships between all entities. Result Governance gains visibility into the complete operational relationship structure before authority and accountability analysis proceeds. Canonical Closing Statement Relationship Identification Integrity Module (RIIM) defines the structural conditions under which operational relationships between actors remain identifiable, distinguishable, traceable, reconstructable, and operationally valid throughout governance analysis. Governance cannot analyze what it cannot see. Relationship identification therefore becomes the first operational step of accountability governance. title: RIM — Redemption Integrity Module
text: RIM — Redemption Integrity Module Parent Standard: Transparency & Probabilistic Integrity Standard Methodology Sign: Fair Win Model™ (FWM™) Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Redemption Integrity Type: Probabilistic Integrity Module Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 9 May 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · Transparency & Probabilistic Integrity Standard · TVL® · INTEGROS® · ArtData® · UCL™ Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English ( UCL™ ) Canonical Definition Redemption Integrity Module defines the structural conditions under which prize claims, reward claims, validation events, expired claims, invalid claims, fraudulent claims, and completed redemptions remain traceable, distinguishable, and auditor-verifiable throughout the operational lifecycle of a probabilistic system. A system satisfies RIM only if: redemption events remain traceable valid, invalid, expired, fraudulent, and completed claim states are distinguishable reward-state changes caused by redemption remain reviewable redemption records do not silently distort remaining-state reality claim handling remains structurally aligned with lifecycle auditability conditions A system that cannot distinguish and verify redemption states does not satisfy RIM. Module Function RIM defines the redemption-state integrity layer of probabilistic transparency. It ensures that prize or reward availability is not reduced through opaque, ambiguous, or unreviewable claim handling. The module applies wherever probabilistic systems must process reward claims and maintain a trustworthy distinction between what was redeemed, what was merely claimed, what was invalid, and what remains available. Minimum Implementation Framework (MIF) Step 1 — Define Redemption States The organization must define the operational states through which a reward claim may pass. Minimum requirement: claim states are explicit valid, invalid, expired, fraudulent, and completed conditions are distinguishable undefined redemption states are excluded from valid operation Step 2 — Define Claim Validation Conditions The system must define how reward claims are validated. Minimum requirement: validation conditions are explicit accepted and rejected claims are distinguishable unverifiable or ambiguous validation is excluded from valid redemption logic Step 3 — Define Redemption Event Recording The system must define how redemption events are recorded and reviewable. Minimum requirement: redemption events are traceable reward tier and claim state are linked to recorded events silent or missing redemption records are excluded from valid integrity conditions Step 4 — Define Fraud and Expiry Distinction The system must define how fraudulent, invalid, expired, or otherwise non-completed claims are distinguished from valid redemption. Minimum requirement: fraud and expiry states are explicitly separated invalid claims do not silently reduce valid remaining-state reality claim-state distortion is excluded from valid operation Step 5 — Preserve Redemption-State Consistency The system must preserve consistency between redemption records and the current remaining reward state. Minimum requirement: completed redemption affects remaining-state reality in a reviewable way invalid or fraudulent claims do not create false depletion redemption integrity remains auditor-verifiable Step 6 — Restrict Invalid Redemption Handling The system must not be treated as valid if redemption events are opaque, ambiguous, untraceable, or structurally inconsistent with remaining-state reality. Minimum requirement: invalid redemption conditions are identifiable ambiguous or distorted claim handling is blocked or invalidated claim processing alone does not justify missing redemption integrity Use Case 1 — Lottery Prize Claim Verification Scenario A lottery operator receives prize claims during operation and must preserve a trustworthy distinction between valid redemptions, invalid submissions, expired entitlements, and fraudulent claims. Application RIM is used to ensure: redemption states are explicitly defined valid and invalid claims are structurally separated redemption events remain traceable remaining-state depletion reflects only valid completed redemption Result The operator gains a stronger basis for proving that remaining prize reality reflects actual valid redemption rather than ambiguous or distorted claim handling. Use Case 2 — Digital Reward Claim Lifecycle Scenario A digital reward system processes claim attempts, verification states, expirations, and fraud checks while needing to keep current remaining availability materially accurate. Application RIM is used to ensure: claim-state logic is explicit fraudulent or expired claims remain distinguishable completed redemption is properly recorded remaining-state reality remains aligned with verified claim outcomes Result The platform gains a structurally governed redemption layer instead of relying on opaque claim processing that may distort real remaining availability. Canonical Closing Statement If redemption states cannot be distinguished and verified, remaining-state reality cannot remain materially fair. Related Documents → Transparency & Probabilistic Integrity Standard

title: RIM — Rollback & Integrity Module
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS RIM — Rollback & Integrity Module OriginID: OOF-OID-GOV-SESCS-RIM-2026-04-09-0001 Category: Governance & Enforcement Module: Rollback & Integrity Module (RIM) Type: Recovery & Integrity Control Module Standard: Self-Evolving Systems Control Standard (SESCS) Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical Module Effective Date: 9 April 2026 Authority: OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Protection: MIP™ — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Compatibility: SESCS · MCM · MLM · MVM · RAM · TSA · MTVF · EVIP · ArtData · AI Governance Systems · ORGS Canonical Definition System Rollback & Integrity Module (RIM) defines the mandatory capability of a system to restore previous valid states and maintain structural integrity after mutations or system failures. Base Without rollback and integrity control: system errors become permanent damage cannot be reversed system degradation accumulates recovery is impossible A system that cannot recover cannot be trusted. Protocol Any system MUST: maintain recoverable system states enable rollback to previous valid state verify integrity after rollback prevent propagation of corrupted states Absence of rollback results in: Irreversible System State (ISS) Scope RIM applies to: AI systems with evolving logic autonomous decision systems adaptive infrastructures multi-agent systems runtime mutation environments Methodology capture system state store valid checkpoints detect failure or anomaly initiate rollback restore previous state verify system integrity Rollback Conditions Rollback MUST be triggered when: mutation validation fails post-deployment system behavior becomes unstable contamination is detected (via TSA) system integrity is compromised Integrity Verification After rollback, system MUST: confirm structural consistency verify functional stability validate alignment with system rules Structural Rule (Critical) No system mutation is complete without rollback capability. Checkpoint Requirement System MUST maintain: defined recovery points state history integrity checkpoints MIF — Minimal Implementation Framework Step 1 — State Capture Capture system state. Minimum: defined checkpoint Step 2 — Storage Store recoverable state. Minimum: persistent state record Step 3 — Rollback Mechanism Enable restoration. Minimum: revert capability Step 4 — Integrity Check Verify restored system. Minimum: basic consistency check MIF+ — Extended Implementation Framework Includes all MIF requirements plus: automated rollback triggers multi-state recovery layers distributed checkpoint storage real-time integrity monitoring integration with TSA contamination detection predictive failure rollback continuous system integrity validation Decision Logic System state is: RECOVERABLE → rollback possible IRREVERSIBLE → rollback not possible Use Case 1 — AI System Failure Recovery Scenario AI system mutation introduces instability. Problem system behaves unpredictably no recovery mechanism Application RIM enables: rollback to stable state integrity verification Result system restored failure contained risk minimized Use Case 2 — Contaminated System State Scenario System becomes contaminated (TSA classification). Problem corrupted behavior spreads system cannot self-correct Application RIM ensures: rollback to clean state prevention of contamination propagation Result system integrity restored contamination removed safe operation resumed Compatibility RIM operates with: MCM — defines mutation boundaries MLM — provides mutation history MVM — validates mutations RAM — assigns responsibility TSA — detects contamination MTVF — validation framework Structural Principle A system must be able to return to a valid state. Closing Statement Change without recovery creates irreversible risk. Irreversible risk destroys system integrity. Rollback & Integrity Module (RIM) establishes a non-negotiable condition: Every system must be able to recover, restore, and verify its integrity.
