However, the standards listed below form the official core identity governance structure of OBIDENITY®. Canonical Definition Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture (OBIDENITY®) is the identity governance architecture that defines the structural conditions under which the origin, identity, ownership, authority, permissions, responsibility, provenance, transfer, continuity, and auditability of an identifiable entity remain legitimate, attributable, traceable, verifiable, and continuously governable throughout the complete identity lifecycle. Core Question How can identity remain uniquely identifiable, attributable, governable, transferable, continuous, and independently verifiable throughout its complete lifecycle? Governance Flow Origin → Identity → Ownership → Authority → Permission → Responsibility → Provenance → Transfer → Continuity → Auditability Core Parent Standards 1. Origin Integrity Standard (OIS) Governed Space: Origin Integrity Core Question: Where did the governed identity originate? 2. Identity Integrity Standard (IIS) Governed Space: Identity Integrity Core Question: What exactly is the governed identity? 3. Ownership Integrity Standard (OWIS) Governed Space: Ownership Integrity Core Question: Who legitimately owns the governed identity? 4. Authority Integrity Standard (AIS) Governed Space: Identity Authority Core Question: Who has legitimate authority over the governed identity? 5. Permission Integrity Standard (PIS) Governed Space: Permission Integrity Core Question: Who may legitimately access, use, modify, or interact with the governed identity? 6. Responsibility Integrity Standard (RIS) Governed Space: Identity Responsibility Core Question: Who remains responsible for the governed identity and its governed actions? 7. Provenance Integrity Standard (PRIS) Governed Space: Identity Provenance Core Question: Can the complete history of the governed identity be proven? 8. Transfer Integrity Standard (TIS) Governed Space: Identity Transfer Core Question: How can the governed identity be transferred while preserving governance integrity? 9. Continuity Integrity Standard (CIS) Governed Space: Identity Continuity Core Question: How can the governed identity remain continuous throughout its complete lifecycle? 10. Auditability Integrity Standard (AUDIS) Governed Space: Identity Auditability Core Question: Can every governance aspect of the governed identity be independently verified? Compatible OOF® Architectures OBIDENITY® interoperates with multiple OOF® architectures governing complementary governance, accountability, cognition, memory, behavior, operational reality, and autonomous-system spaces. GOA™ — Governance Architecture provides the constitutional governance layer defining how governance authority, boundaries, scope, delegation, accountability, validation, integrity, transparency, continuity, and interoperability are structured. ORA™ — Operational Reality Architecture governs operational reality, operational validity, responsibility, authority, evidence, coordination, and recovery across complex operational environments. AGA™ — Accountability Governance Architecture governs accountability relationships, authority validation, responsibility assignment, decision accountability, evidence accountability, continuity, and accountability chains. AIG® — AI Governance Architecture governs the behavioral conditions under which AI behavior remains bounded, auditable, evidence-supported, trusted, correctable, interoperable, and safe. CLIA® — Cognitive Governance Intelligence Architecture governs cognition, interpretation, reasoning, cognitive reality modeling, Human-AI cognition, collective cognition, and cognitive evolution. MGIA™ — Memory Governance Intelligence Architecture governs memory integrity, agent memory, user memory, collective memory, temporal continuity, multimodal memory, and memory evolution. ASGA™ — Autonomous Systems Governance Architecture governs autonomous operational identity, authority, execution, constraints, risk, coordination, escalation, accountability, compatibility, and evolution. OBIDENITY® serves as the foundational identity governance architecture that establishes who or what exists, where it originated, to whom it belongs, under whose authority it operates, what permissions apply, who remains responsible, how its history is preserved, how it may transfer, how continuity survives change, and how the complete identity lifecycle can be independently verified. Architectural Position OBIDENITY® governs the complete origin-bound identity governance lifecycle. The architecture progresses through: Origin Integrity → Identity Integrity → Ownership Integrity → Identity Authority → Permission Integrity → Identity Responsibility → Identity Provenance → Identity Transfer → Identity Continuity → Identity Auditability Together these standards govern how identity originates, becomes identifiable, connects to ownership, receives authority, operates through permissions, remains connected to responsibility, develops provenance, transfers across legitimate environments, preserves continuity through change, and remains independently auditable throughout its complete lifecycle. OBIDENITY® is not limited to one identity type. It may govern: human identity, organizational identity, AI identity, autonomous-agent identity, robotic identity, asset identity, document identity, product identity, digital-twin identity, cross-platform identity, inherited identity, and future forms of governable identity. The architecture is implementation-neutral. A governed identity may be represented through centralized infrastructure, distributed systems, enterprise platforms, public registries, digital credentials, physical identifiers, cryptographic systems, or future technologies. The implementation may change. The governance identity must remain continuously connected to its origin, relationships, history, and evidence. Strategic Position Identity systems traditionally focus on identification, authentication, access, or credential management. OBIDENITY® defines a broader governance space. It governs not only whether an entity can be recognized, but also: where the identity originated, whether the identity is unique, who owns it, who controls it, who may use or modify it, who remains responsible, whether its history can be proven, whether it can be transferred, whether it survives succession, inheritance, cloning, merging, replacement, and technological change, and whether every identity governance relationship can be independently audited. This creates a persistent governance layer that may remain valid across platforms, organizations, jurisdictions, technologies, operational environments, and generations. OBIDENITY® therefore transforms identity from a platform-dependent identifier into a continuously governable lifecycle entity. Canonical Principle OBIDENITY® does not govern identity technology itself. OBIDENITY® governs the structural conditions under which identity remains origin-bound, uniquely identifiable, attributable, ownable, authorized, permissioned, responsible, historically provable, transferable, continuous, and independently verifiable throughout its complete lifecycle.

title: About Integrity Assurance Standard - (IAS)
text: OOF™ About Integrity Assurance Standard - (IAS) About Integrity Assurance Standard - (IAS) What Is Integrity Assurance Standard? Integrity Assurance Standard (IAS) is the tenth Parent Standard of INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture. It governs how integrity is continuously verified, maintained, demonstrated, and assured after successful integrity restoration. IAS recognizes that integrity is not permanently guaranteed simply because it has once been restored. Instead, integrity must remain continuously observable, measurable, governable, and supported by objective evidence throughout the complete operational lifecycle of every governed entity. Canonical Definition Integrity Assurance Standard (IAS) defines the governance conditions required to continuously verify, monitor, maintain, demonstrate, and assure integrity following successful integrity restoration. It establishes the assurance principles, monitoring requirements, validation mechanisms, evidence models, governance controls, and continuous oversight necessary to ensure that approved integrity conditions remain preserved throughout the complete lifecycle of a governed entity. Why IAS Exists Successful restoration marks the return of integrity, but not the end of integrity governance. Operational environments constantly evolve. Systems change, new risks emerge, configurations are modified, users interact differently, and external conditions shift over time. Without continuous assurance, integrity may gradually degrade without timely detection. IAS exists to ensure that restored integrity remains continuously verified, objectively demonstrated, and permanently governed. What IAS Governs IAS governs: Continuous integrity assurance Ongoing integrity monitoring Assurance validation Assurance evidence Assurance reporting Governance oversight Long-term integrity preservation Use Case 1 — Autonomous AI GovernanceScenario An autonomous AI platform has successfully completed integrity restoration after a verified integrity breach and resumes normal operation. Application IAS continuously monitors integrity conditions, validates operational behavior, verifies assurance evidence, and detects emerging integrity risks before they become governance failures. Result Integrity remains continuously demonstrable through objective monitoring, governance oversight, and auditable assurance evidence. Use Case 2 — Critical InfrastructureScenario A national energy grid restores operational integrity after a cybersecurity incident and returns to continuous service. Application IAS governs ongoing integrity monitoring, assurance validation, evidence collection, and governance reporting to ensure restored integrity remains continuously preserved despite operational changes. Result The infrastructure maintains long-term operational trust through continuous integrity assurance supported by transparent governance and objective evidence. Architectural Position IAS represents the final governed space within INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture, completing the full integrity governance lifecycle. Governance Flow Definition → Structure → Conditions → Measurement → State → Deviation → Breach → Response → Restoration → Assurance Canonical Closing Statement Integrity Assurance Standard establishes the canonical governance framework for continuously verifying, maintaining, and demonstrating integrity throughout the complete lifecycle of every governed entity. By defining how restored integrity is continuously assured through monitoring, validation, evidence, and governance oversight, IAS enables sustained trust, operational resilience, accountable governance, and continuous integrity preservation across all operational domains.

title: About Integrity Breach Standard - (IBS)
text: OOF™ About Integrity Breach Standard - (IBS) About Integrity Breach Standard - (IBS) Determining When Integrity Has Been Materially Compromised Not every integrity deviation constitutes an integrity breach. Governance requires a clear and objective determination of the point at which integrity is no longer considered preserved. This distinction enables consistent governance decisions, timely intervention, regulatory compliance, and organizational accountability. What Is Integrity Breach Standard? Integrity Breach Standard (IBS) is the seventh Parent Standard of INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture. It establishes the canonical governance conditions required to identify, verify, classify, assess, and govern integrity breaches throughout the complete lifecycle of a governed entity. Canonical Definition Integrity Breach Standard (IBS) defines the governance conditions required to identify, verify, classify, assess, and govern integrity breaches by establishing breach determination criteria, evidence requirements, severity models, and governance rules throughout the complete lifecycle of a governed entity. Why IBS Exists Detecting integrity deviations is only the beginning of governance. Organizations must also determine when a deviation has crossed the governance threshold and become a material integrity breach requiring formal governance action. Building upon the integrity deviation framework established by IDS, IBS defines the governance criteria used to determine when integrity has been materially compromised. This provides a standardized foundation for initiating incident management, accountability processes, regulatory reporting, and recovery activities. What IBS Governs IBS governs the complete lifecycle of integrity breaches, including: breach identification breach verification breach classification breach severity assessment breach evidence breach documentation breach governance. This governed space ensures that integrity breaches are recognized, evaluated, and governed consistently using objective evidence and standardized governance rules. Architectural Position Within INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture, IBS is the seventh Parent Standard in the governance flow: Definition → Structure → Conditions → Measurement → State → Deviation → Breach → Response → Restoration → Assurance IBS establishes the canonical transition from integrity deterioration to formal integrity failure, creating the governance foundation upon which response, restoration, and long-term assurance are built. Canonical Closing Statement Integrity Breach Standard establishes the canonical governance framework for identifying, verifying, classifying, assessing, and governing material integrity failures. By defining the point at which integrity is no longer considered preserved, IBS enables objective breach determination, accountable governance, structured response, and resilient recovery throughout the complete lifecycle of every governed entity.

title: About Integrity Condition Standard - (ICS)
text: OOF™ About Integrity Condition Standard - (ICS) About Integrity Condition Standard - (ICS) Preserving Integrity Through Conditions Integrity cannot be preserved by definition and structure alone. Every governed entity depends on a set of conditions that must remain continuously valid for integrity to exist. When these conditions are no longer satisfied, integrity begins to degrade regardless of how well the entity was originally designed. What Is Integrity Condition Standard? Integrity Condition Standard (ICS) is the third Parent Standard of INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture. It establishes the canonical governance conditions required to preserve integrity by defining the rules, constraints, dependencies, and operational requirements that must remain continuously satisfied throughout the complete lifecycle of a governed entity. Canonical Definition Integrity Condition Standard (ICS) defines the mandatory governance conditions that must remain continuously satisfied for a governed entity to preserve integrity by governing its rules, constraints, dependencies, and operational requirements throughout its complete lifecycle. Why ICS Exists A governed entity may have a well-defined integrity model and a structurally sound architecture, yet still lose integrity if the conditions required to preserve it are no longer maintained. Building upon the structural foundation established by STIS, ICS defines the mandatory conditions required for integrity to remain valid throughout the governed lifecycle. ICS exists to establish those mandatory governance conditions before integrity is measured, monitored, classified, or evaluated. What ICS Governs ICS governs the conditions required to preserve integrity, including: integrity conditions governance rules operational constraints dependency conditions boundary conditions integrity prerequisites operational validity. This governed space ensures that integrity is maintained through explicitly governed conditions rather than assumptions. Architectural Position Within INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture, ICS is the third Parent Standard in the governance flow: Definition → Structure → Conditions → Measurement → State → Deviation → Breach → Response → Restoration → Assurance ICS transforms a structurally sound integrity model into one that remains continuously valid by governing the conditions required for its preservation before integrity measurement begins. Canonical Closing Statement Integrity Condition Standard establishes the mandatory governance conditions that preserve integrity throughout the complete lifecycle of a governed entity. By governing the rules, constraints, dependencies, and operational requirements upon which integrity depends, ICS provides the essential foundation for every subsequent integrity measurement, evaluation, response, restoration, and assurance activity within INTEGROS® Integrity Governance Architecture.

title: About Integrity Definition Standard - (INDS)
text: OOF™ About Integrity Definition Standard - (INDS) About Integrity Definition Standard - (INDS) Defining Integrity Integrity cannot be governed until its meaning has been clearly established. Every governed entity requires a shared understanding of what integrity represents before it can be measured, evaluated, preserved, restored, or independently verified. What Is Integrity Definition Standard? Integrity Definition Standard (INDS) is the foundational Parent Standard of INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture. It establishes the canonical governance conditions required to formally define integrity for any governed entity, creating the reference point for all subsequent integrity governance activities. Canonical Definition Integrity Definition Standard (INDS) defines the structural conditions under which the meaning of integrity is formally established for any governed entity, enabling integrity to be consistently identified, interpreted, measured, governed, and independently verified throughout its complete lifecycle. Why INDS Exists Different organizations, systems, and industries often use the word integrity with different meanings. Without a common definition, integrity cannot be governed consistently, measurements become incomparable, and governance decisions lose their reliability. INDS exists to establish a single governed reference that defines what integrity means before any assessment or governance process begins. What INDS Governs INDS governs the definition of integrity, including: integrity meaning integrity boundaries integrity criteria integrity context integrity scope integrity interpretation governance reference conditions. This governed space creates the foundation upon which every other integrity governance activity depends. Architectural Position Within INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture, INDS is the first Parent Standard in the governance flow: Definition → Structure → Conditions → Measurement → State → Deviation → Breach → Response → Restoration → Assurance Every subsequent Parent Standard relies on the integrity definition established by INDS. Canonical Closing Statement Integrity Definition Standard establishes the governed meaning of integrity before integrity is measured, evaluated, preserved, restored, or assured. By defining integrity first, INDS provides the foundational reference upon which the entire INTEGROS® Integrity Governance Architecture is built.

title: About Integrity Deviation Standard - (IDS)
text: OOF™ About Integrity Deviation Standard - (IDS) About Integrity Deviation Standard - (IDS) Detecting Integrity Before It Fails Integrity rarely disappears without warning. In most governed systems, integrity gradually deviates from its approved operational state before a complete integrity breach occurs. Detecting these deviations early enables organizations to intervene before operational integrity is compromised. What Is Integrity Deviation Standard? Integrity Deviation Standard (IDS) is the sixth Parent Standard of INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture. It establishes the canonical governance conditions required to detect, classify, evaluate, monitor, and manage deviations from approved integrity states throughout the complete lifecycle of a governed entity. Canonical Definition Integrity Deviation Standard (IDS) defines the governance conditions required to detect, classify, evaluate, and manage deviations from an approved integrity state by establishing deviation criteria, severity levels, evaluation methods, and governance rules throughout the complete lifecycle of a governed entity. Why IDS Exists Knowing the current integrity state is not sufficient for effective governance. Organizations must also recognize when integrity begins to move away from its approved state, even before operational failure occurs. Building upon the integrity states established by ISS, IDS defines how integrity deviations are identified, evaluated, and governed before they evolve into integrity breaches. This enables proactive governance, continuous monitoring, early intervention, and systematic risk reduction. What IDS Governs IDS governs the complete lifecycle of integrity deviations, including: deviation detection deviation classification deviation severity deviation evaluation deviation monitoring deviation tracking deviation reporting. This governed space ensures that integrity deviations are recognized consistently and managed before they become integrity breaches. Architectural Position Within INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture, IDS is the sixth Parent Standard in the governance flow: Definition → Structure → Conditions → Measurement → State → Deviation → Breach → Response → Restoration → Assurance IDS establishes the canonical governance framework for recognizing and managing integrity deterioration before breach management becomes necessary. Canonical Closing Statement Integrity Deviation Standard establishes the canonical governance framework for detecting, classifying, evaluating, and managing departures from approved integrity states. By governing integrity deviations before they develop into integrity breaches, IDS enables proactive governance, early intervention, operational resilience, and continuous preservation of integrity throughout the complete lifecycle of every governed entity.

title: About Integrity Governance Architecture (INTEGROS®)
text: OOF™ About Integrity Governance Architecture (INTEGROS®) About Integrity Governance Architecture (INTEGROS®) Governing Integrity Across the Complete Operational Lifecycle Systems evolve continuously. Technologies change. Organizations change. Operational environments change. Risks change. Integrity must remain governable. Integrity Governance Architecture (INTEGROS®) was created to provide a stable integrity governance architecture that remains applicable regardless of how technologies, systems, organizations, and operational environments evolve. INTEGROS® does not define software architectures, technical controls, organizational procedures, security products, regulatory frameworks, or implementation technologies. INTEGROS® governs integrity. Why INTEGROS® Exists Most integrity-related initiatives focus on security, compliance, quality, reliability, audit, risk, data accuracy, or technical control. These perspectives are important, but none of them alone fully answers a fundamental governance question: How should integrity itself be defined, measured, governed, restored, and continuously assured? INTEGROS® addresses this question by defining the governable integrity spaces that exist throughout the complete integrity lifecycle. Rather than standardizing one technical solution, INTEGROS® standardizes the governance conditions under which integrity can be formally defined, structurally organized, objectively measured, operationally verified, restored after breach, and continuously assured. Integrity Before Implementation The objective of INTEGROS® is not to prescribe how a system must be built. The objective is to define how integrity must remain governable. Every governed entity depends on integrity. Every integrity condition may change. Every change may create deviation. Every deviation may become a breach. Every breach requires response. Every response must support restoration. Every restoration must lead to continuous assurance. INTEGROS® therefore treats integrity as an independent governance domain. The Integrity Governance Architecture INTEGROS® consists of ten independent integrity governance spaces. Each space answers one architectural question. Each space governs one integrity condition. Each space has a defined beginning, operational purpose, and governance boundary. Each space begins where the previous integrity governance requirement has been sufficiently established. Together, these spaces form the complete integrity governance architecture. The architecture progresses through: Integrity Definition → Integrity Structure → Integrity Conditions → Integrity Measurement → Integrity State → Integrity Deviation → Integrity Breach → Integrity Response → Integrity Restoration → Integrity Assurance This progression represents the complete governance journey of integrity—from formally defining what integrity means to continuously demonstrating that it remains valid throughout ongoing operations. Integrity Spaces Rather Than Technical Components INTEGROS® does not organize integrity governance around software components, departments, products, or isolated controls. Instead, it organizes governance around distinct integrity spaces. Each integrity space represents an independent governance responsibility that exists regardless of any specific system, vendor, platform, sector, technology, or implementation method. Because integrity spaces are technology-neutral and domain-independent, INTEGROS® remains applicable as technologies, operational models, regulatory environments, and governance requirements continue to evolve. A Methodology Rather Than an Implementation INTEGROS® is a governance methodology. It is not a technical implementation framework. The architecture defines which integrity conditions must exist, how they relate to one another, where governance responsibility begins, and what must be objectively demonstrated. Organizations remain free to determine how those conditions are implemented within their own technical, operational, legal, regulatory, and organizational environments. This separation allows INTEGROS® to remain stable while implementation methods, technologies, and operational systems continue to evolve. From Definition to Assurance Integrity cannot be governed as a single undivided concept. Before integrity can be measured, it must be defined. Before it can be evaluated, its structure and conditions must be established. Before a deviation can be governed, the current integrity state must be known. Before a breach can be declared, the deviation must be validated. Before integrity can be restored, the breach must be governed through response. Before integrity can be trusted over time, restoration must be followed by continuous assurance. INTEGROS® transforms these dependencies into a structured and navigable governance lifecycle. Who May Benefit INTEGROS® may support: organizations governing complex operational systems public institutions regulators integrity governance teams auditors and assurance providers enterprise architects AI system operators autonomous system developers digital asset and identity environments healthcare organizations financial institutions industrial operators critical infrastructure providers multi-system and cross-organizational ecosystems. Relationship to Other OOF® Architectures INTEGROS® governs integrity. It operates alongside complementary OOF® architectures. GOA™ governs governance structure, authority, scope, delegation, and continuity. ORA™ governs operational reality, operational validity, execution, and coordination. OBIDENITY® governs origin, identity, ownership, authority, provenance, transfer, and continuity. AGA™ governs accountability relationships, responsibility allocation, delegation, and ownership structures. AIG® governs AI behavior. CLIA® governs cognition, reasoning, interpretation, and cognitive integrity. MGIA™ governs memory, memory continuity, and memory integrity. ASGA™ governs autonomous systems, autonomous agents, and autonomous operational environments. ART™ governs continuous auditability and evidence across operational lifecycles. Together, these architectures create a structured methodology for governing increasingly complex operational, intelligent, autonomous, and digital environments. The Long-Term Vision As AI systems, autonomous systems, digital assets, critical infrastructure, and complex organizations become increasingly interconnected, integrity governance will become as important as technical capability, security, compliance, and operational performance. The long-term objective of INTEGROS® is to provide a common integrity governance language through which organizations can identify, define, measure, classify, protect, restore, and continuously assure integrity across changing technologies and operational environments. INTEGROS® is intended to make integrity governable before failure, during deviation, after breach, throughout restoration, and across continuous operation. Canonical Principle Systems, technologies, and operational environments will continue to change. Integrity governance must remain stable. INTEGROS® therefore governs the integrity conditions that remain valid regardless of future technologies, implementations, and operational models. Canonical Closing Statement Integrity Governance Architecture (INTEGROS®) provides the governance foundation through which integrity can be formally defined, structurally organized, objectively measured, operationally evaluated, protected against deviation, governed through breach response, restored through evidence, and continuously assured. By defining the governable spaces of integrity, INTEGROS® establishes a technology-neutral methodology for ensuring that governed entities remain verifiable, resilient, recoverable, accountable, and trustworthy throughout their complete operational lifecycle.

title: About Integrity Measurement Standard - (IMS)
text: OOF™ About Integrity Measurement Standard - (IMS) About Integrity Measurement Standard - (IMS) Measuring Integrity Objectively Integrity cannot be effectively governed through assumptions or subjective judgment. Once integrity has been defined, supported by an appropriate structure, and preserved through mandatory governance conditions, it must be measured objectively to determine whether it is being maintained throughout the lifecycle of a governed entity. What Is Integrity Measurement Standard? Integrity Measurement Standard (IMS) is the fourth Parent Standard of INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture. It establishes the canonical governance conditions required to objectively measure integrity by defining the metrics, indicators, thresholds, evaluation models, and scoring mechanisms used to assess integrity consistently throughout the complete lifecycle. Canonical Definition Integrity Measurement Standard (IMS) defines the governance conditions required to objectively measure integrity by establishing metrics, indicators, thresholds, evaluation models, and scoring mechanisms throughout the complete lifecycle of a governed entity. Why IMS Exists A governed entity may have a clearly defined integrity model, a structurally sound architecture, and valid operating conditions, but governance still requires objective evidence of whether integrity is actually being maintained. Building upon the integrity conditions established by ICS, IMS defines how integrity is objectively measured and evaluated. IMS exists to transform integrity from a governance concept into measurable operational reality before integrity states, deviations, and breaches are identified. What IMS Governs IMS governs the objective measurement of integrity, including: integrity metrics integrity indicators measurement models evaluation methods integrity thresholds integrity scoring measurement consistency. This governed space ensures that integrity is measured objectively, consistently, and independently across all governed entities. Architectural Position Within INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture, IMS is the fourth Parent Standard in the governance flow: Definition → Structure → Conditions → Measurement → State → Deviation → Breach → Response → Restoration → Assurance IMS transforms governed integrity conditions into measurable evidence, providing the objective foundation required for integrity state classification and every subsequent governance activity. Canonical Closing Statement Integrity Measurement Standard establishes the governance framework required to measure integrity objectively and consistently. By governing metrics, indicators, thresholds, evaluation models, and scoring mechanisms, IMS provides the measurable foundation upon which integrity state evaluation, deviation detection, breach identification, restoration, and assurance are built throughout the complete lifecycle of every governed entity.

title: About Integrity Response Standard - (IRS)
text: OOF™ About Integrity Response Standard - (IRS) About Integrity Response Standard - (IRS) Understanding Governed Integrity Response A verified integrity breach is not the end of governance—it marks the beginning of a governed operational response. Without a standardized response methodology, organizations often react inconsistently, causing delayed containment, unclear accountability, ineffective communication, and unnecessary operational damage. Integrity Response Standard establishes the governance framework that transforms reactive incident handling into a controlled, accountable, and auditable response process. What Is Integrity Response Standard? Integrity Response Standard (IRS) defines the governance principles required to authorize, coordinate, execute, monitor, and govern responses to verified integrity breaches. It ensures that every response follows an approved governance methodology rather than ad hoc operational decisions. Canonical Definition Integrity Response Standard defines the governance conditions required to authorize, coordinate, execute, monitor, document, and govern responses to verified integrity breaches. It establishes the response principles, operational procedures, accountability requirements, escalation mechanisms, communication rules, and governance controls required to contain integrity failures, minimize operational impact, and preserve governance continuity throughout the complete lifecycle of a governed entity. Why IRS Exists Recognizing an integrity breach alone does not protect a governed entity. Governance requires a standardized mechanism for determining how organizations respond, who is authorized to respond, when escalation is required, which actions are permitted, and how every response is documented and audited. IRS provides this canonical governance framework. What IRS Governs IRS governs the complete operational response lifecycle, including: response authorization response coordination operational containment escalation stakeholder communication response documentation governance oversight. Use Case 1 — Autonomous AI Operations An autonomous AI platform executes actions outside its approved governance boundaries. After the breach is verified, IRS governs the authorization of containment actions, coordinates operational response teams, documents every decision, and ensures that the incident is managed consistently under approved governance procedures before restoration begins. Use Case 2 — Critical Infrastructure A national energy operator confirms an integrity breach affecting operational control systems. IRS governs emergency response coordination, executive accountability, regulatory communication, operational containment, and complete audit documentation, ensuring that critical services remain under controlled governance during the incident. Architectural Position Within INTEGROS®, IRS represents the eighth governed space. It follows Integrity Breach Standard (IBS) and provides the governance transition from breach determination to controlled operational response before Integrity Restoration Standard (IRS2) begins. Governance Flow Definition → Structure → Conditions → Measurement → State → Deviation → Breach → Response → Restoration → Assurance Canonical Closing Statement Integrity Response Standard provides the canonical governance framework for responding to verified integrity breaches through authorized, coordinated, accountable, and auditable operational actions. It ensures that every integrity breach is managed consistently before restoration begins, preserving governance continuity throughout the complete lifecycle of every governed entity.

title: About Integrity Restoration Standard - (IRRS)
text: OOF™ About Integrity Restoration Standard - (IRRS) About Integrity Restoration Standard - (IRRS) Understanding Governed Integrity Restoration Responding to an integrity breach does not automatically restore integrity. Once a breach has been contained, governance must ensure that integrity has been objectively re-established before normal operations resume. Restoration requires more than recovery—it requires validated evidence, accountable governance, and confirmation that approved integrity conditions have been fully restored. Integrity Restoration Standard transforms operational recovery into a governed and auditable restoration process. What Is Integrity Restoration Standard? Integrity Restoration Standard (IRRS) defines the governance principles required to restore integrity following a verified integrity breach and completed response activities. It ensures that restoration is performed through a standardized governance methodology supported by objective validation, documented evidence, and accountable decision-making. Canonical Definition Integrity Restoration Standard (IRRS) defines the governance conditions required to restore integrity following a verified integrity breach and completed response activities. It establishes the restoration principles, recovery procedures, validation requirements, accountability mechanisms, evidence requirements, and governance controls required to return a governed entity to an approved state of integrity while ensuring that restoration is objective, verifiable, and fully auditable throughout the complete lifecycle of the governed entity. Why IRRS Exists Containing an integrity breach is not the same as restoring integrity. Organizations require a standardized governance framework that defines how integrity is re-established, who validates the restoration, what evidence is required, when restoration is considered complete, and how restored integrity is documented for future governance and audit purposes. IRRS provides this canonical governance framework. What IRRS Governs IRRS governs the complete integrity restoration lifecycle, including: restoration planning restoration execution integrity recovery restoration validation restoration evidence restoration documentation restoration governance. Use Case 1 — Autonomous AI GovernanceScenario A verified integrity breach has been contained, and autonomous AI services have resumed limited operation. Before full production is restored, the organization must demonstrate that governance conditions, operational integrity, and system trustworthiness have been objectively re-established. Application IRRS governs the restoration process by coordinating recovery activities, validating restored integrity, documenting restoration evidence, and confirming that all approved integrity conditions have been satisfied before normal operation resumes. Result Integrity is restored through a governed, evidence-based, and fully auditable process, allowing autonomous operations to resume with documented confidence and accountability. Use Case 2 — Critical Infrastructure RecoveryScenario A national energy operator successfully contains an integrity breach affecting operational control systems. Critical services must now be restored without introducing additional operational risk. Application IRRS governs the restoration methodology, validates recovery activities, confirms that operational integrity has been re-established, and documents objective evidence supporting the return to normal operations. Result Critical infrastructure returns to service through a controlled restoration process supported by governance, accountability, operational resilience, and complete auditability. Architectural Position Within INTEGROS®, IRRS represents the ninth governed space. It follows Integrity Response Standard (IRS) and provides the governance transition from controlled response to Integrity Assurance Standard (IAS), ensuring that integrity has been objectively restored before continuous assurance begins. Governance Flow Definition → Structure → Conditions → Measurement → State → Deviation → Breach → Response → Restoration → Assurance Canonical Closing Statement Integrity Restoration Standard provides the canonical governance framework for restoring integrity following verified breaches and governed responses through validated, accountable, evidence-based, and auditable restoration activities. It ensures that integrity is objectively re-established before continuous assurance begins, preserving governance continuity throughout the complete lifecycle of every governed entity.

title: About Integrity State Standard - (ISS)
text: OOF™ About Integrity State Standard - (ISS) About Integrity State Standard - (ISS) Understanding the Current Condition of Integrity Objective measurements alone do not describe the actual condition of integrity. Governance requires a standardized representation of integrity that communicates whether a governed entity currently operates with preserved, degraded, compromised, or restored integrity. What Is Integrity State Standard? Integrity State Standard (ISS) is the fifth Parent Standard of INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture. It establishes the canonical governance conditions required to determine, classify, manage, and communicate the current operational state of integrity throughout the complete lifecycle of a governed entity. Canonical Definition Integrity State Standard (ISS) defines the governance conditions required to determine, classify, and maintain the current operational state of integrity by establishing standardized integrity states, state transition rules, and governance criteria throughout the complete lifecycle of a governed entity. Why ISS Exists After integrity has been defined, structured, protected by governance conditions, and objectively measured, governance still requires a clear answer to one essential question: What is the current integrity condition? Building upon the objective measurements established by IMS, ISS transforms integrity measurements into standardized operational integrity states. This enables organizations, autonomous systems, regulators, auditors, and governance frameworks to communicate integrity consistently using a common operational language. What ISS Governs ISS governs the classification and lifecycle management of integrity states, including: integrity state determination, integrity state classification, operational integrity status, state transition governance, integrity state consistency, lifecycle state management, integrity state reporting. This governed space ensures that integrity is represented consistently across all operational, organizational, digital, and autonomous environments. Architectural Position Within INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture, ISS is the fifth Parent Standard in the governance flow: Definition → Structure → Conditions → Measurement → State → Deviation → Breach → Response → Restoration → Assurance ISS establishes the canonical operational representation of integrity before deviations, breaches, governance responses, restoration activities, and long-term assurance are performed. Canonical Closing Statement Integrity State Standard establishes the canonical governance framework for determining, classifying, and managing the current operational condition of integrity. By governing integrity states, state transitions, and classification criteria, ISS provides the standardized representation upon which integrity deviation detection, breach identification, governance response, restoration, and long-term assurance are built throughout the complete lifecycle of every governed entity.

title: About Structural Integrity Standard - (STIS)
text: OOF™ About Structural Integrity Standard - (STIS) About Structural Integrity Standard - (STIS) Preserving Integrity Through Structure Integrity is not preserved by definition alone. Every governed entity depends on a structure capable of maintaining integrity as it operates, evolves, and interacts with other entities. Without a coherent structure, even a well-defined integrity model will eventually degrade. What Is Structural Integrity Standard? Structural Integrity Standard (STIS) is the second Parent Standard of INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture. It establishes the canonical governance conditions required to ensure that the structure of a governed entity is capable of preserving integrity consistently throughout its complete lifecycle. Canonical Definition Structural Integrity Standard (STIS) defines the structural conditions required for a governed entity to preserve integrity by governing its organization, components, relationships, dependencies, and structural coherence throughout its complete lifecycle. Why STIS Exists Integrity can only exist when supported by a stable and governable structure. Weak relationships, hidden dependencies, fragmented components, or inconsistent organization can undermine integrity even when its definition is correct. Governance Flow Position Definition → Structure → Conditions → Measurement → State → Deviation → Breach → Response → Restoration → Assurance Standard Abstract Restoring integrity is not the final governance objective. Integrity must continue to be demonstrated over time through continuous monitoring, objective validation, governance oversight, and auditable evidence. Without continuous assurance, restored integrity may gradually degrade without detection. Building upon the restored integrity established by IRRS, Integrity Assurance Standard defines how integrity is continuously preserved, verified, and demonstrated throughout ongoing operations. IAS transforms integrity from a one-time achievement into a continuously governed operational condition. Operational Role Integrity Assurance Standard governs the continuous assurance of integrity after restoration. It establishes the governance framework required to monitor integrity conditions, validate ongoing compliance, detect emerging risks, maintain assurance evidence, and preserve confidence that approved integrity conditions remain continuously satisfied. This governed space ensures that integrity remains continuously verified, preserved, and demonstrable across all operational environments. Organizations require a standardized governance framework that continuously demonstrates that integrity remains preserved, identifies early signs of degradation, and provides objective assurance to stakeholders, regulators, auditors, and governance authorities. IAS exists because Integrity Assurance represents the tenth governed space of INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture, providing the canonical governance framework for continuously preserving and demonstrating integrity after restoration. Canonical Closing Statement Integrity Assurance Standard establishes the canonical governance framework for continuously verifying, maintaining, and demonstrating integrity throughout the complete lifecycle of every governed entity. By defining how restored integrity is continuously assured through monitoring, validation, evidence, and governance oversight, IAS enables sustained trust, operational resilience, accountable governance, and continuous integrity preservation across all operational domains. Canonical Definition Integrity Breach Standard (IBS) defines the governance conditions required to identify, verify, classify, assess, and govern integrity breaches. It establishes the criteria, breach determination rules, evidence requirements, severity models, and governance controls required to recognize when integrity has been materially compromised throughout the complete lifecycle of a governed entity. Governance Flow Position Definition → Structure → Conditions → Measurement → State → Deviation → Breach → Response → Restoration → Assurance Standard Abstract Not every integrity deviation results in an integrity breach. A breach represents the point at which integrity is no longer considered preserved according to approved governance conditions. Recognizing this transition consistently is essential for effective governance, operational resilience, regulatory compliance, and accountability. Building upon the integrity deviations established by IDS, Integrity Breach Standard defines when integrity has been materially compromised and breach governance becomes necessary. IBS transforms integrity failure from subjective interpretation into a standardized governance determination supported by objective evidence. Operational Role Integrity Breach Standard governs the identification and management of integrity breaches. It establishes the governance framework required to determine when integrity has been materially violated, classify the breach, evaluate its impact, and initiate formal breach governance procedures. This governed space ensures that integrity breaches are recognized, documented, and governed consistently across all operational environments. Without standardized breach criteria, organizations cannot determine when integrity has actually failed, when emergency governance should begin, or when formal accountability mechanisms must be activated. IBS exists because Integrity Breach represents the seventh governed space of INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture, providing the canonical governance framework for recognizing material integrity failures before response and restoration activities begin. Canonical Closing Statement Integrity Breach Standard establishes the canonical governance framework for identifying, verifying, classifying, and governing material integrity failures. By defining when integrity deviations become integrity breaches, IBS enables objective breach determination, accountable governance, timely intervention, and structured recovery throughout the complete lifecycle of every governed entity. Canonical Definition Integrity Condition Standard (ICS) defines the mandatory governance conditions that must remain continuously satisfied for a governed entity to preserve its integrity throughout its complete lifecycle. It establishes the governing rules, constraints, dependencies, and operational conditions under which integrity remains valid, measurable, and governable. Governance Flow Position Definition → Structure → Conditions → Measurement → State → Deviation → Breach → Response → Restoration → Assurance Standard Abstract A defined integrity model and a structurally sound architecture alone do not guarantee that integrity will be preserved. Integrity exists only while specific governance conditions continue to be satisfied. Building upon the structural foundation established by STIS, Integrity Condition Standard defines the mandatory conditions required for integrity to remain valid throughout the governed lifecycle. ICS establishes these mandatory governance conditions and provides the operational foundation upon which integrity can later be measured, monitored, evaluated, and protected. When one or more mandatory conditions cease to exist, integrity enters a governable state of degradation that can subsequently be detected, classified, and managed by later standards within INTEGROS®. Operational Role Integrity Condition Standard governs the mandatory conditions required to preserve integrity. It establishes the governance rules that determine whether integrity remains continuously valid before integrity is measured, classified, or evaluated. Operational Space ICS governs: integrity conditions governance constraints integrity rules dependency conditions boundary conditions operational validity integrity prerequisites. This governed space ensures that integrity is maintained through continuously satisfied governance conditions rather than assumptions. Why This Standard Exists Integrity is not maintained simply because it has been defined or supported by an appropriate structure. It remains valid only while its governing conditions continue to exist. ICS exists because Integrity Conditions represent the third governed space of INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture, establishing the mandatory governance requirements that preserve integrity before measurement and state evaluation begin. Scope This standard may be applied across: AI systems autonomous systems organizational governance digital identities digital assets operational processes software systems cognitive systems governance frameworks any governed entity requiring integrity governance. Relationship to Other OOF® Architectures ICS governs the governance conditions that preserve integrity. It interoperates with: GOA™ for governance rules OBIDENITY® for identity integrity conditions ART™ for evidence supporting integrity conditions ORA™ for operational conditions AGA™ for accountability conditions AIG® for behavioral conditions CLIA® for cognitive conditions MGIA™ for memory conditions ASGA™ for autonomous system operating conditions. Together these architectures ensure that integrity remains continuously governed through explicitly defined conditions across every governed domain. Foundational Principle Integrity exists only while its governing conditions remain true. When mandatory integrity conditions are no longer satisfied, integrity begins to degrade regardless of the underlying structure. Canonical Closing Statement Integrity Condition Standard establishes the mandatory governance conditions required for integrity to remain continuously valid. By governing the rules, constraints, dependencies, and operational requirements that preserve integrity, ICS provides the essential bridge between structural integrity and measurable integrity throughout the complete lifecycle of every governed entity. INDS governs integrity definition. The standard establishes the canonical governance conditions required to determine what integrity means before integrity can be measured, evaluated, protected, restored, or assured. Integrity cannot be governed until integrity has been defined. INDS establishes that foundation. Governance Flow Position Definition → Structure → Conditions → Measurement → State → Deviation → Breach → Response → Restoration → Assurance Standard Abstract Every governed entity depends upon integrity. However, integrity cannot be evaluated unless its meaning is explicitly defined. Different domains often interpret integrity differently. This creates inconsistency, ambiguity, and incompatible governance decisions. INDS establishes a canonical integrity definition before any governance activity begins. It serves as the foundational layer upon which every subsequent integrity governance activity depends. Operational Role Integrity Definition Standard provides the governance layer responsible for defining the canonical meaning of integrity for any governed entity. Its role is to establish the structural governance foundation that enables all subsequent integrity governance processes to operate consistently. Operational Space INDS governs: integrity definition integrity meaning integrity boundaries integrity criteria integrity context integrity scope integrity interpretation integrity governance foundation. This governed space ensures that integrity possesses one formally governed meaning before measurement, evaluation, restoration, or assurance occur. Why This Standard Exists Integrity cannot be measured if it has never been defined. It cannot be protected if its governing conditions remain unknown. It cannot be restored if no reference state exists. INDS exists because Integrity Definition represents the first governable space of INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture. It interoperates with: GOA™ for governance structure OBIDENITY® for identity integrity ART™ for audit evidence ORA™ for operational integrity AGA™ for accountability integrity AIG® for behavioral integrity CLIA® for cognitive integrity MGIA™ for memory integrity ASGA™ for autonomous system integrity. Together these architectures ensure that integrity is consistently defined before it is governed within each operational domain. Foundational Principle Integrity begins with definition. A governed entity cannot preserve, measure, restore, or demonstrate integrity until the meaning of integrity has been formally established. Canonical Closing Statement Integrity is not created by measurement or verification. It begins with a shared definition. Integrity Definition Standard establishes the canonical governance foundation upon which every subsequent integrity decision, evaluation, restoration, and assurance process depends throughout the complete lifecycle of any governed entity. Canonical Definition Integrity Response Standard (IRS) defines the governance conditions required to authorize, coordinate, execute, monitor, document, and govern responses to verified integrity breaches. It establishes the response principles, operational procedures, accountability requirements, escalation mechanisms, communication rules, and governance controls required to contain integrity failures, minimize operational impact, and preserve governance continuity throughout the complete lifecycle of a governed entity. Governance Flow Position Definition → Structure → Conditions → Measurement → State → Deviation → Breach → Response → Restoration → Assurance Standard Abstract Recognizing an integrity breach alone is not sufficient. Once a breach has been verified, governance must transition from detection to controlled operational action. Every response must be timely, proportionate, accountable, transparent, and fully auditable to prevent further integrity degradation and protect the governed entity. Building upon the verified integrity breaches established by IBS, Integrity Response Standard defines how governed entities respond to integrity failures before restoration activities begin. IRS transforms operational reaction into a standardized governance process supported by documented authority, controlled execution, and objective accountability. Operational Role Integrity Response Standard governs the execution and management of integrity responses. It establishes the governance framework required to authorize response activities, coordinate operational actions, contain integrity failures, manage escalation, communicate with stakeholders, and document response execution under controlled governance. Operational Space IRS governs: response authorization response coordination response execution containment escalation stakeholder communication response documentation. This governed space ensures that every verified integrity breach is managed through a consistent, accountable, transparent, and auditable governance response across all operational environments. Why This Standard Exists A verified integrity breach requires more than recognition—it requires governed action. Without standardized response governance, organizations risk inconsistent decision-making, delayed containment, uncontrolled escalation, fragmented accountability, and increased operational damage. IRS exists because Integrity Response represents the eighth governed space of INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture, providing the canonical governance framework for responding to verified integrity breaches before integrity restoration and long-term assurance activities begin. Scope This standard may be applied across: AI systems autonomous systems organizations digital identities digital assets software systems operational processes governance frameworks cognitive systems critical infrastructure any governed entity requiring standardized integrity response governance. Foundational Principle A verified integrity breach requires a governed response—not an improvised reaction. Every integrity response shall be authorized, proportionate, accountable, evidence-based, and fully auditable. Canonical Closing Statement Integrity Response Standard establishes the canonical governance framework for authorizing, coordinating, executing, and governing responses to verified integrity breaches. By defining how governed entities respond to material integrity failures, IRS enables controlled containment, accountable operational action, governance continuity, and structured transition toward integrity restoration throughout the complete lifecycle of every governed entity. Canonical Definition Integrity Restoration Standard (IRRS) defines the governance conditions required to restore integrity following a verified integrity breach and completed response activities. It establishes the restoration principles, recovery procedures, validation requirements, accountability mechanisms, evidence requirements, and governance controls required to return a governed entity to an approved state of integrity while ensuring that restoration is objective, verifiable, and fully auditable throughout the complete lifecycle of the governed entity. Governance Flow Position Definition → Structure → Conditions → Measurement → State → Deviation → Breach → Response → Restoration → Assurance Standard Abstract Responding to an integrity breach does not automatically restore integrity. After containment and response, governance must ensure that integrity has been objectively re-established through controlled restoration activities supported by evidence, validation, and accountability. Building upon the governed responses established by IRRS, Integrity Restoration Standard defines how integrity is systematically restored before long-term integrity assurance begins. IRRS transforms operational recovery into a standardized governance process that confirms integrity has been re-established according to approved governance conditions. Operational Role Integrity Restoration Standard governs the restoration and recovery of integrity following verified breaches. It establishes the governance framework required to plan restoration activities, recover governed entities, validate restored integrity, document recovery, and prepare the entity for continuous integrity assurance. Operational Space IRRS governs: restoration planning restoration execution recovery validation integrity re-establishment restoration evidence restoration documentation restoration governance. This governed space ensures that integrity restoration is performed consistently, objectively, and under approved governance across all operational environments. Why This Standard Exists Containing an integrity breach is not equivalent to restoring integrity. Without standardized restoration governance, organizations cannot objectively demonstrate that integrity has been fully re-established, operational risks have been eliminated, and governance conditions have been satisfied. IRRS exists because Integrity Restoration represents the ninth governed space of INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture, providing the canonical governance framework for restoring integrity before continuous assurance activities begin. Scope This standard may be applied across: AI systems autonomous systems organizations digital identities digital assets software systems operational processes governance frameworks cognitive systems critical infrastructure any governed entity requiring standardized integrity restoration governance. Foundational Principle Integrity is not restored when the incident ends—it is restored when governed evidence objectively demonstrates that approved integrity conditions have been re-established. Canonical Closing Statement Integrity Restoration Standard establishes the canonical governance framework for restoring integrity following verified breaches and governed responses. By defining how integrity is objectively re-established, validated, documented, and governed, IRRS enables consistent recovery, accountable restoration, operational resilience, and structured transition to continuous integrity assurance throughout the complete lifecycle of every governed entity. title: INTEGROS® Architecture Map
text: OOF™ INTEGROS® Architecture Map INTEGROS® Architecture Map Integrity Governance Architecture — Integrity Governance Layer Official Integrity Governance Reference Map for AI Systems, Autonomous Systems, Digital Assets, Organizations, Critical Infrastructure, and Future Operational Environments INTEGROS® serves as the official OOF® integrity governance reference map used to identify, define, classify, navigate, validate, and understand governable integrity spaces across AI systems, autonomous systems, digital assets, organizations, critical infrastructure, and future operational environments. The purpose of INTEGROS® is not to define the technical implementation of a system. The purpose of INTEGROS® is to identify, define, separate, and map the governable spaces through which integrity is established, evaluated, protected, restored, and continuously assured. INTEGROS® serves as the official integrity governance reference map for: AI Systems Autonomous Systems Autonomous Agents Digital Assets Digital Identity Environments Enterprise Systems Government Systems Healthcare Infrastructure Financial Infrastructure Industrial Systems Critical Infrastructure Multi-System Environments Future Operational Ecosystems Core Architectural Principle Every integrity governance space answers one primary governance question. No integrity governance space duplicates the purpose of another integrity governance space. Every integrity governance space has a defined beginning, a defined operational purpose, and a defined governance boundary. Every integrity governance space begins where the preceding integrity governance requirement has been sufficiently established. Together, these integrity governance spaces form the official integrity governance reference map of INTEGROS®. Official Integrity Governance Flow Integrity Definition → Integrity Structure → Integrity Conditions → Integrity Measurement → Integrity State → Integrity Deviation → Integrity Breach → Integrity Response → Integrity Restoration → Integrity Assurance 1. Integrity Definition Standard (INDS) Governed Space: Integrity Definition Core Question How can integrity be formally defined as a governable operational reality? Canonical Definition Integrity Definition Standard (INDS) defines the governance conditions under which integrity is formally identified, described, bounded, classified, documented, and established as a governable operational concept for a specific governed entity. Governance Boundary Begins when a governed entity requires a formal and operationally usable definition of integrity. Ends when integrity has been sufficiently defined, bounded, classified, and documented to support structural governance. 2. Integrity Structure Standard (STIS) Governed Space: Integrity Structure Core Question How should integrity be structurally organized so that it can be consistently governed? Canonical Definition Integrity Structure Standard (STIS) defines the governance conditions under which the components, relationships, dependencies, layers, and structural elements constituting integrity are identified, organized, validated, and documented. Governance Boundary Begins when the formally defined concept of integrity requires a structural model. Ends when the components and relationships constituting integrity have been sufficiently organized and validated to support the definition of integrity conditions. 3. Integrity Conditions Standard (ICS) Governed Space: Integrity Conditions Core Question Under which governed conditions can integrity legitimately exist, be preserved, and remain operationally valid? Canonical Definition Integrity Conditions Standard (ICS) defines the governance conditions, requirements, dependencies, thresholds, and operational circumstances under which integrity may legitimately exist, remain valid, and be preserved. Governance Boundary Begins when the structure of integrity has been established and the conditions required for its valid existence must be defined. Ends when the required integrity conditions have been identified, validated, documented, and made suitable for objective measurement. 4. Integrity Measurement Standard (IMS) Governed Space: Integrity Measurement Core Question How can integrity be objectively measured, evaluated, and demonstrated? Canonical Definition Integrity Measurement Standard (IMS) defines the governance conditions under which integrity indicators, metrics, thresholds, measurement methods, evidence sources, and evaluation procedures are established and applied. Governance Boundary Begins when approved integrity conditions require objective measurement. Ends when valid measurement methods and sufficient measurement results exist to determine the integrity state of a governed entity. 5. Integrity State Standard (ISS) Governed Space: Integrity State Core Question What is the current integrity state of a governed entity, and how can that state be objectively determined? Canonical Definition Integrity State Standard (ISS) defines the governance conditions under which the current integrity state of a governed entity is assessed, classified, validated, monitored, and documented through approved integrity measurements and evidence. Governance Boundary Begins when sufficient integrity measurements exist to determine the current state of integrity. Ends when the integrity state has been objectively assessed, classified, validated, and made available for ongoing governance evaluation. 6. Integrity Deviation Standard (IDS) Governed Space: Integrity Deviation Core Question When does integrity begin to deviate from approved conditions, and how can that deviation be governed before it becomes a breach? Canonical Definition Integrity Deviation Standard (IDS) defines the governance conditions under which departures from approved integrity conditions are identified, assessed, validated, monitored, classified, and documented before or without automatically constituting a formal integrity breach. Governance Boundary Begins when the observed or measured integrity state no longer fully conforms to approved integrity conditions. Ends when the deviation has been resolved, accepted under governed conditions, or formally determined to constitute an integrity breach. 7. Integrity Breach Standard (IBS) Governed Space: Integrity Breach Core Question When does an integrity deviation become a governed integrity breach requiring formal governance intervention? Canonical Definition Integrity Breach Standard (IBS) defines the governance conditions under which an integrity deviation is formally identified, validated, assessed, classified, documented, and recognized as an integrity breach requiring governed intervention. Governance Boundary Begins when an integrity deviation reaches an approved breach condition, threshold, severity, or governance significance. Ends when the breach has been formally validated, classified, documented, and transferred into the governed integrity response process. 8. Integrity Response Standard (IRS) Governed Space: Integrity Response Core Question How should verified integrity breaches be governed, contained, and managed to minimize operational impact? Canonical Definition Integrity Response Standard (IRS) defines the governance conditions under which verified integrity breaches are authorized for intervention, coordinated, contained, escalated, managed, executed, and documented through an accountable response process. Governance Boundary Begins when an integrity breach has been formally validated and requires governance action. Ends when the immediate effects of the breach have been contained, response actions have been completed, and the governed entity is ready to enter integrity restoration. 9. Integrity Restoration Standard (IRRS) Governed Space: Integrity Restoration Core Question How can integrity be objectively restored after a verified breach while preserving governance accountability and evidence? Canonical Definition Integrity Restoration Standard (IRRS) defines the governance conditions under which integrity is planned for restoration, operationally re-established, validated, evidenced, approved, and documented after a verified integrity breach and governed response. Governance Boundary Begins when the immediate integrity response has been completed and restoration of approved integrity conditions becomes possible. Ends when approved integrity conditions have been demonstrably re-established, validated, evidenced, documented, and formally accepted. 10. Integrity Assurance Standard (IAS) Governed Space: Integrity Assurance Core Question How can restored integrity remain continuously verified, demonstrable, and governably assured throughout the complete operational lifecycle? Canonical Definition Integrity Assurance Standard (IAS) defines the governance conditions under which integrity is continuously monitored, validated, evidenced, reported, supervised, and maintained after restoration or initial integrity establishment. Governance Boundary Begins when integrity has been formally established or successfully restored and requires continuous assurance. Continues throughout the remaining operational lifecycle of the governed entity while integrity must remain verifiable, demonstrable, and governably maintained. Core Governed Integrity Spaces Integrity Definition Integrity Structure Integrity Conditions Integrity Measurement Integrity State Integrity Deviation Integrity Breach Integrity Response Integrity Restoration Integrity Assurance Architectural Position INTEGROS® governs the complete integrity governance lifecycle. The architecture progresses through: Integrity Definition → Integrity Structure → Integrity Conditions → Integrity Measurement → Integrity State → Integrity Deviation → Integrity Breach → Integrity Response → Integrity Restoration → Integrity Assurance Together, these integrity governance spaces govern how integrity is formally defined, structurally organized, conditionally established, objectively measured, operationally determined, monitored for deviation, classified when breached, governed through response, re-established through restoration, and continuously maintained through assurance. INTEGROS® therefore provides a complete governance path from the first definition of integrity to its continuous operational preservation. What INTEGROS® Defines INTEGROS® defines: where the governance of integrity begins how integrity is formally defined which structural elements constitute integrity which conditions must exist for integrity to remain valid how integrity is objectively measured how the current integrity state is determined where integrity deviation begins when a deviation becomes a formal integrity breach how verified integrity breaches enter governed response how integrity is objectively restored how restored integrity is continuously assured. INTEGROS® provides the official integrity governance language used for integrity-space identification, integrity lifecycle navigation, governance classification, structural diagnosis, and integrity architecture design across complex operational environments. Compatible OOF® Architectures GOA™ — Governance Architecture ORA™ — Operational Reality Architecture OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture AGA™ — Accountability Governance Architecture AIG® — AI Governance Architecture CLIA® — Cognitive Governance Intelligence Architecture MGIA™ — Memory Governance Intelligence Architecture ASGA™ — Autonomous Systems Governance Architecture ART™ — Audit in Real Time Architecture Canonical Principle INTEGROS® does not define system functionality, software implementation, organizational performance, behavioral legitimacy, or governance authority. INTEGROS® governs the integrity conditions under which governed entities remain formally defined, structurally coherent, objectively measurable, operationally verifiable, recoverable after breach, and continuously assured throughout their complete lifecycle. Canonical Closing Statement INTEGROS® serves as the official integrity governance reference map for AI systems, autonomous systems, digital assets, organizations, critical infrastructure, and future operational environments. By defining the primary governable spaces of integrity, INTEGROS® provides the architecture used to identify, classify, navigate, measure, validate, protect, restore, and continuously assure integrity throughout the complete lifecycle of every governed entity.

text: OOF™ Integrity State Transition Module (ISTM) Integrity State Transition Module (ISTM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority OriginID: OOF-OID-INTEGROS-ISS-ISTM-2026-07-21-0002 Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Integrity State Standard (ISS) Operational Layer: Meta-Integrity Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Integrity Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Integrity State Transitions Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Origin Date: 21 July 2026 Compatibility: OOF Methodology OS · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · ART™ · ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP™ — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL) Governed Space Integrity State Transitions Canonical Definition Integrity State Transition Module (ISTM) defines the governance framework for controlling how integrity moves from one operational state to another. It establishes the transition rules, authorization requirements, validation criteria, and governance controls required to ensure that every integrity state change is legitimate, traceable, and consistently governed throughout the complete lifecycle of a governed entity. Operational Role ISTM governs the transition layer of integrity state management by ensuring that integrity state changes occur only through validated governance processes rather than arbitrary or uncontrolled events. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Define State Transition Rules Identify all permitted integrity state transitions and define the governance conditions under which each transition is allowed. 2. Define Transition Requirements Establish authorization requirements, validation criteria, supporting evidence, approvals, and operational prerequisites required before any integrity state transition may occur. 3. Define Transition Validation Logic Define how transition requests are verified for legitimacy, completeness, consistency, evidence sufficiency, and governance compliance before execution. 4.
