title: Validation Evidence Adequacy Module (VEADM)
text: Validation Evidence Adequacy Module (VEADM) Validation Evidence Adequacy Module (VEADM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VALIDOS™ — Validation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Validation Evidence Fitness Standard (VEFS) Operational Layer: Validation Evidence Fitness Governance Layer Category: AI & Interpretation Subcategory: Validation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Validation Evidence Adequacy Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 9 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS® · ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Validation Evidence Adequacy Canonical Definition Validation Evidence Adequacy Module (VEADM) defines the governance framework for determining whether Relevant, Applicable, and sufficiently Covered Validation Evidence possesses the necessary completeness, representativeness, timeliness, precision, resolution, consistency, and proportional sufficiency to support its assigned validation role at the required Validation Depth. It establishes the conditions under which evidentiary coverage becomes an adequate evidentiary basis rather than merely a populated evidence set. Operational Role VEADM serves as the fourth evidence-qualification gate within the Validation Evidence Fitness Standard. The preceding modules establish: VERM — Does the evidence address the validation question? VEAM — Does the evidence apply to the actual validation conditions? VECM — Does the evidence cover the validation space that must be evidenced? VEADM asks: Is the evidence within that coverage actually adequate for the validation role it must perform? The governed progression is: Covered Validation Evidence → Completeness → Representativeness → Timeliness → Precision → Resolution → Consistency → Proportional Sufficiency → Evidence Adequacy Determination VEADM therefore examines the qualitative and proportional adequacy of the evidence basis after its relevance, applicability, and coverage have been established. Module Operational Space VEADM governs: evidence adequacy, evidence completeness, evidence representativeness, evidence timeliness, evidence recency, evidence precision, evidence resolution, evidence granularity, evidence consistency, evidentiary diversity, evidentiary concentration, evidentiary proportionality, evidentiary sufficiency, adequacy thresholds, adequacy limitations, conditional adequacy, adequacy uncertainty, adequacy degradation, adequacy change, and adequacy traceability. Module Function VEADM applies after the evidence basis has been mapped against the required validation space. Its function is to prevent: covered criteria being assumed adequately evidenced, minimal evidence being treated as sufficient merely because coverage exists, unrepresentative samples supporting broad validation conclusions, stale evidence being used for rapidly changing Validation Objects, low-resolution evidence concealing material differences, imprecise measurements supporting precision-sensitive criteria, internally inconsistent evidence being aggregated without qualification, evidence volume substituting for evidentiary quality, and evidence requirements being satisfied nominally while remaining substantively weak. Coverage and Adequacy Are Different VALIDOS™ establishes: Evidence Coverage asks: Is the required validation space represented by evidence? Evidence Adequacy asks: Is the evidence representing that space sufficiently strong, complete, representative, current, precise, and proportionate for the required validation role? A criterion may therefore possess evidence coverage while remaining inadequately evidenced. For example: A safety criterion may have one relevant and applicable test result. That creates evidence coverage. It may still be inadequate for a high-consequence deployment decision requiring repeated testing across multiple operating conditions. Evidence Completeness Completeness examines whether the available evidence sufficiently addresses the material components of the evidentiary requirement. Completeness may concern: required observations, required measurements, required conditions, required populations, required scenarios, required documentation, required time periods, or other defined evidence elements. Evidence completeness is relative to the governed requirement. It does not mean collecting every possible piece of information. Representativeness Evidence must sufficiently represent the conditions to which the validation conclusion is expected to apply. VEADM assesses whether the evidence basis disproportionately represents: favorable cases, common cases, easy-to-measure cases, accessible populations, normal operating states, or other convenient subsets. Representativeness becomes especially important where validation conclusions are intended to generalize across diverse or changing conditions. Representativeness and Coverage Coverage and representativeness interact but remain distinct. Evidence may technically cover several populations while representing one population with thousands of observations and another with only a handful. VECM may identify that both populations possess evidence coverage. VEADM determines whether that distribution is sufficiently representative for the intended validation conclusion. Evidence Timeliness VEADM evaluates whether evidence is sufficiently current relative to: the Validation Object, Validation Purpose, Validation Scope, operating environment, Validation Criteria, and intended reliance. Evidence may become less adequate as time passes even when it remains relevant and technically applicable. Timeliness requirements may vary significantly between: stable physical characteristics, rapidly changing AI systems, financial environments, cybersecurity conditions, evolving populations, or dynamic operational systems. Evidence Recency Recency is one component of timeliness. Recent evidence is not automatically better evidence. Older evidence may remain highly adequate where the validated condition is stable. Conversely, evidence from several weeks earlier may already be inadequate for a rapidly changing system. VEADM therefore evaluates material recency, not recency for its own sake. Evidence Precision Precision concerns whether evidence provides sufficient exactness for the Validation Criterion being examined. Where validation depends upon thresholds, small deviations may matter. Evidence that is too imprecise may be incapable of distinguishing: Acceptable from: Unacceptable conditions. Required precision must therefore correspond to the validation question. Evidence Resolution Resolution concerns the level at which evidence can reveal meaningful variation. Highly aggregated evidence may conceal: subgroup differences, local failures, temporal instability, edge-case behavior, rare events, component-level failures, or threshold transitions. VEADM determines whether the evidence possesses sufficient resolution for the relevant Validation Criterion and required Validation Depth. Evidence Granularity Granularity concerns how finely evidence is divided or represented. For example: System-level average may be sufficient for one criterion. Another criterion may require: component-level, population-level, transaction-level, or event-level evidence. VEADM prevents coarse evidence from supporting conclusions requiring finer-grained visibility. Evidence Consistency Evidence may contain internal inconsistencies. Consistency assessment asks whether: repeated observations materially agree, measurement processes produce stable outputs, comparable conditions produce comparable evidence, evidence records align where they should, and material divergence is sufficiently understood. Perfect consistency is not required. Real operational systems may legitimately produce variation. The objective is to distinguish explainable variability from unresolved evidentiary inconsistency. Evidence Diversity Some validation questions benefit from evidentiary diversity. Evidence may originate from different: observations, populations, environments, time periods, scenarios, methods, or operational states. Diversity can reduce dependence upon one narrow evidence condition. However: Evidence Diversity ≠ Source Independence Source independence belongs to subsequent Source Reliability governance. VEADM governs diversity of the evidentiary basis itself. Evidence Concentration An evidence basis may be numerically large while concentrated around one narrow condition. For example: One million observations from the same environment may provide excellent evidence of that environment but limited adequacy for a validation covering many environments. VEADM therefore assesses whether concentration weakens the evidence basis relative to the intended validation role. Proportional Sufficiency Evidence adequacy must be proportionate to the consequence and depth of the validation. A low-consequence preliminary validation may require less evidence than: production deployment, regulatory approval, medical use, autonomous decision authority, critical infrastructure operation, or another high-consequence reliance context. VEADM therefore rejects a universal evidence-volume threshold. Sufficiency must be governed relative to the validation requirement. Validation Depth and Adequacy Validation Depth directly affects evidence adequacy. For example: Basic Validation Depth may require evidence sufficient to establish preliminary conformity. Enhanced Validation Depth may require broader coverage, stronger precision, greater representativeness, or additional evidence. High-Assurance Validation Depth may require extensive evidence, multiple conditions, deeper uncertainty analysis, independent corroboration, and stronger operational representation. The exact depth model may be defined elsewhere within VALIDOS™. VEADM consumes the applicable depth requirement. Evidence Adequacy Threshold Where useful, a Validation Criterion may establish an Evidence Adequacy Threshold. The threshold may define minimum acceptable conditions concerning: evidence quantity, sample size, observation period, representativeness, precision, resolution, repeated testing, or other evidentiary requirements. Thresholds must be justified rather than selected merely to fit available evidence. Evidence Sufficiency Evidence is sufficient when the governed evidence basis provides enough legitimate support for its assigned validation role relative to the required Validation Depth. Sufficiency is not identical to certainty. Evidence may be sufficient while some uncertainty remains. The relevant question is whether remaining uncertainty is compatible with the governed validation requirement. Adequacy Limitations Evidence may be adequate while carrying material limitations. Examples include: adequate only for one population, adequate only for normal operation, adequate only within a specified period, adequate only at a defined confidence level, or adequate only when combined with additional evidence. Limitations must remain attached to the adequacy determination. Conditional Adequacy Evidence may receive Conditional Adequacy where it can support validation only if specified conditions remain satisfied. Conditions may include: reduced Validation Scope, restricted reliance, supplementary evidence, additional monitoring, defined operating limits, or future evidence collection. Conditional adequacy must not later be represented as unrestricted evidentiary adequacy. Adequacy Uncertainty Where available information is insufficient to determine whether evidence is adequate, VEADM preserves uncertainty. Possible causes include: unclear evidence requirements, insufficient sample characterization, unknown precision, incomplete temporal information, unresolved inconsistency, or uncertain representativeness. In such cases: Adequacy Undetermined is methodologically preferable to unsupported confidence. Evidence Adequacy Status VEADM may establish: Evidence Adequate The evidence basis is sufficiently complete, representative, timely, precise, resolved, consistent, and proportionate for the assigned validation role. Evidence Conditionally Adequate The evidence basis is adequate only within defined conditions or limitations. Evidence Adequacy Undetermined Available information is insufficient to establish adequacy. Evidence Inadequate The evidence basis does not provide sufficient support for the assigned validation role. These statuses describe evidence adequacy. They do not represent the Validation State of the Validation Object. Adequacy Is Role-Specific VALIDOS™ establishes: Evidence adequacy is not a universal property of an evidence set. The same evidence may be: Adequate for preliminary assessment, Conditionally Adequate for limited deployment, and: Inadequate for high-consequence reliance. Adequacy must therefore remain attached to the validation role for which it was assessed. Adequacy Degradation Evidence adequacy may degrade over time. Degradation may result from: object evolution, operational drift, changing populations, new failure modes, changed environments, aging evidence, expanded Validation Scope, increased Validation Depth, or newly discovered limitations. VEADM therefore treats evidence adequacy as a potentially dynamic condition. Adequacy Change Governance Material changes affecting evidence adequacy must trigger proportionate reassessment. Possible outcomes include: Adequacy Maintained Adequacy Restricted Conditional Adequacy Additional Evidence Required Adequacy Withdrawn This prevents historical adequacy determinations from surviving material change without review. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Establish Adequacy Requirements Determine the evidentiary strength required by the Validation Criteria, Purpose, Scope, Method, and Validation Depth. 2. Assess Completeness Determine whether material evidentiary requirements are sufficiently populated. 3. Assess Representativeness Determine whether evidence sufficiently represents the conditions to which the validation conclusion is expected to apply. 4. Assess Timeliness Determine whether evidence remains sufficiently current. 5. Assess Precision and Resolution Determine whether evidence is sufficiently exact and sufficiently granular for the relevant Validation Criteria. 6. Assess Consistency and Diversity Identify material inconsistencies, concentration, and whether evidentiary diversity is sufficient where required. 7. Assess Proportional Sufficiency Determine whether the complete evidence basis is proportionate to the Validation Depth and intended validation role. 8. Establish Adequacy Status Classify the evidence as: Evidence Adequate, Evidence Conditionally Adequate, Evidence Adequacy Undetermined, or Evidence Inadequate. 9. Preserve Adequacy Traceability Maintain: Evidence Adequacy Record, evidence requirement references, completeness assessment, representativeness assessment, timeliness assessment, precision assessment, resolution assessment, consistency assessment, diversity assessment, concentration record, sufficiency rationale, Validation Depth reference, limitations, conditions, adequacy status, version, reassessment triggers, and sufficient lifecycle traceability. Evidence Adequacy Output VEADM may produce: Evidence Adequacy Assessment, Evidence Completeness Record, Evidence Representativeness Assessment, Evidence Timeliness Assessment, Evidence Precision Record, Evidence Resolution Record, Evidence Consistency Assessment, Evidence Diversity Assessment, Evidence Concentration Record, Evidence Sufficiency Determination, Conditional Adequacy Record, Adequacy Limitation Record, Adequacy Change Record, and Evidence Adequacy Determination. These outputs support the final Evidence Fitness governance stage. Use Case 1 — Medical AI Scenario A diagnostic AI system has relevant and applicable evidence covering all required patient groups. Application VECM establishes population coverage. VEADM then discovers that one clinically important subgroup is represented by only a very small number of observations, insufficient for the required Validation Depth. Result The evidence possesses coverage but remains inadequately representative for unrestricted validation of that subgroup. Use Case 2 — Critical Infrastructure Scenario An autonomous control system possesses evidence covering normal, degraded, emergency, and recovery conditions. Application VEADM determines that emergency-condition evidence was generated several system versions earlier and at substantially lower operating scale. Result The Evidence Coverage Map remains populated, but evidentiary adequacy for current high-consequence operation requires reassessment and potentially new evidence. Architectural Position Validation Evidence Adequacy is the fourth internal governance space of the Validation Evidence Fitness Standard (VEFS). The progression now becomes: Candidate Evidence → Evidence Relevance → Evidence Applicability → Evidence Coverage → Evidence Adequacy VERM determines whether evidence addresses the validation question. VEAM determines whether it applies to the target conditions. VECM determines whether the required validation space is covered. VEADM determines whether the evidence within that coverage is sufficiently strong and proportionate. The final module can then determine whether the complete governed evidence basis is ready to be recognized as fit for subsequent VALIDOS™ validation governance. Foundational Principle Evidence coverage shows where evidence exists; evidence adequacy determines whether what exists is enough. Canonical Closing Statement Validation Evidence Adequacy Module establishes the governance framework through which covered validation evidence is assessed for substantive evidentiary strength. By governing completeness, representativeness, timeliness, precision, resolution, granularity, consistency, diversity, concentration, proportionality, sufficiency, limitations, conditionality, degradation, change, and traceability, VEADM ensures that the presence of evidence across a validation space cannot be mistaken for an evidentiary basis strong enough to support the validation role for which it is intended. title: Validation Evidence Applicability Module (VEAM)
text: Validation Evidence Applicability Module (VEAM) Validation Evidence Applicability Module (VEAM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VALIDOS™ — Validation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Validation Evidence Fitness Standard (VEFS) Operational Layer: Validation Evidence Fitness Governance Layer Category: AI & Interpretation Subcategory: Validation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Validation Evidence Applicability Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 9 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS® · ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Validation Evidence Applicability Canonical Definition Validation Evidence Applicability Module (VEAM) defines the governance framework for determining whether Relevant Validation Evidence generated, observed, measured, recorded, or established under specific conditions can legitimately be applied to the actual Validation Object, version, configuration, population, environment, jurisdiction, operational state, temporal condition, and Validation Scope for which validation is being performed. It establishes the conditions under which evidence relevance becomes Evidence Applicability within a defined validation context. Operational Role VEAM serves as the second evidence-qualification gate within the Validation Evidence Fitness Standard. The preceding Validation Evidence Relevance Module asks: Does this evidence meaningfully address the validation question? VEAM asks: Can this relevant evidence legitimately be applied to this particular Validation Object and the conditions for which the validation conclusion is intended? The governed progression is: Relevant Validation Evidence → Applicability Dimensions → Condition Comparison → Transfer Assessment → Applicability Determination → Applicable Validation Evidence VEAM prevents relevant evidence from being generalized beyond the conditions it can legitimately support. Module Operational Space VEAM governs: evidence applicability, object applicability, version applicability, configuration applicability, population applicability, environmental applicability, jurisdictional applicability, operational applicability, lifecycle applicability, temporal applicability, scale applicability, domain applicability, context applicability, evidence transfer, applicability equivalence, applicability divergence, applicability boundaries, conditional applicability, applicability limitations, applicability uncertainty, applicability change, and applicability traceability. Module Function VEAM applies after evidence has been determined sufficiently relevant to one or more Validation Criteria or evidence requirements. Its function is to prevent: evidence from one object being automatically applied to another, evidence from an old system version being silently transferred to a new version, evidence from one configuration being generalized across materially different configurations, population-specific findings being represented as universal, evidence from controlled environments being assumed valid in real-world environments, jurisdiction-specific evidence being transferred without examining regulatory or contextual differences, evidence from normal operating conditions being applied to extreme conditions, historical evidence being treated as permanently applicable, evidence generated at one scale being generalized to another, and similarity being mistaken for methodological equivalence. Relevance and Applicability Are Different VALIDOS™ establishes a strict distinction: Evidence Relevance asks: Does the evidence address the validation question? Evidence Applicability asks: Does that evidence address the validation question under conditions sufficiently aligned with the actual validation context? Evidence may therefore be relevant but inapplicable. For example: A study examining the same type of AI system may be highly relevant. If it concerns a materially different model version, population, deployment environment, or operating configuration, its applicability may remain limited. Applicability Dimensions VEAM evaluates evidence across the dimensions capable of materially affecting transfer into the governed validation context. These may include: Object Version Configuration Population Environment Jurisdiction Operational State Lifecycle Stage Time Scale Domain Context Not every validation requires every dimension. The applicable dimensions depend upon the Validation Object and Validation Scope. Object Applicability Evidence must possess a legitimate relationship to the actual Validation Object. Evidence generated from: the same object, an equivalent object, a predecessor object, a related object, a representative object, or another object class may possess different degrees of applicability. Object similarity alone does not establish applicability. Material differences must be examined. Version Applicability Validation evidence frequently becomes version-sensitive. A software patch, model update, dataset change, component replacement, algorithm modification, or system redesign may alter whether previous evidence remains applicable. VEAM therefore asks: Does the evidence still describe the version being validated? Where the answer is uncertain, evidence applicability must not be assumed. Configuration Applicability The same Validation Object may operate under materially different configurations. Evidence generated under one configuration may not support another when differences affect the characteristic being validated. Relevant configuration differences may include: model parameters, hardware, software dependencies, safety settings, system permissions, operational constraints, infrastructure, or integration architecture. Applicability must remain configuration-aware. Population Applicability Where evidence concerns people, users, patients, customers, operators, datasets, or other populations, VEAM evaluates whether the represented population corresponds sufficiently to the population within the Validation Scope. Relevant differences may include: age, language, geography, behavior, demographic composition, usage pattern, clinical characteristics, technical capability, or another validation-relevant characteristic. Evidence from one population should not automatically support conclusions about materially different populations. Environmental Applicability Evidence may depend upon the environment in which it was produced. Relevant environmental dimensions may include: physical environment, digital environment, network conditions, infrastructure, weather, operating load, surrounding systems, user behavior, security conditions, or interaction context. Controlled-environment evidence may remain valuable. However, its applicability to operational reality must be explicitly governed. Jurisdictional Applicability Some evidence depends upon jurisdictional conditions. These may include: laws, regulatory requirements, institutional practices, technical standards, healthcare systems, financial structures, documentation requirements, or governance expectations. Evidence valid within one jurisdiction may remain technically relevant while being insufficient for validation under another jurisdictional environment. Operational Applicability Evidence must correspond to the operational conditions represented by the Validation Scope. Evidence generated during: Normal Operation may not automatically apply to: Degraded Operation Emergency Operation Adversarial Conditions or: Maximum Load VEAM prevents one operational state from silently representing all operational states. Lifecycle Applicability Validation Objects may behave differently across lifecycle stages. Evidence from: development, testing, pre-deployment, deployment, mature operation, degraded operation, maintenance, or retirement may have different applicability. Lifecycle transfer requires governance where stage differences are material. Temporal Applicability Evidence exists in time. Its applicability may change because: the Validation Object evolves, populations change, environments change, dependencies change, operating conditions drift, external knowledge improves, or previously unknown failure modes emerge. VEAM therefore evaluates whether historical evidence remains applicable to the current validation. Scale Applicability Evidence produced at one scale may not remain valid at another. Examples include: prototype → production system, small dataset → population-scale deployment, laboratory network → national infrastructure, one autonomous agent → multi-agent ecosystem, low transaction volume → high-volume financial operation. Scale may introduce new dependencies, interactions, failure modes, or emergent behavior. Evidence transfer across scale therefore requires explicit assessment. Domain Applicability A methodology or evidence basis may originate in one domain and be proposed for another. For example: Evidence derived from industrial automation may inform autonomous-system validation. However, domain differences may affect: operating assumptions, risk conditions, user interaction, regulatory expectations, or failure consequences. VEAM governs whether cross-domain evidence transfer remains legitimate. Applicability Equivalence Evidence transfer becomes stronger where the original evidence conditions and target validation conditions can be shown to be materially equivalent for the validation question. Equivalence does not require every characteristic to be identical. It requires that material differences do not invalidate the evidentiary relationship. VEAM therefore distinguishes: Identical Conditions from: Materially Equivalent Conditions and: Materially Different Conditions Applicability Divergence An Applicability Divergence exists where the evidence-generation conditions and target validation conditions differ in a way that may materially affect evidentiary meaning. Divergence does not automatically make evidence unusable. It creates a governance requirement to determine: whether transfer remains legitimate, whether applicability should be conditional, whether additional evidence is required, or whether the evidence must be excluded from the target validation role. Evidence Transfer VEAM governs the transfer of evidence across conditions. The governed relationship is: Source Evidence Context → Material Difference Assessment → Transfer Basis → Target Validation Context Transfer should possess an identifiable methodological basis. Statements such as: "The systems are similar." or: "This worked before." do not by themselves establish evidence applicability. Transfer Conditions Evidence transfer may depend upon conditions such as: verified equivalence, bounded configuration differences, unchanged relevant components, comparable populations, stable operating conditions, supplementary evidence, independent confirmation, or restricted Validation Scope. Transfer conditions must remain attached to the evidence after applicability determination. Applicability Boundary Every evidence item or evidence body may possess a boundary beyond which its applicability cannot be assumed. An Applicability Boundary may define: versions, configurations, populations, environments, time periods, operational states, jurisdictions, scale, or other conditions. The boundary prevents validation conclusions from silently expanding beyond the evidence base. Conditional Applicability Evidence may be classified as applicable only under explicit conditions. Examples include: Applicable only to software version 4.2. Applicable only to represented patient populations. Applicable only under nominal network conditions. Applicable only within the validated operating range. Applicable only when combined with current operational evidence. Conditional applicability must remain visible throughout subsequent VALIDOS™ governance. Applicability Uncertainty Where evidence transfer cannot be confidently established or rejected, VEAM preserves uncertainty. Evidence may receive: Applicability Undetermined rather than being silently accepted or excluded. This is particularly important where: systems are novel, evidence is scarce, conditions are partially comparable, or material differences are poorly understood. Applicability Status Relevant Validation Evidence may receive an applicability status such as: Applicable The evidence can legitimately support the defined validation role under the target conditions. Conditionally Applicable The evidence may support the validation role only within explicit conditions or limitations. Applicability Undetermined Available information is insufficient to establish legitimate applicability. Not Applicable The evidence cannot legitimately be transferred to the target validation context for the proposed role. These statuses remain specific to the evidence-to-context relationship. Applicability Is Relationship-Specific VALIDOS™ establishes: Evidence applicability is not a permanent property of evidence. The same evidence may be: Applicable to Object Version A, Conditionally Applicable to Version B, and: Not Applicable to Version C. Applicability must therefore remain attached to the exact conditions for which it has been assessed. Applicability and Evidence Gaps When relevant evidence is found to be inapplicable, an Evidence Gap may emerge. This is important because evidence may appear to exist until applicability is examined. For example: A system may possess extensive historical testing. If the system has undergone a material architectural change, much of that evidence may no longer apply. VEAM therefore helps distinguish: Apparent Evidence Coverage from: Applicable Evidence Coverage Applicability Change Governance Evidence applicability may change because of: object modification, version change, configuration change, population change, environmental change, jurisdictional change, lifecycle progression, operational drift, scale expansion, changed Validation Scope, or new knowledge concerning material differences. Material changes require proportionate applicability reassessment. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Establish Evidence Origin Conditions Identify the material conditions under which the evidence was generated, observed, measured, or recorded. 2. Establish Target Validation Conditions Identify the corresponding conditions of the actual Validation Object and Validation Scope. 3. Compare Material Dimensions Assess relevant differences across: object, version, configuration, population, environment, jurisdiction, operation, lifecycle, time, scale, domain, and context. 4. Identify Applicability Divergence Determine whether any material difference may affect the evidentiary relationship. 5. Establish Transfer Basis Where evidence is transferred, document the methodological basis supporting that transfer. 6. Establish Applicability Boundary Define the conditions within which evidence may legitimately support validation. 7. Establish Applicability Status Classify the evidence as: Applicable, Conditionally Applicable, Applicability Undetermined, or Not Applicable. 8. Preserve Applicability Traceability Maintain: Evidence Identifier, originating evidence conditions, target validation conditions, material-difference assessment, transfer basis, applicability dimensions, divergence record, applicability boundary, conditions, limitations, status, version, reassessment triggers, and sufficient lifecycle traceability. Applicability Output VEAM may produce: Evidence Applicability Record, Evidence Context Profile, Evidence-to-Target Comparison, Applicability Divergence Record, Evidence Transfer Assessment, Evidence Transfer Basis, Applicability Boundary, Conditional Applicability Record, Applicability Determination, Applicability Change Record, and Applicable Validation Evidence Set. These outputs support subsequent Evidence Fitness governance. Use Case 1 — Updated AI Model Scenario An AI model has previously undergone extensive validation. A new version changes the model architecture and training data. Application The historical evidence remains relevant to the general validation questions. VEAM evaluates whether it remains applicable to the new model version. Evidence relating to unchanged external interfaces may remain applicable, while performance and behavioral evidence affected by the architecture and training changes may require new validation. Result Historical evidence is not discarded wholesale, but neither is it automatically transferred. Applicability is governed at the level of material change. Use Case 2 — Healthcare Deployment Scenario A medical AI system was validated using evidence from hospitals in one country and is proposed for deployment in another. Application VEAM assesses differences in: patient population, clinical workflow, language, healthcare infrastructure, operating conditions, and regulatory context. Result Some evidence may remain Applicable, some may become Conditionally Applicable, and additional local evidence may be required where material Applicability Divergence exists. Architectural Position Validation Evidence Applicability is the second internal governance space of the Validation Evidence Fitness Standard (VEFS). The progression now becomes: Candidate Evidence → Evidence Relevance → Evidence Applicability VERM establishes whether evidence addresses the validation question. VEAM establishes whether that relevant evidence can legitimately be applied to the actual validation conditions. Subsequent Evidence Fitness governance can then determine whether the applicable evidence basis provides sufficient coverage, completeness, representativeness, timeliness, and overall fitness. Foundational Principle Relevant evidence cannot legitimately support a validation conclusion beyond the conditions to which that evidence applies. Canonical Closing Statement Validation Evidence Applicability Module establishes the governance framework through which relevant evidence is tested against the actual conditions of validation before it may support a validation conclusion. By governing object, version, configuration, population, environment, jurisdiction, operation, lifecycle, temporal, scale, domain, and contextual applicability, together with evidence transfer, divergence, boundaries, conditionality, uncertainty, change, and traceability, VEAM prevents validation evidence from being silently generalized beyond the conditions it can legitimately represent. title: Validation Evidence Coverage Module (VECM)
text: Validation Evidence Coverage Module (VECM) Validation Evidence Coverage Module (VECM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VALIDOS™ — Validation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Validation Evidence Fitness Standard (VEFS) Operational Layer: Validation Evidence Fitness Governance Layer Category: AI & Interpretation Subcategory: Validation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Validation Evidence Coverage Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 9 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS® · ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Validation Evidence Coverage Canonical Definition Validation Evidence Coverage Module (VECM) defines the governance framework for determining whether Relevant and Applicable Validation Evidence sufficiently covers the material Validation Criteria, evidence requirements, populations, scenarios, operating conditions, temporal periods, system states, boundaries, and other validation-relevant dimensions established by the governed Validation Scope and required Validation Depth. It establishes the conditions under which individual evidence items become a structured evidentiary coverage model capable of revealing what has been evidenced, what has been only partially evidenced, and what remains unsupported. Operational Role VECM serves as the third evidence-qualification gate within the Validation Evidence Fitness Standard. The preceding modules ask: VERM — Does the evidence address the validation question? VEAM — Can that evidence legitimately apply to the actual validation conditions? VECM asks: Does the resulting applicable evidence basis cover the validation space that must actually be evidenced? The governed progression is: Relevant Evidence → Applicable Evidence → Evidence Requirements → Coverage Mapping → Coverage Assessment → Coverage Gaps → Evidence Coverage Determination VECM transforms evidence from a collection of individual items into a governed map of evidentiary coverage. Module Operational Space VECM governs: evidence coverage, criterion coverage, requirement coverage, scope coverage, population coverage, scenario coverage, operational-condition coverage, system-state coverage, boundary-condition coverage, temporal coverage, lifecycle coverage, environmental coverage, failure-condition coverage, edge-case coverage, coverage depth, coverage distribution, coverage concentration, coverage redundancy, partial coverage, coverage gaps, critical coverage gaps, coverage change, and coverage traceability. Module Function VECM applies after evidence has been established as sufficiently relevant and applicable. Its function is to prevent: large evidence volumes being mistaken for broad validation coverage, repeated evidence for one criterion concealing unsupported criteria, normal-operation evidence being treated as complete operational coverage, majority-population evidence concealing unrepresented populations, average-case evidence concealing edge conditions, favorable scenarios dominating the evidence basis, short observation windows being represented as lifecycle coverage, repeated measurements creating artificial impressions of completeness, and material Evidence Gaps remaining invisible inside complex evidence repositories. Evidence Quantity and Evidence Coverage Are Different VALIDOS™ establishes a strict distinction: Evidence Quantity = How much evidence exists. Evidence Coverage = How much of the required validation space that evidence legitimately represents. A validation may contain millions of observations while providing weak coverage. Conversely, a smaller but deliberately structured evidence set may provide strong coverage of the material validation dimensions. Therefore: Evidence Volume ≠ Evidence Coverage Coverage Begins With Requirements Evidence coverage cannot be meaningfully assessed without knowing what must be covered. VECM derives its coverage structure from: Validation Criteria, evidence requirements, Validation Scope, Validation Depth, Validation Method Framework, object characteristics, relevant operating conditions, and other governed validation requirements. The basic relationship is: Validation Requirement → Required Evidence Dimension → Available Applicable Evidence → Coverage Status Criterion Coverage Every material Validation Criterion should have identifiable evidence coverage. Criterion coverage asks: Does applicable evidence exist? Does it address the complete criterion? Does it address only part of the criterion? Does the evidence cover all material conditions under which the criterion applies? Does required Validation Depth change the amount or diversity of evidence required? A criterion should not be classified as evidenced merely because one related evidence item exists. Requirement Coverage A single Validation Criterion may create multiple evidence requirements. For example: Criterion: Autonomous system maintains safe behavior under degraded operating conditions. Evidence requirements may include: sensor degradation, network interruption, power instability, component failure, partial information, recovery behavior, and escalation behavior. VECM maps coverage at the requirement level where necessary. This prevents broad criterion labels from concealing unsupported subconditions. Scope Coverage Validation Scope defines where the validation conclusion is intended to apply. VECM compares the evidence basis against that scope. Where the scope includes: multiple environments, multiple populations, multiple configurations, multiple jurisdictions, multiple operating states, or multiple lifecycle phases, evidence coverage must reflect those dimensions where they are materially relevant. Population Coverage Where populations matter, VECM evaluates whether applicable evidence sufficiently represents the populations included within the Validation Scope. Coverage may be examined across: user groups, patient groups, languages, geographic regions, behavioral groups, demographic categories, technical capability levels, or other relevant characteristics. VECM does not prescribe which population characteristics must be used. It requires the characteristics material to the validation question to be covered. Scenario Coverage Complex systems may require evidence across multiple scenarios. VECM assesses whether evidence sufficiently covers: expected scenarios, uncommon scenarios, high-impact scenarios, adversarial scenarios, failure scenarios, boundary scenarios, recovery scenarios, and other materially relevant situations. Scenario count alone does not establish scenario coverage. Ten thousand nearly identical scenarios may provide less useful coverage than a deliberately diversified scenario set. Operational-Condition Coverage Systems may operate under materially different conditions. VECM may assess evidence coverage across: Nominal Operation High Load Degraded Operation Failure Conditions Emergency Conditions Recovery Conditions Adversarial Conditions or other defined states. Evidence demonstrating only nominal operation should not silently create the appearance of complete operational validation. System-State Coverage A Validation Object may move through different states. Relevant states may include: initialization, normal operation, transition, degraded operation, fallback, shutdown, recovery, update, or another system-specific state. Where state behavior matters to validation, evidence coverage should reflect the relevant state space. Boundary-Condition Coverage Validation failures frequently emerge near boundaries. These may include: maximum or minimum operating ranges, threshold transitions, resource limits, latency boundaries, capacity limits, confidence thresholds, decision boundaries, or other operational limits. VECM therefore distinguishes ordinary-condition coverage from boundary-condition coverage. Edge-Case Coverage Rare conditions may have disproportionate consequences. Evidence coverage may therefore require explicit treatment of: rare inputs, unusual combinations, extreme conditions, atypical users, low-frequency failures, unexpected interactions, or other edge cases. Edge-case coverage should be proportionate to Validation Purpose, Scope, Depth, risk, and consequence. Failure-Condition Coverage Evidence of successful behavior does not automatically demonstrate behavior during failure. Where relevant, VECM assesses whether the evidence basis includes: known failure modes, plausible failure modes, cascading failures, dependency failures, partial failures, recovery failures, and failure escalation. This is particularly important for autonomous systems, critical infrastructure, healthcare, finance, and high-consequence AI applications. Temporal Coverage A short evidence window may provide strong evidence of immediate performance while weakly representing long-term operation. VECM evaluates whether evidence spans the temporal conditions required by the Validation Scope. Temporal coverage may concern: duration, seasonality, repeated operation, long-term drift, lifecycle stages, update cycles, degradation, or recurring conditions. Temporal coverage is separate from evidence timeliness. Timeliness asks whether evidence is current enough. Temporal coverage asks whether enough of the relevant time dimension has been represented. Lifecycle Coverage Where validation conclusions apply across multiple lifecycle stages, evidence coverage may need to represent: development, testing, deployment, operation, maintenance, modification, degradation, recovery, and retirement. Evidence from one lifecycle stage cannot automatically establish coverage of another. Coverage Depth Coverage is not purely binary. A validation requirement may have: No Coverage Minimal Coverage Partial Coverage Substantial Coverage Required Coverage Achieved or another governed classification. Coverage depth should correspond to the Validation Depth established earlier in VALIDOS™. Coverage Distribution VECM examines how evidence is distributed across the validation space. Evidence may be highly concentrated around: common conditions, favorable outcomes, one population, one configuration, one time period, or one operational environment. This may create an evidentiary imbalance even where total evidence volume appears substantial. Coverage Concentration A Coverage Concentration exists where disproportionate evidence accumulates around a limited part of the Validation Scope. Coverage concentration is not automatically a defect. Some conditions legitimately require more evidence. However, concentration must not conceal unsupported areas. Coverage Redundancy Repeated evidence may increase confidence within an already covered area. But redundancy does not necessarily expand coverage. VECM therefore distinguishes: Evidence Reinforcement from: Evidence Coverage Expansion Repeated tests of the same condition may strengthen confidence in that condition while doing nothing to address another unsupported requirement. Partial Coverage A requirement may be partially evidenced. For example: Evidence may cover system behavior under moderate network degradation but not complete network loss. VECM preserves partial coverage rather than converting it into either complete coverage or no coverage. This allows later validation governance to reason about the actual evidentiary state. Evidence Coverage Gap An Evidence Coverage Gap exists where one or more required validation dimensions lack sufficient applicable evidence. A gap may concern: a Validation Criterion, evidence requirement, population, scenario, system state, operating condition, boundary, failure mode, lifecycle stage, or temporal condition. Coverage gaps must remain explicit. Critical Coverage Gap Not all coverage gaps have equal significance. A Critical Coverage Gap exists where missing evidence concerns a condition capable of materially affecting: validity determination, safety, high-consequence operation, required Validation Depth, intended reliance, or another critical validation requirement. Criticality must be determined through the applicable governance context rather than by evidence volume alone. Coverage Gap Is Not Invalidity VALIDOS™ establishes: Evidence Coverage Gap ≠ Validation Object Invalid A coverage gap means that a required part of the validation space lacks sufficient evidentiary support. The correct governance response may be: collect additional evidence, reduce Validation Scope, restrict reliance, classify uncertainty, perform additional validation, or delay determination. The gap must not automatically become either validity or invalidity. Coverage Map VECM may represent evidence coverage through an Evidence Coverage Map. A conceptual structure may be: Validation Criterion → Evidence Requirement → Required Dimension → Applicable Evidence → Coverage Level → Gap Status This creates a navigable evidentiary structure. For complex systems, coverage maps may become machine-readable and dynamically updated as evidence changes. Coverage Matrix Where appropriate, evidence coverage may be represented through a matrix. For example: Criteria × Populations Criteria × Scenarios Criteria × Operating Conditions Criteria × System States Criteria × Evidence Types Criteria × Time Periods Such matrices can reveal evidence gaps that would remain invisible in ordinary document-based validation. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Establish Required Coverage Dimensions Derive the material coverage requirements from: Validation Criteria, Evidence Requirements, Validation Scope, Validation Depth, and Validation Method Framework. 2. Map Applicable Evidence Associate relevant and applicable evidence with the dimensions it legitimately covers. 3. Assess Coverage Determine whether each material requirement has: sufficient coverage, partial coverage, minimal coverage, or no coverage. 4. Assess Distribution and Redundancy Identify whether evidence is disproportionately concentrated or repeatedly reinforces already-covered areas. 5. Identify Coverage Gaps Record material unsupported or under-supported dimensions. 6. Identify Critical Coverage Gaps Determine which gaps may materially affect subsequent validation governance. 7. Establish Coverage Determination Determine whether the evidence basis provides sufficient coverage relative to the Validation Purpose, Scope, Criteria, Method, and required Depth. 8. Preserve Coverage Traceability Maintain: Evidence Coverage Map, Validation Criterion references, evidence requirement references, applicable evidence references, coverage dimensions, coverage levels, partial coverage, coverage concentrations, redundancies, Evidence Coverage Gaps, Critical Coverage Gaps, changes, version, and sufficient lifecycle traceability. Evidence Coverage Status VECM may establish a coverage status such as: Coverage Sufficient Material evidence requirements possess sufficient coverage for the governed validation stage. Coverage Conditionally Sufficient Coverage is sufficient only within defined boundaries, limitations, or reduced scope. Coverage Incomplete Material evidence requirements remain partially unsupported. Coverage Critically Incomplete One or more critical evidence requirements lack sufficient coverage. Coverage Undetermined Available information is insufficient to determine evidentiary coverage. These statuses describe the evidence basis. They do not represent the Validation State of the Validation Object. Coverage Change Governance Evidence coverage may change because of: new evidence, evidence removal, evidence invalidation, applicability change, Validation Criteria change, Validation Scope change, Validation Depth change, new system states, newly identified failure modes, expanded populations, changed operating environments, or newly discovered validation requirements. Material changes require the Evidence Coverage Map to be reassessed. Coverage and Subsequent Validation Governance VECM does not decide the final Validation Determination. Instead, it provides later VALIDOS™ stages with explicit information concerning: what is evidenced, how strongly it is covered, where evidence is concentrated, where evidence remains partial, and where evidence is absent. This allows later governance to distinguish: Evidence-supported conclusions from: Assumed conclusions. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle System Scenario An autonomous system has millions of kilometers of evidence from normal road conditions. Application VECM maps evidence across: weather conditions, road types, traffic density, sensor degradation, emergency scenarios, unusual objects, nighttime conditions, and failure states. Result The evidence volume is extremely large, but the Coverage Map reveals weak evidence for several rare high-consequence conditions. The validation therefore possesses high evidence volume but incomplete evidence coverage. Use Case 2 — Financial AI Scenario An AI system used for financial decision support has strong evidence across ordinary market conditions. Application VECM examines coverage across: stable markets, high volatility, liquidity stress, market discontinuity, unusual correlation structures, and historical crisis conditions. Result Strong normal-market evidence does not automatically establish coverage of stress conditions included within the Validation Scope. Architectural Position Validation Evidence Coverage is the third internal governance space of the Validation Evidence Fitness Standard (VEFS). The evidence-governance progression now becomes: Candidate Evidence → Evidence Relevance → Evidence Applicability → Evidence Coverage VERM determines whether evidence addresses the validation question. VEAM determines whether that evidence applies to the actual validation context. VECM determines whether the resulting evidence basis sufficiently covers the required validation space. Subsequent modules can then govern the remaining dimensions necessary for an overall Evidence Fitness Determination. Foundational Principle Evidence abundance cannot compensate for evidence absence where validation actually matters. Canonical Closing Statement Validation Evidence Coverage Module establishes the governance framework through which relevant and applicable evidence is mapped against the complete evidentiary space required by validation. By governing criterion, requirement, scope, population, scenario, operational, system-state, boundary, edge-case, failure, temporal, lifecycle, depth, distribution, redundancy, partial coverage, gaps, critical gaps, change, and traceability, VECM ensures that validation confidence reflects what the evidence genuinely covers rather than how much evidence happens to exist. title: Validation Evidence Fitness Determination Module (VEFDM)
text: Validation Evidence Fitness Determination Module (VEFDM) Validation Evidence Fitness Determination Module (VEFDM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VALIDOS™ — Validation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Validation Evidence Fitness Standard (VEFS) Operational Layer: Validation Evidence Fitness Governance Layer Category: AI & Interpretation Subcategory: Validation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Validation Evidence Fitness Determination Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 9 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS® · ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Validation Evidence Fitness Determination Canonical Definition Validation Evidence Fitness Determination Module (VEFDM) defines the governance framework for integrating evidence relevance, applicability, coverage, adequacy, limitations, gaps, contradictions, uncertainty, and validation-role requirements into a formal determination of whether the complete governed evidence basis is sufficiently fit to progress within the VALIDOS™ validation lifecycle. It establishes the final evidence-fitness governance gate between Evidence Qualification and subsequent Validation Source Reliability Governance. Operational Role VEFDM serves as the fifth and final internal governance space of the Validation Evidence Fitness Standard. The preceding modules establish: VERM — Validation Evidence Relevance VEAM — Validation Evidence Applicability VECM — Validation Evidence Coverage VEADM — Validation Evidence Adequacy VEFDM asks: Considering the complete governed evidence basis, is the evidence sufficiently fit for the validation role it is expected to perform? The governed progression is: Relevant Evidence → Applicable Evidence → Covered Evidence → Adequate Evidence → Integrated Fitness Assessment → Evidence Fitness Determination VEFDM does not determine whether the Validation Object is valid. It determines whether the evidence basis is sufficiently fit to continue supporting the validation process. Module Operational Space VEFDM governs: integrated evidence fitness, evidence-fitness determination, evidence-fitness status, evidence-fitness conditions, evidence-fitness limitations, evidence-fitness uncertainty, evidence-fitness conflicts, evidence-fitness gaps, evidence-fitness dependencies, evidence-fitness proportionality, evidence-fitness restrictions, evidence-fitness readiness, evidence-fitness change, evidence-fitness expiration, evidence-fitness reassessment, evidence-fitness withdrawal, evidence-fitness continuity, evidence-fitness traceability, and transition to subsequent validation governance. Module Function VEFDM applies after the material evidence basis has been assessed for relevance, applicability, coverage, and adequacy. Its function is to prevent: individually acceptable evidence assessments from being mistaken for overall evidence fitness, unresolved Evidence Gaps from disappearing during aggregation, conditional evidence becoming represented as unconditional evidence, evidence limitations being detached from later validation stages, contradictory evidence being silently averaged away, evidence uncertainty being converted into unsupported confidence, strong evidence in one area compensating automatically for critical weakness in another, evidence fitness being inferred from quantity, evidence fitness being confused with source trustworthiness, and evidence qualification being confused with Validation Determination. Evidence Fitness as an Integrated Condition Evidence Fitness is not established by one characteristic. VALIDOS™ treats it as an integrated governance condition. The evidence basis must be considered across: Relevance Applicability Coverage Adequacy together with material: Limitations Gaps Contradictions Uncertainty Dependencies and: Validation Role Requirements Evidence may perform strongly in several dimensions while remaining unfit because of one material unresolved condition. Fitness Integration Principle VEFDM establishes: Evidence fitness should not be calculated through blind averaging. A high score in one dimension must not automatically neutralize a critical failure in another. For example: Highly relevant and precise evidence cannot compensate for the complete absence of evidence concerning a critical safety condition. Likewise, broad coverage cannot compensate for evidence that does not apply to the actual Validation Object. Fitness determination must therefore remain sensitive to materiality. Evidence Fitness Inputs VEFDM may consume governed outputs including: Evidence Relevance Determinations, Evidence Applicability Determinations, Evidence Coverage Maps, Evidence Coverage Gaps, Critical Coverage Gaps, Evidence Adequacy Assessments, Evidence Limitations, Evidence Contradictions, Validation Criteria, Validation Purpose, Validation Scope, Validation Depth, Validation Method Framework, and other validation-role requirements. These inputs form the basis of the integrated Evidence Fitness Determination. Fitness Materiality Not every evidentiary weakness has equal significance. VEFDM distinguishes between conditions that are: immaterial, minor, material, critical, or execution-blocking. Materiality may depend upon: the affected Validation Criterion, Validation Purpose, Validation Depth, consequence of error, intended reliance, evidence substitutability, and the availability of compensating evidence. A critical evidentiary weakness must not disappear merely because the remainder of the evidence basis is strong. Evidence Fitness and Critical Criteria Certain Validation Criteria may be designated as critical. Where evidence supporting a critical criterion is: irrelevant, inapplicable, critically incomplete, inadequate, or materially uncertain, the complete evidence basis may be prevented from receiving unrestricted Evidence Fit status. This preserves the significance of critical validation requirements. Evidence Fitness Conditions Evidence may be fit only within defined conditions. Conditions may include: restricted Validation Scope, limited population, defined operating environment, specific object version, specified configuration, limited time period, additional monitoring, supplementary evidence, additional validation, or restricted downstream reliance. Such conditions form part of the Evidence Fitness Determination itself. They must remain attached to the evidence basis throughout subsequent validation governance. Evidence Fitness Limitations A limitation differs from a condition. A condition specifies what must remain true for the fitness determination to apply. A limitation identifies a known boundary or weakness in what the evidence can establish. Examples include: limited long-term evidence, restricted edge-case representation, unresolved low-frequency behavior, limited geographic representation, or constrained historical depth. Limitations must survive transition into subsequent VALIDOS™ stages. Evidence Fitness Uncertainty VEFDM preserves uncertainty where the evidence basis cannot support a stronger conclusion. Uncertainty may result from: incomplete evidence, applicability uncertainty, conflicting evidence, insufficient representativeness, measurement uncertainty, unknown system behavior, or unresolved evidentiary dependencies. VALIDOS™ establishes: Uncertainty must not be converted into evidence fitness merely because a decision is operationally convenient. Evidence Contradiction Integration Material contradictory evidence must remain visible during the final fitness determination. VEFDM evaluates whether contradiction: can be sufficiently explained, reflects different conditions, requires additional evidence, creates a material limitation, creates uncertainty, requires reduced Validation Scope, or prevents an Evidence Fit determination. VEFDM does not determine the ultimate truth of conflicting claims. It determines what the unresolved contradiction means for evidence fitness. Evidence Gap Integration Evidence gaps identified earlier must be carried into the final fitness assessment. VEFDM distinguishes: Non-Material Evidence Gap Material Evidence Gap Critical Evidence Gap A non-material gap may permit unrestricted fitness. A material gap may require conditional fitness. A critical gap may prevent the evidence basis from being considered fit for the intended validation role. Evidence Fitness Dependencies Evidence fitness may depend upon additional conditions that have not yet been fully resolved. Dependencies may include: pending evidence, future operational observations, required external records, additional population data, updated measurements, completion of a defined test, or another evidentiary prerequisite. Dependencies must remain visible rather than being treated as completed evidence. Evidence Fitness Proportionality VEFDM determines fitness relative to the actual validation role. The same evidence basis may be: Fit for exploratory analysis, Conditionally Fit for controlled pilot deployment, and: Unfit for unrestricted high-consequence operation. Therefore: Evidence Fitness is proportional to the validation role and required Validation Depth. Evidence Fitness Status VEFDM may establish the following canonical evidence-fitness states: Evidence Fit The governed evidence basis is sufficiently relevant, applicable, covered, adequate, and methodologically usable for the defined validation role. Evidence Conditionally Fit The evidence basis may support the defined validation role only under explicit conditions, limitations, restrictions, or additional controls. Evidence Fitness Undetermined Available information does not permit a defensible Evidence Fitness Determination. Evidence Insufficient The evidence basis contains material gaps or inadequacies preventing sufficient evidentiary support for the defined validation role. Evidence Unfit The evidence basis cannot legitimately perform the proposed validation role. These states apply to the evidence basis. They do not constitute the Validation State of the Validation Object. Evidence Fitness Determination A formal Evidence Fitness Determination should identify, where applicable: Validation Object, Validation Purpose, Validation Scope, Validation Depth, relevant Validation Criteria, applicable Validation Method Framework, evidence basis assessed, relevance status, applicability status, coverage status, adequacy status, material limitations, material gaps, contradictions, uncertainty, dependencies, conditions, restrictions, Evidence Fitness Status, determination basis, effective period, and reassessment triggers. Evidence Fitness Record The determination should produce a persistent Evidence Fitness Record. The record provides a governed reference connecting the evidence qualification stage to subsequent VALIDOS™ governance. This allows later stages to determine: which evidence was considered fit, for which validation role, under which conditions, within which boundaries, with which limitations, and at which point in time. Evidence Fitness Is Not Source Reliability VEFDM preserves a strict architectural boundary: Evidence Fit ≠ Source Reliable An evidence item may be: relevant, applicable, well-covered, and adequate while the trustworthiness of its originating source remains unresolved. The subsequent Validation Source Reliability Standard governs that independent question. Therefore, successful completion of VEFS does not authorize VALIDOS™ to assume source trustworthiness. Evidence Fitness Is Not Validation Execution Evidence Fitness also does not demonstrate that validation has been properly executed. VEFDM establishes: The evidence basis is fit to participate in validation. Validation Execution must subsequently establish: The governed validation process was actually performed according to the approved validation structure. These are separate governance conditions. Evidence Fitness Is Not Validation Determination VALIDOS™ establishes: Evidence Fit ≠ Validation Object Valid A strong evidence basis may ultimately demonstrate that the Validation Object fails one or more Validation Criteria. That is entirely compatible with Evidence Fit status. Evidence Fitness concerns the quality of the evidentiary basis. Validation Determination concerns what the governed validation process demonstrates about the Validation Object. Evidence Fitness Readiness An Evidence Fitness Determination creates readiness for the evidence basis to progress to subsequent validation governance. Where the evidence basis is: Evidence Fit or appropriately: Evidence Conditionally Fit it may proceed subject to applicable conditions. Where it is: Evidence Insufficient or: Evidence Unfit additional evidence governance may be required before progression. Conditional Progression Conditionally Fit evidence may progress only when its conditions remain visible and enforceable. Examples include: limited-scope validation, additional source verification, supplementary evidence collection, restricted operational assumptions, or enhanced validation controls. The downstream validation process must not silently discard these conditions. Evidence Fitness Expiration Evidence Fitness is not necessarily permanent. A determination may expire because of: elapsed time, object change, version change, configuration change, Validation Scope change, Validation Criteria change, Validation Depth change, new contradictory evidence, evidence degradation, new operational information, or another material change. Expiration conditions should be identifiable where relevant. Evidence Fitness Reassessment Material change may trigger reassessment. Possible reassessment outcomes include: Fitness Maintained Fitness Modified Conditional Fitness Additional Evidence Required Fitness Suspended Fitness Withdrawn This prevents outdated Evidence Fitness Determinations from remaining operationally active after their evidentiary basis has materially changed. Evidence Fitness Withdrawal An Evidence Fitness Determination may require withdrawal where: critical evidence becomes invalid, evidence applicability is lost, a material error is discovered, a critical gap emerges, evidence manipulation is identified, or another condition destroys the basis of the previous determination. Withdrawal must remain traceable. Evidence Fitness Continuity Where evidence progresses into later validation stages, its: identity, fitness status, conditions, limitations, gaps, uncertainty, restrictions, and applicable version should remain preserved. This creates Evidence Fitness Continuity across the VALIDOS™ lifecycle. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Consolidate Evidence Fitness Inputs Collect the governed outputs of: Evidence Relevance, Evidence Applicability, Evidence Coverage, and Evidence Adequacy. 2. Identify Material Conditions Identify: limitations, gaps, contradictions, uncertainty, dependencies, and restrictions. 3. Assess Materiality Determine which conditions are immaterial, material, critical, or progression-blocking. 4. Assess Validation-Role Proportionality Compare the complete evidence basis against: Validation Purpose, Validation Scope, Validation Criteria, Validation Depth, and intended validation role. 5. Establish Evidence Fitness Status Classify the evidence basis as: Evidence Fit, Evidence Conditionally Fit, Evidence Fitness Undetermined, Evidence Insufficient, or Evidence Unfit. 6. Establish Conditions and Boundaries Where applicable, define: fitness conditions, limitations, restrictions, validity period, and permitted downstream use. 7. Establish Reassessment Triggers Identify material changes requiring Evidence Fitness reassessment. 8. Create Evidence Fitness Record Preserve: Evidence Fitness Determination Identifier, Validation Object reference, Validation Purpose and Scope, Validation Criteria references, Validation Method Framework reference, evidence basis, relevance determination, applicability determination, coverage determination, adequacy determination, limitations, gaps, contradictions, uncertainty, dependencies, restrictions, fitness status, determination basis, effective period, reassessment triggers, version, changes, and sufficient lifecycle traceability. Evidence Fitness Governance Flow VEFDM completes the VEFS internal progression: Candidate Evidence → Relevance → Applicability → Coverage → Adequacy → Integrated Fitness Assessment → Evidence Fitness Determination → Qualified Evidence Basis This closes the evidence-fitness governance stage. Governance Outputs VEFDM may produce: Evidence Fitness Determination, Evidence Fitness Record, Qualified Evidence Basis, Evidence Fitness Status, Evidence Fitness Conditions Record, Evidence Fitness Limitation Record, Evidence Gap Integration Record, Evidence Contradiction Record, Evidence Uncertainty Record, Evidence Fitness Restriction Record, Evidence Fitness Expiration Condition, Evidence Fitness Reassessment Trigger, Evidence Fitness Change Record, Evidence Fitness Withdrawal Record, and Evidence Fitness Continuity Reference. Use Case 1 — Autonomous AI System Scenario An autonomous AI system has highly relevant and applicable operational evidence with strong coverage across normal and degraded conditions. However, evidence concerning one critical emergency override condition remains inadequate. Application VEFDM integrates the otherwise strong evidence basis with the critical inadequacy. Result The evidence cannot receive unrestricted Evidence Fit status merely because most other dimensions are strong. Depending upon Validation Purpose and required Validation Depth, it may receive: Evidence Conditionally Fit or: Evidence Insufficient until the critical evidentiary requirement is addressed. Use Case 2 — Financial Model Validation Scenario A financial model possesses extensive historical evidence with strong relevance, applicability, coverage, and adequacy for ordinary and stressed market conditions. New market behavior emerges that was not represented in the original evidence basis. Application The new condition creates a potential change in Evidence Fitness. Result VEFDM triggers reassessment rather than assuming that the historical Evidence Fitness Determination remains permanently valid. Architectural Position Validation Evidence Fitness Determination is the fifth and final internal governance space of the Validation Evidence Fitness Standard (VEFS). The complete VEFS progression is: Validation Evidence Relevance → Validation Evidence Applicability → Validation Evidence Coverage → Validation Evidence Adequacy → Validation Evidence Fitness Determination Together, these five governed spaces transform available information into a formally qualified evidence basis. The architectural transition is: Available Information ↓ Relevant Evidence ↓ Applicable Evidence ↓ Covered Evidence Basis ↓ Adequate Evidence Basis ↓ Qualified Evidence Basis ↓ Evidence Fitness Determination The resulting evidence basis can then proceed to the next VALIDOS™ governance question: Can the sources behind that evidence be sufficiently relied upon? Foundational Principle Evidence becomes fit for validation only when the complete evidentiary basis is fit for the role it is expected to perform. Canonical Closing Statement Validation Evidence Fitness Determination Module completes the evidence-fitness governance lifecycle within VALIDOS™ by integrating relevance, applicability, coverage, adequacy, limitations, gaps, contradictions, uncertainty, dependencies, proportionality, conditions, restrictions, change, and traceability into a formal Evidence Fitness Determination. VEFDM ensures that evidence progresses through validation only when its complete governed basis is demonstrably fit for the specific role it is expected to perform, while preserving a strict separation between evidence fitness, source reliability, validation execution, and the ultimate Validation Determination.
