title: Validation Execution Basis & Authorization Module (VEBAM)
text: Validation Execution Basis & Authorization Module (VEBAM) Validation Execution Basis & Authorization Module (VEBAM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VALIDOS™ — Validation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Validation Execution Standard (VEXS) Operational Layer: Validation Execution Governance Layer Category: AI & Interpretation Subcategory: Validation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Validation Execution Basis & Authorization Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 11 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS® · ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Validation Execution Basis & Authorization Canonical Definition Validation Execution Basis & Authorization Module (VEBAM) defines the governance framework for assembling, verifying, freezing, authorizing, and preserving the complete governed basis from which a specific Validation Execution may legitimately begin. It establishes the conditions under which the outputs of preceding VALIDOS™ governance stages become an identifiable, versioned, execution-ready, and authorized Validation Execution Basis. Operational Role VEBAM serves as the first internal governance space of the Validation Execution Standard. The preceding VALIDOS™ Parent Standards establish: Validation Object Validation Purpose & Scope Validation Criteria Validation Method Validation Evidence Fitness and: Validation Source Reliability VEBAM asks: Are the required validation components sufficiently established, mutually connected, current, and authorized for this specific Validation Execution to begin? The governed progression is: Governed Validation Components → Execution Prerequisite Review → Basis Assembly → Basis Consistency Check → Execution Instance Definition → Authorization Assessment → Basis Freeze → Authorized Validation Execution Basis VEBAM does not perform the validation. It establishes the governed starting condition from which validation may be performed. Module Operational Space VEBAM governs: Validation Execution Basis, execution prerequisites, execution readiness, execution authorization, execution instance identity, Validation Object reference, object-version reference, Validation Purpose reference, Validation Scope reference, Validation Depth reference, Validation Criteria references, Validation Method reference, Validation Evidence references, Validation Source references, Source Reliability conditions, execution-role requirements, resource readiness, instrument readiness, system readiness, environment prerequisites, authorization authority, authorization scope, authorization conditions, basis completeness, basis consistency, basis versioning, basis freeze, basis change, authorization change, authorization withdrawal, and execution-basis traceability. Module Function VEBAM applies immediately before operational validation execution begins. Its function is to prevent: execution beginning against an undefined Validation Object, execution using the wrong object version, obsolete Validation Criteria being used, unapproved methods entering execution, Validation Scope remaining ambiguous, insufficient Validation Depth being silently accepted, unqualified evidence entering execution, Source Reliability conditions being lost, execution beginning before required prerequisites exist, incompatible validation components being assembled, execution roles remaining undefined, unavailable resources being assumed available, unauthorized validation activity being represented as governed validation, and the validation basis changing silently after execution begins. Validation Execution Basis The Validation Execution Basis is the governed collection of validation components upon which a specific execution instance depends. It may contain: Validation Object reference, object version or state, Validation Purpose, Validation Scope, Validation Depth, applicable Validation Criteria, approved Validation Method, qualified Validation Evidence, Source Reliability information, source conditions, execution requirements, participant requirements, system requirements, instrument requirements, environmental requirements, execution controls, restrictions, and authorization conditions. The Validation Execution Basis creates the methodological starting state for execution. Execution Basis Is Not a Validation Plan A Validation Execution Basis and a validation plan are related but not identical. A plan may describe intended activities. The Execution Basis establishes the governed methodological conditions that authorize those activities to begin. VALIDOS™ therefore distinguishes: Execution Plan → What is intended to occur from: Validation Execution Basis → What governed validation structure permits execution to occur A plan cannot override the governed Validation Execution Basis. Execution Instance Identity Each material Validation Execution should be sufficiently identifiable as a distinct execution instance. An Execution Instance may be associated with: an identifier, Validation Object, object version, Validation Method version, execution date or period, responsible execution entity, environment, or another distinguishing attribute. This allows multiple executions of the same Validation Object to remain distinguishable. Object Reference VEBAM requires the Execution Basis to identify the exact Validation Object against which execution is authorized. The reference should remain connected to the object established under the Validation Object Standard. Where object identity cannot be sufficiently established, execution should not silently proceed. Object Version & State Reference Where validation depends upon version, configuration, release, state, or temporal condition, the relevant object instance must be explicit. VALIDOS™ establishes: Authorization to validate one object state does not automatically authorize validation of another materially different state. Purpose Continuity The Validation Purpose established earlier must remain connected to execution. Execution activity should not silently drift toward a different purpose. For example: Validation authorized to determine: functional performance should not silently become validation of: regulatory compliance unless the required governance basis for that purpose has also been established. Scope Continuity The authorized Validation Scope establishes what execution may legitimately cover. VEBAM therefore identifies: included scope, excluded scope, applicable boundaries, temporal boundaries, system boundaries, population boundaries, or other relevant limits. This creates the baseline against which later execution deviations can be assessed. Validation Depth Continuity Validation Depth affects how extensively the Validation Object must be examined. VEBAM ensures that the required depth remains attached to execution. Execution should not silently substitute: limited validation for: deep validation while preserving the appearance of the original validation objective. Criteria Set The applicable Validation Criteria must be sufficiently established before execution begins. VEBAM creates an identifiable criteria set connecting the Execution Basis to the criteria that execution is expected to evaluate. The criteria set may include: mandatory criteria, conditional criteria, optional supporting criteria, criterion priority, criterion applicability, or other governed relationships. Criteria Version Where Validation Criteria change over time, the applicable criteria version must remain explicit. This prevents a later criteria revision from being incorrectly represented as the basis under which an earlier execution occurred. Method Reference The Validation Execution Basis must identify the approved Validation Method. Where multiple methods exist, the exact: method, version, configuration, procedure, test protocol, analytical process, or other relevant methodological instance should be sufficiently identifiable. Method Eligibility Continuity Where the Validation Method Standard established eligibility conditions, those conditions must remain satisfied when execution begins. A method that was previously eligible may become inappropriate if: the Validation Object changes, the Validation Scope changes, evidence availability changes, environmental conditions change, or required systems become unavailable. VEBAM therefore checks that the methodological basis remains current. Validation Evidence Reference Evidence intended for execution should remain connected to the evidence objects qualified under Validation Evidence Fitness governance. The Execution Basis may identify: required evidence, supporting evidence, optional evidence, evidence versions, evidence limitations, evidence validity periods, and Evidence Fitness conditions. This prevents unqualified evidence from entering execution without visibility. Source Reliability Reference Where evidence depends upon Validation Sources, VEBAM preserves the relevant Source Reliability conditions. These may include: Source Reliability Status, source-role restrictions, required corroboration, reliability limitations, independence conditions, source version, source validity period, or reassessment requirements. Prerequisite Governance Before execution begins, VEBAM determines whether material prerequisites have been sufficiently established. Prerequisites may include: approved method, qualified evidence, reliable or conditionally reliable sources, available instruments, required systems, required data, competent participants, required access, environmental conditions, authorization, or another validation-specific requirement. Prerequisite Status A prerequisite may be classified as: Satisfied Conditionally Satisfied Unsatisfied or: Undetermined A critical Unsatisfied or Undetermined prerequisite may prevent authorization. Resource Readiness Validation execution may require resources such as: personnel, compute, laboratories, testing environments, datasets, instruments, infrastructure, time, or external services. VEBAM determines whether required resources are sufficiently available for the intended execution. Resource availability does not itself establish methodological validity. It establishes execution readiness. Instrument Readiness Where instruments materially affect validation, readiness may require: correct instrument identity, calibration, required configuration, operating range, maintenance status, software version, or another applicable condition. An instrument that exists but is not ready should not be assumed execution-ready. System Readiness Validation may depend upon: software, testing platforms, AI systems, simulation environments, data pipelines, monitoring systems, or infrastructure. VEBAM may establish whether required systems are available in the correct state and configuration. Environment Readiness Some Validation Methods require defined environmental conditions. These may include: physical conditions, network conditions, operational state, simulation settings, controlled access, geographic conditions, or another relevant environment. VEBAM establishes whether the required environment is sufficiently available before execution begins. Participant Readiness Where human or machine participants perform material validation roles, VEBAM may establish: required role, identity, authority, competence requirement, availability, system permission, or another prerequisite. Participant readiness does not replace Source Capability or accountability governance. It ensures that required execution roles can actually be performed. Basis Completeness A Validation Execution Basis should contain sufficient information for execution to begin without relying upon material unstated assumptions. Possible completeness conditions include: Basis Complete Basis Conditionally Complete Basis Partially Complete Basis Incomplete Basis Completeness Undetermined Completeness requirements should remain proportionate to validation consequence. Basis Consistency A complete basis may still contain contradictions. VEBAM therefore assesses whether its components are materially consistent. Examples of inconsistency include: criteria requiring evidence not available, method incompatible with object type, Validation Depth inconsistent with method capability, evidence version inconsistent with object version, Source Reliability restriction incompatible with intended source role, or scope broader than authorized execution capability. Material inconsistencies must remain visible. Basis Conflict A Basis Conflict exists where two or more governed execution components impose materially incompatible requirements. A conflict may require: correction, escalation, method revision, scope revision, evidence replacement, source reassessment, or another governance action. Execution should not resolve material Basis Conflicts silently. Execution Readiness VEBAM may establish an Execution Readiness condition such as: Execution Ready All material prerequisites and basis requirements are sufficiently established. Execution Conditionally Ready Execution may proceed only under explicit conditions. Execution Readiness Undetermined Available information is insufficient to establish readiness. Execution Not Ready Material prerequisites remain unsatisfied. Readiness does not itself authorize execution where separate authorization is required. Execution Authorization Execution Authorization establishes that a defined Validation Execution Instance may legitimately proceed under the approved Validation Execution Basis. Authorization should identify, where applicable: authorization authority, authorized Validation Object, authorized scope, authorized method, applicable conditions, restrictions, effective period, and authorization status. Authorization Authority The entity granting authorization must possess sufficient authority for the relevant validation context. Authority may derive from: governance structure, organizational role, contractual authority, regulatory authority, methodological governance, delegated authority, or another legitimate basis. VEBAM does not create external legal authority. It records and governs the authority relationship used to initiate validation execution. Authorization Scope Authorization should be bounded. It may authorize: one Validation Object, one object version, one Validation Scope, one Validation Method, one execution environment, one execution period, or another defined set of conditions. Authorization should not silently extend beyond its governed scope. Conditional Authorization Execution may be authorized subject to conditions. Examples include: specific evidence must remain available, a source requires independent corroboration, execution must occur within a defined environment, a specified participant must be present, or a particular control must remain active. Conditional authorization remains valid only while its material conditions remain satisfied. Authorization Status VEBAM may establish: Authorized Conditionally Authorized Authorization Pending Authorization Denied Authorization Suspended or: Authorization Withdrawn These statuses govern permission to execute. They do not represent Validation State. Basis Freeze Immediately before execution begins, the material Validation Execution Basis should be sufficiently frozen or version-fixed. A Basis Freeze establishes the exact governed configuration under which execution began. This may include: object version, criteria version, method version, evidence set, source conditions, execution requirements, and authorization conditions. Freeze does not prohibit change. It makes subsequent change visible. Why Basis Freeze Matters Without a Basis Freeze, a validation process may change its methodological foundation during execution while later presenting the final configuration as if it had governed the complete process. VEBAM prevents this. VALIDOS™ establishes: Execution history must preserve the basis that actually governed execution at the time it occurred. Basis Versioning Materially different Execution Bases should remain distinguishable. For example: Execution Basis 1.0 Execution Basis 1.1 Execution Basis 2.0 The versioning structure may vary by implementation. The governance requirement is that material basis changes remain reconstructable. Basis Change After Basis Freeze, a material change may involve: Validation Object, scope, criteria, method, evidence, source, environment, participant, instrument, system, or authorization condition. Such change becomes an execution-governance event. Depending upon materiality, it may require: updated authorization, controlled deviation, new Basis version, execution restart, partial re-execution, or complete revalidation. Authorization Change Authorization may change because of: scope expansion, scope reduction, new authority, changed method, object change, source change, environmental change, or another material condition. Authorization changes should remain historically traceable. Authorization Suspension Execution authorization may be temporarily suspended where a material condition arises that requires review. Examples include: prerequisite failure, instrument issue, source reliability concern, unexpected object change, safety concern, or governance conflict. Suspension does not automatically terminate the validation. It pauses authorization until the relevant condition is resolved. Authorization Withdrawal Authorization may be withdrawn where the basis for legitimate execution no longer exists. Withdrawal may require: stopping execution, preserving existing records, assessing already performed activities, and determining whether reauthorization or new execution is necessary. Unauthorized Execution Validation activity performed without required authorization may still produce factual observations. However, it should not automatically be represented as a governed VALIDOS™ Validation Execution. VALIDOS™ therefore distinguishes: Activity Occurred from: Governed Validation Execution Authorized Authorization Does Not Guarantee Valid Execution Authorization establishes permission to begin. It does not prove that execution will later be: complete, conformant, correctly sequenced, deviation-free, or methodologically valid. Therefore: Authorized Execution ≠ Conformant Execution Subsequent VEXS modules govern actual execution behavior. Basis Traceability VEBAM creates traceability between: Validation Object → Purpose & Scope → Criteria → Method → Evidence → Sources → Execution Requirements → Authorization → Execution Instance This becomes the baseline against which actual execution can later be compared. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Identify Validation Execution Instance Create a distinguishable reference for the intended execution. 2. Assemble Validation Execution Basis Connect the relevant: Validation Object, Purpose, Scope, Depth, Criteria, Method, Evidence, Sources, conditions, and restrictions. 3. Verify Prerequisites Determine whether required execution prerequisites are satisfied. 4. Assess Basis Completeness Determine whether the basis contains sufficient information for execution. 5. Assess Basis Consistency Identify contradictions, incompatibilities, or Basis Conflicts. 6. Determine Execution Readiness Establish whether execution is Ready, Conditionally Ready, Undetermined, or Not Ready. 7. Establish Execution Authorization Determine whether the defined execution instance may legitimately begin. 8. Freeze and Version the Basis Preserve the exact governed basis applicable at execution start. 9. Preserve Lifecycle Traceability Maintain: Execution Instance reference, Validation Object reference, object version, Purpose, Scope, Depth, Criteria set, Method reference, Evidence references, Source Reliability references, prerequisites, readiness status, authorization, conditions, restrictions, Basis version, Basis Freeze, changes, suspensions, withdrawals, and sufficient lifecycle traceability. Governance Outputs VEBAM may produce: Validation Execution Instance Identifier, Validation Execution Basis, Validation Execution Basis Record, Execution Prerequisite Register, Execution Prerequisite Status, Execution Resource Readiness Record, Instrument Readiness Record, System Readiness Record, Environment Readiness Record, Participant Readiness Record, Basis Completeness Assessment, Basis Consistency Assessment, Basis Conflict Record, Execution Readiness Status, Validation Execution Authorization, Authorization Scope, Authorization Condition Record, Authorization Status, Validation Execution Basis Version, Basis Freeze Record, Basis Change Record, Authorization Change Record, Authorization Suspension Record, Authorization Withdrawal Record, and Execution Basis Traceability Record. Use Case 1 — AI Model Validation Scenario An organization intends to validate a new AI model release. The validation methodology has already been approved. Application VEBAM establishes that: the Validation Object is Model Version 4.2, the approved criteria apply to Version 4.2, the correct benchmark evidence is available, source-reliability conditions remain current, the required testing environment is ready, and the approved method version is identifiable. The complete basis is frozen as Execution Basis 1.0 and authorized. Result Validation begins against a reconstructable methodological baseline rather than a loosely defined testing plan. Use Case 2 — Industrial Equipment Validation Scenario A validation is scheduled for an industrial component. The required measurement instrument exists, but its calibration expired before execution. Application VEBAM identifies the calibration requirement as an unsatisfied execution prerequisite. Result The validation remains: Execution Not Ready until the instrument condition is resolved. The existence of the instrument is not mistaken for instrument readiness. Use Case 3 — Healthcare Validation Scenario A healthcare validation has an approved method, qualified evidence, and competent participants. However, one critical evidence source has become subject to a newly identified Source Reliability restriction requiring independent corroboration. Application VEBAM propagates the new source condition into the Execution Basis. Result Execution may become: Conditionally Ready and: Conditionally Authorized subject to the required corroboration. The earlier source assessment is not silently treated as permanently valid. Architectural Position Validation Execution Basis & Authorization is the first internal governance space of the Validation Execution Standard (VEXS). It establishes the transition: Governed Validation Design → Authorized Validation Execution Basis The next execution-governance stage can then ask: How is that authorized basis instantiated into actual validation activity against the Validation Object under real execution conditions? The VEXS internal progression therefore begins: Execution Basis & Authorization → Execution Instantiation & Control → Execution Observation & Traceability → Deviation & Exception Governance → Execution Completeness & Conformity Foundational Principle Validation execution should not begin until the basis governing what may be executed is identifiable, internally coherent, sufficiently ready, and appropriately authorized. Canonical Closing Statement Validation Execution Basis & Authorization Module establishes the governed starting condition for operational validation within VALIDOS™ by transforming previously established Validation Object, Purpose, Scope, Criteria, Method, Evidence, and Source Reliability information into an identifiable, consistent, versioned, execution-ready, and authorized Validation Execution Basis. Through prerequisite governance, readiness assessment, authorization, basis freezing, version control, change governance, and lifecycle traceability, VEBAM ensures that validation execution begins from a reconstructable methodological foundation rather than from procedural assumption, incomplete preparation, or undefined authority. title: Validation Execution Completeness & Conformity Module (VECCM)
text: Validation Execution Completeness & Conformity Module (VECCM) Validation Execution Completeness & Conformity Module (VECCM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VALIDOS™ — Validation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Validation Execution Standard (VEXS) Operational Layer: Validation Execution Governance Layer Category: AI & Interpretation Subcategory: Validation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Validation Execution Completeness & Conformity Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 11 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS® · ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Validation Execution Completeness & Conformity Canonical Definition Validation Execution Completeness & Conformity Module (VECCM) defines the governance framework for determining whether a Validation Execution Instance has performed the materially required validation activities with sufficient completeness, conformity, continuity, control, reconstructability, and resolution of material deviations to support progression into formal Validation Determination. It establishes the final execution-governance gate through which the Actual Validation Execution Record is compared against the Authorized Validation Execution Basis and classified according to its methodological fitness for subsequent determination. Operational Role VECCM serves as the fifth and final internal governance space of the Validation Execution Standard. The preceding modules establish: VEBAM — Validation Execution Basis & Authorization VEICM — Validation Execution Instantiation & Control VEOTM — Validation Execution Observation & Traceability VEDEGM — Validation Execution Deviation & Exception Governance VECCM asks: Considering what was authorized, what was actually performed, what can be reconstructed, and which deviations remain, is the complete validation execution sufficiently complete and conformant to support a legitimate Validation Determination? The governed progression is: Authorized Execution Basis → Actual Execution Record → Completeness Assessment → Conformity Assessment → Residual Deviation Assessment → Reconstruction Assessment → Determination Readiness → Execution Conformity Determination VECCM does not determine whether the Validation Object satisfies the Validation Criteria. It determines whether the validation execution itself is methodologically usable for that later determination. Module Operational Space VECCM governs: execution completeness, execution conformity, execution coverage, required-activity completion, criteria-execution completeness, method-step completeness, execution continuity, object continuity, scope conformity, method conformity, evidence-use conformity, source-condition conformity, configuration conformity, control conformity, sequence conformity, participant-role conformity, reconstruction sufficiency, traceability sufficiency, residual deviation impact, unresolved exception impact, execution integrity readiness, conditional conformity, execution invalidity, Determination Readiness, Determination Block, execution completion status, execution conformity status, execution reassessment, and execution-conformity traceability. Module Function VECCM applies when material validation execution activities have ended, been terminated, or reached a stage where progression to Validation Determination is being considered. Its function is to prevent: partially executed validation being represented as complete, complete activity counts being mistaken for methodological conformity, unresolved deviations disappearing at execution closure, missing criteria being hidden by successful execution elsewhere, scope reduction being forgotten, wrong object versions being overlooked, incomplete traceability being ignored, source restrictions being lost, execution under changed configurations being treated as equivalent, failed or omitted activities being silently excluded, and a final Validation Determination being issued where the execution record cannot legitimately support one. Completeness and Conformity Are Different VALIDOS™ establishes a strict distinction: Execution Completeness asks: Were the materially required validation activities actually performed? Execution Conformity asks: Were those activities performed with sufficient correspondence to the Authorized Validation Execution Basis? A validation execution may therefore be: Complete but Non-Conformant or: Conformant in performed activities but Incomplete overall For example: Every executed test may follow the method perfectly, while one mandatory test was never performed. That execution is not complete. Likewise, every required activity may have occurred, but several were conducted against the wrong configuration. That execution may be complete but materially non-conformant. Execution Completeness Execution Completeness evaluates whether all materially required validation activities have been addressed. This may include completeness across: Validation Scope, Validation Criteria, method steps, required evidence interactions, required source interactions, required operating conditions, required scenarios, required repetitions, required observations, required reviews, and required controls. Completeness should remain proportionate to the approved Validation Purpose and Validation Depth. Required Activity Completion A required activity may be classified as: Completed Conditionally Completed Partially Completed Not Completed Not Applicable or: Completion Undetermined These classifications should remain traceable to the execution basis. Criteria Execution Completeness Every material Validation Criterion requiring execution should have sufficient execution activity associated with it. VECCM asks: Was the criterion actually examined? Were all required activities performed? Were required conditions represented? Was execution sufficient for later criterion determination? Are material parts of the criterion still unsupported? This does not determine whether the criterion was satisfied. Method-Step Completeness Where the Validation Method requires a defined sequence or set of steps, VECCM determines whether materially required steps were completed. Missing non-critical procedural detail may not always block determination. Missing a methodologically essential step may. Materiality must therefore remain explicit. Scope Completeness Validation execution must be compared against the approved Validation Scope. Possible conditions include: Scope Fully Executed Scope Conditionally Executed Scope Partially Executed Scope Materially Reduced or: Scope Execution Undetermined Where actual execution covers less than the authorized scope, later Validation Determination must remain bounded accordingly. Validation Depth Completeness VECCM assesses whether execution achieved the required Validation Depth. A validation may perform all nominal activities while failing to achieve the depth required for: high-consequence reliance, enhanced assurance, regulatory use, critical deployment, or another governed purpose. Therefore: Activity Completion ≠ Required Validation Depth Achieved Execution Conformity Execution Conformity evaluates the degree to which Actual Validation Execution corresponds to the Authorized Validation Execution Basis. Conformity may include: correct Validation Object, correct object version, approved scope, approved method, approved configuration, required sequence, required evidence, governed sources, required controls, authorized participants, required environment, and applicable restrictions. Object Conformity VECCM verifies whether execution remained sufficiently connected to the Validation Object authorized for validation. Relevant questions include: Was the correct object examined? Was the correct version used? Did the object materially change during execution? Were material state changes governed? Did outputs remain attributable to the correct object state? A critical object mismatch may invalidate affected execution. Scope Conformity Execution may move outside or inside the authorized scope. VECCM determines whether: required scope was preserved, unauthorized scope expansion occurred, material scope reduction occurred, exclusions were governed, and actual scope can be reliably defined. Method Conformity VECCM evaluates whether the instantiated and performed method remained sufficiently aligned with the approved Validation Method. This includes consideration of: required method steps, parameters, sequence, repetition, comparison structure, analytical conditions, simulation conditions, or another method-specific requirement. Configuration Conformity Validation may depend materially upon: model configuration, system settings, instrument settings, environment settings, software versions, dataset versions, or simulation configurations. VECCM determines whether actual configurations remained sufficiently aligned with those authorized. Evidence-Use Conformity VECCM assesses whether validation used evidence in accordance with its approved role and Evidence Fitness conditions. This may include: correct evidence identity, evidence version, permitted role, applicability conditions, temporal validity, scope limitations, and any conditional fitness requirements. Source-Condition Conformity Where sources were subject to Source Reliability conditions, VECCM determines whether execution respected those conditions. For example: A source approved only with independent corroboration should not be treated as unrestricted if the required corroboration was never performed. Control Conformity Required controls may include: access controls, logging, environmental control, sequence control, oversight, configuration locks, safety controls, or validation-specific controls. VECCM determines whether required controls were sufficiently active across the activities they were intended to govern. Sequence Conformity Where sequence matters methodologically, VECCM assesses whether activities occurred in the required order. Sequence deviation may affect only one activity or the validity of a larger methodological chain. Participant-Role Conformity VECCM may assess whether material validation activities were performed by participants or systems possessing the required execution role. This may include: authorization, role boundaries, competence conditions, independence requirements, or permitted intervention rights where those conditions formed part of the Execution Basis. Execution Continuity Execution Continuity concerns whether the validation process remained sufficiently connected across its material stages. Continuity may be affected by: long interruptions, object changes, evidence replacement, source change, environment change, configuration change, participant change, or execution restart. A resumed execution should not automatically be treated as continuous where material conditions changed. Traceability Sufficiency VECCM consumes VEOTM outputs to determine whether the execution history is sufficiently traceable for conformity assessment. A validation may have been performed correctly but lack sufficient records to demonstrate that fact. VALIDOS™ establishes: Correct Execution That Cannot Be Demonstrated ≠ Fully Governed Execution where demonstrability is required for the intended validation role. Reconstruction Sufficiency VECCM asks whether a qualified reviewer or system can sufficiently reconstruct: what occurred, against which object, using which method, with which evidence, from which sources, under which conditions, in what sequence, with which deviations, and with which outputs. Reconstruction need not be perfect. It must be sufficient for the intended Validation Determination. Residual Deviation Assessment VECCM consumes the complete deviation and exception record established under VEDEGM. It determines what residual effects remain after: correction, compensation, re-execution, escalation, or closure. A closed deviation may still leave a material methodological limitation. Resolved Does Not Mean Immaterial VALIDOS™ establishes: Deviation Resolved ≠ Deviation Never Mattered A resolved deviation may continue to affect: scope, interpretation, confidence, evidence use, or later reliance. Residual impact must remain visible. Unresolved Deviation A material unresolved deviation may prevent unrestricted Execution Conformity. Depending upon materiality, it may lead to: Conditional Conformity, Non-Conformity, Determination Block, or Execution Invalidity. Cumulative Deviation Assessment VECCM evaluates whether multiple minor or moderate deviations collectively create a material conformity problem. This prevents fragmented exception handling from missing system-level execution degradation. Execution Completeness Status VECCM may establish: Execution Complete All materially required validation activities have been sufficiently performed. Execution Conditionally Complete Execution is complete only within explicit boundaries, limitations, or reduced scope. Execution Partially Complete Material validation activities remain unperformed. Execution Incomplete The execution cannot reasonably be treated as complete for the intended Validation Purpose. Execution Completeness Undetermined Available records are insufficient to establish completeness. Execution Conformity Status VECCM may establish: Execution Conformant Actual validation execution sufficiently corresponds to the Authorized Validation Execution Basis for the intended determination. Execution Conditionally Conformant Execution may support Validation Determination only under explicit conditions, limitations, scope restrictions, or interpretive boundaries. Execution Conformity Undetermined Available information is insufficient to establish whether execution was sufficiently conformant. Execution Non-Conformant Material execution conditions departed from the authorized basis sufficiently to prevent unrestricted methodological reliance. Execution Invalid Critical execution deficiencies prevent the affected execution from legitimately supporting the intended Validation Determination. These states describe execution. They do not describe the Validation Object. Conditional Conformity Conditional Conformity may arise where: one validation condition remains limited, scope was reduced, one source required restriction, a deviation was compensated but leaves residual uncertainty, a subset of criteria remains usable, or validation can support only a narrower determination than originally intended. Conditions must remain attached to the subsequent Validation Determination. Partial Execution Validity Where execution is partly valid and partly invalid, VALIDOS™ should avoid unnecessary all-or-nothing treatment where methodological separation is possible. VECCM may identify: Valid Execution Portion and: Invalid or Unusable Execution Portion provided the boundaries can be reliably established. This supports precise remediation and partial re-execution. Execution Invalidity Execution Invalidity should be reserved for conditions that fundamentally prevent legitimate methodological use of affected execution. Potential causes include: wrong Validation Object, critical object-version mismatch, critical method failure, irrecoverable sequence corruption, critical evidence discontinuity, critical source-condition failure, untraceable critical activity, severe uncontrolled deviation, or inability to reconstruct the execution sufficiently. Invalid Execution Does Not Mean Invalid Object VALIDOS™ establishes one of its strongest distinctions: Execution Invalid ≠ Validation Object Invalid Invalid execution means the validation process cannot legitimately establish the intended conclusion. The Validation Object may still satisfy or fail the Validation Criteria. VALIDOS™ simply does not claim to know on the basis of that execution. Conformant Execution Can Demonstrate Failure Conversely: Execution Conformant + Criterion Failure = Legitimate Negative Validation Finding A validation process should not be judged by whether it produces a positive result. It should be judged by whether it produces a legitimate result. Determination Readiness VECCM creates the final execution gate into Validation Determination. A Validation Execution Instance may be considered Determination Ready where sufficient basis exists to determine: what was executed, which criteria were examined, which execution outputs exist, how complete execution was, how conformant execution was, which deviations occurred, what limitations remain, and which portions of the execution may legitimately support determination. Determination Readiness Status Possible statuses may include: Determination Ready Execution is sufficiently complete, conformant, reconstructable, and governed to support Validation Determination. Determination Conditionally Ready Determination may proceed only within explicit conditions, restrictions, limitations, or reduced scope. Determination Readiness Undetermined Available execution information is insufficient to determine readiness. Determination Not Ready Material execution deficiencies must be resolved before legitimate determination can occur. Determination Blocked One or more critical execution conditions prevent Validation Determination from legitimately proceeding. Determination Block A Determination Block prevents the architecture from converting deficient execution into a validity conclusion. Potential triggers include: critical missing validation activity, wrong Validation Object, critical scope failure, execution invalidity, unreconstructable critical activity, unresolved critical deviation, critical method substitution, or another execution condition destroying the methodological basis for determination. Determination Block Is Not Object Failure A Determination Block means: VALIDOS™ cannot legitimately determine the object's validation result from this execution. It does not mean: The object failed validation. This preserves methodological neutrality. Execution Completion Record VECCM may establish a formal Validation Execution Completion Record containing: Execution Instance, Validation Object reference, actual scope, actual Validation Depth, executed criteria, method execution summary, evidence used, sources used, execution outputs, deviations, exceptions, residual limitations, Execution Completeness Status, Execution Conformity Status, reconstruction status, Determination Readiness, and any Determination Block. Execution Closure Execution may be formally closed when: active execution has ended, material outputs are preserved, material deviations have status, completeness is assessed, conformity is assessed, residual limitations are recorded, and Determination Readiness has been established. Closure does not erase the possibility of later reassessment. Execution Reassessment Execution completeness or conformity may require reassessment if: new execution records emerge, a previously unknown deviation is discovered, a source is later found unreliable, evidence fitness changes, a configuration discrepancy is discovered, a traceability error is corrected, or another material fact changes the execution picture. Execution Conformity Change A prior Conformant determination may become: Conditionally Conformant Non-Conformant or: Invalid if new material information emerges. Likewise, an initially uncertain execution may later become conformant after missing records or corrective execution become available. Historical Execution Preservation Reassessment should not erase earlier conformity determinations. The record should preserve: Original Determination → New Information → Reassessment → Revised Determination This creates methodological continuity and auditability. Execution Handoff to Validation Determination VECCM closes the Validation Execution lifecycle and passes forward a structured execution basis containing: actual performed activities, execution outputs, execution limitations, conformity conditions, residual deviations, scope boundaries, completeness status, and Determination Readiness. The next Parent Standard can then ask: What does this governed validation record actually demonstrate about the Validation Object? Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Establish Actual Execution Scope Determine what portion of the authorized validation scope was actually executed. 2. Assess Required Activity Completion Determine whether materially required validation activities and method steps were completed. 3. Assess Criteria Execution Completeness Determine whether each applicable Validation Criterion possesses sufficient execution activity for later determination. 4. Assess Execution Conformity Compare Actual Validation Execution against the Authorized Validation Execution Basis across: object, scope, method, configuration, evidence, sources, sequence, controls, environment, and participant roles. 5. Assess Reconstruction & Traceability Determine whether material execution history can be sufficiently reconstructed. 6. Integrate Deviations & Exceptions Assess unresolved, residual, cumulative, and critical execution deviations. 7. Establish Completeness Status Classify execution completeness. 8. Establish Conformity Status Classify execution conformity. 9. Establish Determination Readiness Determine whether Validation Determination may: proceed, proceed conditionally, remain pending, or be blocked. 10. Preserve Lifecycle Traceability Maintain: Execution Instance, Authorized Execution Basis, Actual Execution Scope, executed criteria, completed method steps, evidence used, sources used, execution outputs, traceability assessment, reconstruction assessment, deviations, exceptions, residual limitations, Execution Completeness Status, Execution Conformity Status, Determination Readiness, Determination Blocks, reassessments, versions, and sufficient lifecycle continuity. Governance Outputs VECCM may produce: Validation Execution Completeness Assessment, Required Activity Completion Map, Validation Criteria Execution Completeness Map, Method-Step Completion Record, Actual Validation Scope Record, Validation Depth Execution Assessment, Object Conformity Assessment, Scope Conformity Assessment, Method Conformity Assessment, Configuration Conformity Assessment, Evidence-Use Conformity Assessment, Source-Condition Conformity Assessment, Control Conformity Assessment, Sequence Conformity Assessment, Participant-Role Conformity Assessment, Execution Continuity Assessment, Traceability Sufficiency Assessment, Reconstruction Sufficiency Assessment, Residual Deviation Assessment, Cumulative Deviation Assessment, Execution Completeness Status, Execution Conformity Status, Valid Execution Portion Record, Invalid Execution Portion Record, Validation Execution Completion Record, Determination Readiness Status, Determination Block, Execution Closure Record, Execution Reassessment Record, and Execution Conformity Change Record. Use Case 1 — AI Model Validation Scenario An AI model completes 98 of 100 planned validation activities. The two omitted tests concern a critical autonomous-escalation criterion. All other activities were performed correctly. Application VECCM does not classify the execution as complete merely because 98% of activities were performed. The missing activities are evaluated according to their methodological significance. Result Execution may be: Partially Complete and: Determination Not Ready for the affected criterion despite otherwise strong execution conformity. Use Case 2 — Industrial System Validation Scenario All required industrial validation tests are completed, but one section of testing was performed after an unauthorized configuration change. Application VECCM distinguishes completeness from conformity. Result Execution may be: Execution Complete but: Execution Conditionally Conformant or: Execution Non-Conformant for the affected section, depending upon materiality. The relevant portion may require re-execution without discarding unaffected activities. Use Case 3 — Autonomous Validation Agent Scenario An autonomous validation agent completes every required test and generates extensive records. Later review discovers that several high-risk tests used an unapproved tool outside the authorized execution configuration. Application VECCM integrates: complete activity coverage, traceability, the tool-related deviation, affected criteria, and residual methodological impact. Result The validation cannot derive unrestricted confidence merely from complete automation. The affected execution portion is classified according to conformity rather than activity count. Architectural Position Validation Execution Completeness & Conformity is the fifth and final internal governance space of the Validation Execution Standard (VEXS). The complete VEXS progression is: Validation Execution Basis & Authorization → Validation Execution Instantiation & Control → Validation Execution Observation & Traceability → Validation Execution Deviation & Exception Governance → Validation Execution Completeness & Conformity Together, these five governed spaces transform an approved validation design into a demonstrable and methodologically classified Validation Execution Record. The lifecycle progresses: Authorized Validation Basis ↓ Controlled Execution Instance ↓ Observed & Reconstructable Execution ↓ Governed Deviations & Exceptions ↓ Execution Completeness & Conformity ↓ Determination Readiness The next VALIDOS™ Parent Standard can therefore address a fundamentally different question: What does the complete governed validation record actually demonstrate about the Validation Object? Foundational Principle Validation execution becomes usable for determination only when what was required, what was performed, and what can be demonstrated are sufficiently aligned. Canonical Closing Statement Validation Execution Completeness & Conformity Module completes the execution-governance lifecycle within VALIDOS™ by determining whether actual validation activity is sufficiently complete, conformant, reconstructable, controlled, and methodologically usable for subsequent Validation Determination. By governing required-activity completion, criteria execution, scope and depth, object and method conformity, evidence and source conditions, configurations, controls, sequencing, traceability, residual deviations, conditional conformity, execution invalidity, Determination Readiness, Determination Blocks, reassessment, and lifecycle continuity, VECCM ensures that VALIDOS™ advances from execution to determination only when the operational validation record can legitimately support the conclusion it is being asked to produce. title: Validation Execution Deviation & Exception Governance Module (VEDEGM)
text: Validation Execution Deviation & Exception Governance Module (VEDEGM) Validation Execution Deviation & Exception Governance Module (VEDEGM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VALIDOS™ — Validation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Validation Execution Standard (VEXS) Operational Layer: Validation Execution Governance Layer Category: AI & Interpretation Subcategory: Validation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Validation Execution Deviation & Exception Governance Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 11 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS® · ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Validation Execution Deviation & Exception Governance Canonical Definition Validation Execution Deviation & Exception Governance Module (VEDEGM) defines the governance framework for identifying, classifying, assessing, authorizing, containing, correcting, escalating, documenting, and resolving material departures, anomalies, interruptions, substitutions, control losses, unexpected conditions, execution failures, and other exceptions occurring during a Validation Execution Instance. It establishes the conditions under which differences between the Authorized Validation Execution Basis and Actual Validation Execution become explicit, traceable, and governable execution events rather than hidden methodological drift. Operational Role VEDEGM serves as the fourth internal governance space of the Validation Execution Standard. The preceding modules establish: VEBAM — What basis authorizes validation execution? VEICM — How is that basis instantiated and controlled? VEOTM — What actually occurred, and can execution be reconstructed? VEDEGM asks: Where did actual execution depart from the governed basis, what exceptions occurred, how material were they, and what governance response is required? The governed progression is: Observed Execution → Difference Detection → Deviation Identification → Exception Classification → Materiality Assessment → Authorization Assessment → Impact Assessment → Response & Escalation → Resolution → Execution Deviation Record VEDEGM does not issue the final Execution Conformity Determination. It establishes the governed deviation and exception record upon which that determination depends. Module Operational Space VEDEGM governs: execution deviations, execution exceptions, anomaly detection, execution divergence, execution drift, procedural deviation, sequence deviation, scope deviation, object deviation, configuration deviation, evidence substitution, source substitution, method-step substitution, instrument substitution, participant substitution, environment deviation, access deviation, control loss, control degradation, control bypass, interruption, execution failure, unexpected condition, deviation authorization, exception authorization, deviation materiality, exception materiality, deviation impact, exception impact, deviation containment, corrective execution, compensating controls, escalation, resolution, unresolved deviations, cumulative deviation, deviation recurrence, deviation closure, and deviation-and-exception traceability. Module Function VEDEGM applies whenever actual validation execution differs materially or potentially materially from the approved Execution Basis or expected execution conditions. Its function is to prevent: deviations remaining undocumented, execution drift being normalized, unauthorized substitutions becoming invisible, interruptions being treated as irrelevant, failed validation activities being silently omitted, control losses being forgotten after recovery, deviations being accepted without impact assessment, authorized changes being treated as methodologically harmless automatically, repeated minor deviations accumulating without governance, anomalous outputs being ignored because the final result appears favorable, and execution exceptions being converted directly into Validation Object failure or success. Deviation and Exception Are Related but Distinct VALIDOS™ distinguishes: Execution Deviation from: Execution Exception An Execution Deviation is a departure from an approved, expected, required, or controlled execution condition. An Execution Exception is a material event, anomaly, failure, interruption, unexpected state, or condition requiring governance attention whether or not it represents a formal departure from the approved method. For example: A different instrument than the one approved may be a deviation. An unexpected system crash during an approved test may be an exception. An event may be both. Deviation Detection Deviation governance begins with the ability to compare: Authorized Execution Basis against: Observed Actual Execution Relevant signals may come from: execution records, control-state logs, operator observations, automated monitoring, object-state changes, configuration snapshots, evidence-use records, source-use records, method-step traceability, or another execution artifact. Deviation Identity A material deviation should be sufficiently identifiable. A Deviation Record may establish: Deviation Identifier, Execution Instance, affected activity, affected criterion, expected condition, actual condition, time, actor or system, affected evidence, affected source, affected method step, affected control, initial classification, and current status. Deviation Types VEDEGM may distinguish different deviation types. Object Deviation The Validation Object, version, configuration, or state differs from the authorized basis. Scope Deviation Execution moves outside, omits, narrows, or otherwise alters the approved Validation Scope. Method Deviation Actual execution departs from the approved Validation Method. Sequence Deviation Required validation activities occur in a materially different order. Configuration Deviation A system, model, instrument, environment, or validation configuration changes materially. Evidence Deviation Different, missing, expired, altered, or unqualified evidence is used. Source Deviation A source changes, becomes unavailable, exceeds its approved role, or loses a required reliability condition. Participant Deviation A material execution role is performed by a different or unauthorized participant or system. Control Deviation A required execution control becomes inactive, degraded, bypassed, or unavailable. Environment Deviation Execution occurs under conditions materially different from those required. These categories may overlap. Execution Exception Types Execution exceptions may include: system failure, instrument failure, missing data, missing evidence, infrastructure outage, safety event, control failure, unexpected system behavior, extreme observation, contradictory output, anomalous measurement, operator error, AI failure, autonomous-system escalation, resource failure, or another unplanned condition. An exception may require governance even where no method rule was formally violated. Deviation Materiality Not every deviation has equal significance. VEDEGM may classify deviation materiality as: Immaterial Minor Material Critical Execution-Invalidating Materiality should be assessed relative to: Validation Purpose, Validation Scope, Validation Depth, affected Validation Criteria, affected method step, evidence criticality, source criticality, consequence of error, recoverability, and impact on later Validation Determination. Immaterial Deviation An Immaterial Deviation has no reasonable material effect on the legitimacy, scope, interpretation, or reconstructability of validation execution. It may still be recorded where required for traceability. Minor Deviation A Minor Deviation represents a limited departure that does not materially undermine the validation but may require documentation, correction, or additional review. Material Deviation A Material Deviation can reasonably affect: methodological interpretation, criterion evaluation, evidence use, execution completeness, execution conformity, or permissible Validation Determination. Material deviations require explicit impact governance. Critical Deviation A Critical Deviation materially threatens the legitimacy of one or more critical validation activities. It may require: execution pause, re-execution, scope restriction, escalation, method reassessment, or Determination Block. Execution-Invalidating Deviation An Execution-Invalidating Deviation prevents affected execution activity—or in severe cases the complete execution— from legitimately supporting the intended Validation Determination. Invalidation should remain bounded to the affected execution scope where possible. Exception Materiality Exceptions may also require materiality classification. An unexpected event can be highly significant even if it does not violate an explicit execution rule. For example: A never-before-observed autonomous behavior during a properly executed safety test may be methodologically important despite perfect execution conformity. VEDEGM therefore governs both rule departure and unexpected operational significance. Authorized Deviation A deviation may be authorized before or during execution. Authorization should identify: the proposed deviation, rationale, authority, affected execution activities, affected criteria, expected methodological effect, compensating controls, permitted duration, and applicable conditions. Pre-Authorized Deviation Some Validation Execution Bases may anticipate defined alternative paths. For example: If Instrument A becomes unavailable, Instrument B may be used if Calibration Condition X is satisfied. Where these alternatives are established beforehand, the resulting change may be treated as a governed Pre-Authorized Deviation. Post-Event Authorization A deviation discovered after it occurred cannot be made methodologically harmless merely by approving it retrospectively. Post-event governance may determine whether the deviation is: acceptable, correctable, conditionally usable, requiring repetition, or invalidating. VALIDOS™ therefore establishes: Retrospective Authorization ≠ Erasure of Deviation Unauthorized Deviation An Unauthorized Deviation occurs where actual execution departs materially from the governed basis without applicable authorization. This may require: immediate correction, pause, escalation, repetition, scope restriction, or execution invalidation. Deviation Cause VEDEGM may identify the cause of a deviation. Possible causes include: human error, system error, software defect, resource limitation, environmental change, unavailable evidence, source failure, configuration drift, unclear instructions, methodological ambiguity, external event, safety intervention, unauthorized action, or deliberate modification. Cause identification can inform corrective and preventive governance. Deviation Impact Assessment A Deviation Impact Assessment asks: Which execution activity was affected? Which Validation Criterion was affected? Which evidence was affected? Which source conditions changed? Did the deviation affect method validity? Did it affect object state? Did it affect scope? Did it affect sequence? Did it affect traceability? Can affected activity be isolated? Can the effect be corrected? Does re-execution become necessary? Localized Impact Some deviations affect only one narrow execution activity. Where the affected portion can be reliably isolated, VALIDOS™ should avoid invalidating unaffected execution unnecessarily. This supports proportionate governance. Systemic Impact A deviation may have systemic effects where it influences: multiple method steps, multiple criteria, the complete evidence basis, the object state, the execution environment, or the validity of the complete execution sequence. Systemic deviations may require wider re-execution or reassessment. Cumulative Deviation Several small deviations may collectively create a material execution problem. VALIDOS™ therefore establishes: Minor Deviation + Minor Deviation + Minor Deviation ≠ Necessarily Minor Overall VEDEGM may assess cumulative effect across an Execution Instance. Deviation Recurrence Repeated occurrence of the same deviation may indicate: weak control, flawed procedure, inadequate training, unstable environment, unsuitable method, or systematic execution drift. Recurrence may increase materiality even when individual instances appear minor. Execution Drift Execution Drift is a progressive departure from the approved Execution Basis rather than one discrete event. Examples include: incremental parameter changes, repeated informal exceptions, expanding access, shifting scope, changing evidence sources, evolving configurations, or altered participant roles. VEDEGM governs accumulated drift as a material execution condition. Evidence Substitution Evidence Substitution occurs where approved evidence is replaced by another evidence item or body. VEDEGM determines whether the substitute is: already qualified, equivalent, conditionally acceptable, requiring new Evidence Fitness assessment, or unacceptable. Substitution must not silently inherit the fitness status of the replaced evidence. Source Substitution Where a source changes, the replacement source must not automatically inherit the reliability status of the original source. A material source substitution may require: new identity assessment, provenance assessment, capability assessment, independence assessment, or complete Source Reliability reassessment. Instrument Substitution An alternative instrument may differ in: range, calibration, precision, resolution, method, software, or operating conditions. Instrument substitution therefore requires equivalence assessment where material. Participant Substitution A substitute participant may require assessment of: role authority, competence, independence, access, and execution permissions. The presence of another qualified person does not automatically establish role equivalence. Environment Exception Unexpected environmental conditions may materially affect validation. Examples include: temperature change, network instability, load variation, system outage, unusual user conditions, or external interference. VEDEGM determines whether execution may continue and how affected activity must be treated. Control Loss A required control may become: Degraded Lost Bypassed or: Unavailable VEDEGM evaluates: when the loss occurred, which activities were affected, whether control recovery occurred, whether affected outputs remain usable, and whether re-execution is necessary. Control Bypass Control Bypass occurs where a required control is intentionally or unintentionally circumvented. Where the bypass is unauthorized or materially affects execution integrity, it may constitute a critical deviation. Execution Interruption An interruption stops or materially disrupts execution. VEDEGM governs: interruption cause, duration, execution state, object-state effect, evidence continuity, control continuity, whether execution can resume, and whether previous activity remains valid. Execution Resume Assessment Before execution resumes after a material interruption, VEDEGM may require assessment of: object continuity, configuration continuity, environment continuity, control restoration, evidence continuity, source continuity, and method-state continuity. A restart from an altered state may not be methodologically equivalent to uninterrupted execution. Execution Failure An Execution Failure occurs where a required validation activity cannot be completed sufficiently. Examples include: test cannot run, required evidence unavailable, instrument failure, model crashes, system inaccessible, required source unavailable, or procedure cannot be completed. VALIDOS™ establishes: Execution Failure ≠ Validation Object Failure The failure concerns the validation process. Corrective Execution A deviation or exception may permit corrective action. Corrective execution may include: repeating a step, replacing an invalid measurement, restoring a control, correcting configuration, rerunning a test, replacing a participant, restoring evidence continuity, or another governed correction. Corrective Action Does Not Erase History Where a deviation is corrected, the original event remains part of the execution history. VALIDOS™ establishes: Correction ≠ Historical Deletion The execution record should preserve: Original Condition → Deviation → Corrective Action → Corrected Condition Compensating Control Where a deviation cannot be removed, a compensating control may reduce its methodological impact. Examples include: independent corroboration, additional testing, enhanced monitoring, reduced Validation Scope, additional review, duplicated measurement, or stricter reliance restrictions. A compensating control must be proportionate to the deviation. Deviation Escalation Material deviations may require escalation where they exceed the authority or capability of the execution actor. Escalation may involve: validation supervisor, methodology authority, governance authority, independent reviewer, safety authority, or another defined role. VEDEGM does not define universal organizational hierarchies. It requires material escalation pathways to remain governed. Exception Escalation Trigger Triggers may include: critical object change, critical control loss, unknown evidence substitution, source compromise, repeated deviation, safety event, high-consequence anomaly, unauthorized scope expansion, or inability to determine execution impact. Deviation Resolution A deviation may be resolved through: Accepted as Immaterial Corrected Compensated Re-Executed Scope Restricted Conditionally Accepted Escalated Execution Portion Invalidated or: Unresolved Resolution must remain traceable to the impact assessment. Unresolved Deviation An unresolved material deviation must not disappear simply because execution ends. It should propagate into: Execution Completeness assessment, Execution Conformity assessment, Determination Readiness, or later Validation Determination limitations. Deviation Closure A deviation may be closed when sufficient information exists to establish: what occurred, why it occurred, what it affected, what response occurred, whether correction or control was sufficient, and what residual limitation remains. Closure does not necessarily mean the deviation became immaterial. Deviation Status VEDEGM may establish statuses such as: Open Under Assessment Contained Corrective Action Required Corrected Conditionally Accepted Escalated Resolved Closed with Residual Limitation or: Execution-Invalidating Exception Status An exception may be: Observed Under Investigation Controlled Resolved Escalated Unresolved or: Critical These states support execution governance without becoming Validation Object states. Deviation and Traceability Deviation governance depends upon VEOTM traceability. A deviation that cannot be sufficiently reconstructed may itself create a Traceability Gap. Conversely, strong traceability may allow a deviation's effect to be isolated and preserve unaffected validation activity. Deviation and Execution Conformity VEDEGM does not itself issue final Execution Conformity. It provides the structured input needed to determine: which deviations occurred, their materiality, whether they were corrected, what remains unresolved, and whether execution can still legitimately support later determination. Deviation Is Not Validation Determination A material deviation may weaken or invalidate execution. It does not directly determine whether the Validation Object itself satisfies or fails a Validation Criterion. VALIDOS™ preserves: Execution Deviation ≠ Object Invalidity Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Detect Deviation or Exception Identify actual execution conditions differing from the governed basis or requiring exceptional governance attention. 2. Create Deviation / Exception Record Record the affected execution activity, expected condition, actual condition, time, actor, object state, and relevant relationships. 3. Classify Type Determine whether the event concerns: object, scope, method, sequence, evidence, source, configuration, participant, environment, control, interruption, failure, anomaly, or another exception type. 4. Assess Materiality Classify the event according to its potential methodological impact. 5. Assess Authorization Determine whether the deviation was: pre-authorized, authorized during execution, retrospectively assessed, or unauthorized. 6. Assess Impact Determine which criteria, methods, evidence, sources, outputs, and execution activities are affected. 7. Establish Response Determine whether to: continue, pause, correct, compensate, repeat, restrict, escalate, terminate, or invalidate affected activity. 8. Track Resolution Maintain the event until sufficient resolution or explicit unresolved status is established. 9. Preserve Residual Limitations Carry unresolved or residual methodological effects forward. 10. Preserve Lifecycle Traceability Maintain: Deviation or Exception Identifier, Execution Instance, event type, expected condition, actual condition, affected object state, affected scope, method step, criterion, evidence, source, participant, control, materiality, cause, authorization status, impact, response, corrective action, compensating controls, escalation, resolution, residual limitation, status, recurrence, cumulative impact, version, and sufficient lifecycle traceability. Governance Outputs VEDEGM may produce: Validation Execution Deviation Register, Validation Execution Exception Register, Deviation Classification Record, Exception Classification Record, Deviation Materiality Assessment, Exception Materiality Assessment, Deviation Authorization Record, Unauthorized Deviation Record, Deviation Impact Assessment, Exception Impact Assessment, Execution Drift Record, Evidence Substitution Record, Source Substitution Record, Instrument Substitution Record, Participant Substitution Record, Environment Exception Record, Control Loss Record, Control Bypass Record, Execution Interruption Record, Execution Failure Record, Corrective Execution Record, Compensating Control Record, Deviation Escalation Record, Exception Escalation Record, Cumulative Deviation Assessment, Deviation Recurrence Record, Deviation Resolution Record, Residual Limitation Record, Deviation Closure Record, and Deviation & Exception Traceability Record. Use Case 1 — AI Model Validation Scenario During validation of an AI model, one approved benchmark becomes temporarily unavailable and the execution team replaces it with a similar benchmark. Application VEDEGM records the substitution as an Evidence and Method-related Deviation. The replacement benchmark does not automatically inherit the qualification status of the approved benchmark. Its effect on: criteria coverage, Evidence Fitness, method comparability, and execution validity is assessed. Result Execution may continue only if the substitution is sufficiently governed, or the affected validation activity may require later re-execution. Use Case 2 — Industrial Validation Scenario A required sensor temporarily loses calibration during a critical measurement sequence. Application VEDEGM identifies: Control Loss, affected measurement period, affected Validation Criteria, affected outputs, and time of calibration recovery. Result Measurements generated during the affected period remain distinguishable from valid measurements and may require repetition rather than contaminating the complete execution record. Use Case 3 — Autonomous Validation Agent Scenario An autonomous validation agent encounters an unexpected system condition and uses a tool outside the execution path anticipated by the Validation Method. Application VEDEGM determines whether the action was within delegated authority, whether it changed the methodological basis, what outputs were affected, and whether human escalation was required. Result The event becomes a governed execution exception rather than an invisible autonomous adaptation. Architectural Position Validation Execution Deviation & Exception Governance is the fourth internal governance space of the Validation Execution Standard (VEXS). The progression now becomes: Execution Basis & Authorization → Execution Instantiation & Control → Execution Observation & Traceability → Execution Deviation & Exception Governance VEBAM establishes: What authorizes execution? VEICM establishes: How is execution instantiated and controlled? VEOTM establishes: What actually happened? VEDEGM establishes: Where did execution differ, what exceptional conditions occurred, and how were those differences governed? The fifth and final VEXS module can then determine: Was the overall execution sufficiently complete and conformant to support Validation Determination? Foundational Principle Execution deviations do not destroy validation merely by occurring; they destroy validation when their existence, materiality, impact, and resolution are not governable. Canonical Closing Statement Validation Execution Deviation & Exception Governance Module establishes the controlled exception layer of VALIDOS™ validation execution by governing departures, anomalies, substitutions, interruptions, failures, control losses, unexpected conditions, authorization, materiality, impact, corrective action, compensation, escalation, recurrence, cumulative effects, resolution, residual limitations, and traceability. VEDEGM ensures that operational variation does not disappear into execution history and that neither deviation nor exception is allowed to influence Validation Determination without first becoming an explicit and governable methodological condition.
