title: Validation State Governance Standard
text: Validation State Governance Standard Validation State Governance Standard Standard ID: VSGS OriginID: OOF-OID-AI-VALIDOS-VSGS-2026-08-12-0009 Architecture: VALIDOS™ — Validation Governance Architecture Category: AI & Interpretation Subcategory: Validation Governance Type: Parent Standard Governed Space: Validation State Governance Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 12 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS® · ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Canonical Definition Validation State Governance Standard (VSGS) defines the governance conditions under which Validation Objects are assigned, maintained, transitioned, restricted, suspended, invalidated, expired, superseded, and reclassified across formal Validation States based upon applicable Validation Determinations, object identity, object version, scope, conditions, lifecycle events, material change, temporal validity, unresolved limitations, and revalidation requirements. Canonical Definition Extension A Validation Determination describes what a governed validation event demonstrated. A Validation State describes the current formal validation condition of the Validation Object. These are not the same. A system may receive a Positive Validation Determination today. Tomorrow: the object may change, its configuration may change, relevant evidence may become outdated, a source may become unreliable, an operational environment may materially change, a validation condition may no longer hold, the determination may expire, or new contradictory information may emerge. The original determination remains historically valid as a record of what the validation event demonstrated. But the Validation State of the object may no longer remain unchanged. Validation State Governance Standard therefore governs the transition: Validation Determination → Validation State → Validation State Change → Validation State Continuity The standard establishes the conditions necessary to determine: which Validation Determination governs the current object state, whether the determination remains applicable, whether the Validation Object remains materially equivalent to the validated object, whether determination conditions remain satisfied, whether temporal validity remains active, whether material change has occurred, whether new evidence or information affects the state, whether revalidation is required, whether the current state must be restricted, whether the state must be suspended, whether prior validation has expired, whether validation has been invalidated, whether a newer determination supersedes an earlier state, and what formal Validation State the Validation Object currently holds. VSGS does not determine whether reliance upon that state is permitted. It governs the current validation condition of the object itself. Core Question What formal Validation State does the Validation Object currently hold, and under which conditions may that state remain, change, expire, suspend, or require revalidation? Purpose The purpose of Validation State Governance Standard is to prevent historical validation conclusions from being treated as permanently current. The standard addresses a fundamental lifecycle problem: Validated once does not mean validated forever. Validation Objects evolve. Systems change. Models are updated. Data changes. Dependencies change. Operating environments change. Threat conditions change. Regulatory requirements change. Evidence ages. New information appears. Validation State Governance ensures that validation remains connected to the current reality of the Validation Object rather than only to a historical validation event. Governance Objective VSGS establishes a governed Validation State layer capable of maintaining a current and traceable validation condition across the complete lifecycle of a Validation Object. The standard seeks to ensure that: every formal Validation State is connected to a legitimate Validation Determination, Validation State remains object-specific, Validation State remains version-specific where required, scope and conditions remain attached, state validity periods remain visible, state changes are governed, material object changes are detected, revalidation triggers are identifiable, outdated determinations do not remain silently active, suspended states remain distinguishable from invalidated states, expired validation remains distinguishable from negative validation, superseded determinations remain historically visible, and the current Validation State can be reconstructed throughout the object lifecycle. Operational Role Validation State Governance Standard serves as the lifecycle-state layer of VALIDOS™. The preceding standards establish: Validation Object → Validation Purpose & Scope → Validation Criteria → Validation Method → Validation Evidence Fitness → Validation Source Reliability → Validation Execution → Validation Determination VSGS then asks: What Validation State should the object now hold, and how does that state evolve over time? Its structural progression is: Validation Determination → State Eligibility Assessment → Validation State Assignment → State Activation → State Monitoring → State Change Detection → State Transition → State Continuity The resulting state becomes the governed basis upon which Validation Reliance & Revalidation governance can operate. Governance Scope Validation State Governance Standard governs: Validation State definition, state assignment, state activation, state applicability, state scope, state conditions, state limitations, state restrictions, state effective point, state validity period, state expiration, state suspension, state resumption, state invalidation, state supersession, state withdrawal, state transition, state continuity, state history, state change detection, object-change detection, material-change assessment, state reassessment, revalidation-required status, state uncertainty, state authority where applicable, and Validation State traceability. Validation State A Validation State is the formal lifecycle condition assigned to a Validation Object based upon the currently applicable governed validation record. A Validation State is not merely a label. It should remain connected to: Validation Object, object version, applicable determination, Validation Purpose, Validation Scope, Validation Depth, conditions, restrictions, limitations, effective point, validity period, change triggers, and revalidation requirements. Validation Determination and Validation State VALIDOS™ establishes a strict architectural distinction: Validation Determination asks: What did the governed validation event demonstrate? Validation State asks: What validation condition does the Validation Object currently hold? A determination is an event-level conclusion. A state is a lifecycle-level condition. This distinction allows historical validation evidence to remain intact while current validation status changes. Canonical Validation States VSGS may establish formal Validation States including: Validation Required The Validation Object requires formal validation before an applicable governed validation state can be established. Validation Pending Validation has been initiated or scheduled but has not yet produced a formal Validation Determination sufficient for state assignment. Partially Validated Only part of the Validation Object, Validation Scope, criterion structure, operating environment, population, or other governed domain possesses a positive or conditional validation basis. Conditionally Validated The Validation Object possesses a positive validation basis only while explicit conditions, limitations, restrictions, or operating boundaries remain satisfied. Validated The Validation Object possesses a currently applicable Positive Validation Determination sufficient to support an active Validation State within the defined scope, version, depth, and validity conditions. Validation Conflicted Material unresolved validation conflict prevents one coherent unrestricted state from being represented. Validation Suspended A previously active Validation State has been temporarily placed into non-active status because material uncertainty, change, investigation, or unresolved condition requires reassessment. Invalidated A previously supported Validation State has lost its governing validation basis because the validation conclusion or its applicability has been materially destroyed. Validation Expired The temporal validity or defined lifecycle period of the active validation state has ended. Revalidation Required Material change, expiration, new evidence, changed risk, changed environment, or another governed trigger requires new validation before the object can regain or maintain an applicable validation state. Additional state subcategories may be defined where justified by domain-specific requirements. State Assignment A Validation State should not be assigned directly from intuition, reputation, or historical claims. State Assignment should derive from: applicable Overall Validation Determination, current Validation Object identity, current object version, current scope, current conditions, current environment, current validity period, and any material changes occurring after determination. Positive Determination and Validated State A Positive Validation Determination may support assignment of: Validated but only where: the determination remains applicable, the object remains materially equivalent, scope remains valid, determination conditions remain satisfied, no suspension or invalidation condition exists, and the validation has not expired. Therefore: Positive Validation Determination ≠ Automatically Permanent Validated State Conditional Determination and State A Conditional Validation Determination may normally support: Conditionally Validated rather than unrestricted: Validated The conditions defining that state must remain attached. If the conditions cease to hold, the state may transition. Partial Determination and State A Partial Validation Determination may support: Partially Validated where only defined portions of the object or scope possess sufficient validation basis. The validated and non-validated portions must remain distinguishable. Negative Determination and State A Negative Validation Determination does not necessarily imply that the object must be permanently categorized as Invalidated. The actual state may depend upon whether: the object was previously Validated, this is the first validation, scope differs, only one domain failed, the determination is partial, or remediation is underway. VSGS therefore governs lifecycle meaning separately from the determination itself. Indeterminate Determination and State An Indeterminate Validation Determination may produce: Validation Pending, Validation Conflicted, Validation Suspended, Revalidation Required, or another appropriate state depending upon context. It should not automatically become: Validated or: Invalidated. Validation State Scope Every state must remain bounded to the scope supported by its governing determination. A system may simultaneously be: Validated for Function A and: Validation Required for Function B where these scopes can be legitimately separated. VSGS therefore permits multidimensional Validation State where necessary. Validation State Depth State should remain connected to the Validation Depth supporting it. For example: Validated — Preliminary Depth and: Validated — High-Assurance Depth may represent materially different assurance conditions. The state should not imply stronger validation than its determination supports. State Conditions A Validation State may depend upon conditions. Examples include: specific system configuration, continued human oversight, defined operating environment, specific population, continued source availability, active safety control, restricted autonomy, specific jurisdiction, or ongoing monitoring. Conditions form part of the state. State Restrictions Restrictions define what the Validation State must not be interpreted to cover. Examples include: not valid for autonomous deployment, not valid outside defined temperature range, not validated for pediatric use, not validated for Version 5, not validated outside defined jurisdiction, or not valid after material modification. State Limitation A Validation State may remain active while carrying known limitations. Limitations may concern: evidence depth, rare-event coverage, population representation, long-term operating data, external validation, or unresolved low-level uncertainty. Limitations remain visible throughout the state lifecycle. State Effective Point A Validation State should have an identifiable point at which it becomes active. This may be: determination issuance, determination approval, state assignment, deployment approval, or another governed event. VSGS distinguishes state effective point from determination date where necessary. State Validity Period Some Validation States may be time-bounded. Validity may be expressed through: fixed expiration date, maximum validity period, event-based validity, version-based validity, condition-based validity, or continuous validity subject to monitoring. Not every object requires fixed-time expiration. The validity model should match the nature of the Validation Object. State Expiration A Validation State becomes Validation Expired when its defined validity period or applicability condition ends without sufficient renewal or revalidation. Expiration does not mean the object failed validation. VALIDOS™ establishes: Validation Expired ≠ Validation Failed Expiration means the previous validation basis is no longer sufficient to represent the object as currently validated. Material Change A Material Change is a change capable of affecting whether the existing Validation State remains applicable. Material changes may include: model update, software update, architecture change, dataset change, configuration change, hardware replacement, operating environment change, population expansion, new use case, jurisdiction change, source change, evidence change, method change, risk change, or newly discovered failure condition. Material Change Assessment Not every change requires revalidation. VSGS therefore distinguishes: Immaterial Change Minor Validation-Relevant Change Material Change Critical Validation-Relevant Change The appropriate response depends upon whether the existing validation basis still represents the changed object. Object Equivalence After change, VSGS may assess whether the changed object remains sufficiently equivalent to the validated object. Possible outcomes include: Validation Equivalence Maintained Validation Equivalence Conditionally Maintained Validation Equivalence Undetermined Validation Equivalence Lost Loss of equivalence may trigger revalidation. State Change Trigger A State Change Trigger is an event requiring reassessment of the current Validation State. Triggers may include: object modification, new evidence, critical incident, source reliability change, determination reassessment, operating environment change, new regulation, changed Validation Purpose, scope expansion, time expiration, repeated anomaly, drift, or another material development. State Reassessment State reassessment determines whether the current Validation State should: remain unchanged, become conditional, become partial, be suspended, expire, be invalidated, require revalidation, or transition to another formal state. State Transition A Validation State may transition through governed paths. Examples include: Validation Required → Validation Pending → Validated Validated → Conditionally Validated Validated → Validation Suspended Validated → Validation Expired Validated → Revalidation Required Conditionally Validated → Validated Conditionally Validated → Validation Suspended Validation Suspended → Validated Validation Suspended → Revalidation Required Revalidation Required → Validation Pending Validation Pending → Validated Validated → Invalidated Transitions must remain traceable. State Transition Is Not Free-Form VALIDOS™ may define permitted state transitions. For example: A Validation Object should not ordinarily transition directly from: Validation Required to: Validated without an applicable Validation Determination. Likewise: Validation Expired should not become: Validated merely because the object has not changed. The validation basis must be restored. Validation Suspended Suspension is temporary. It may be appropriate where: serious new evidence emerges, incident investigation is underway, source reliability is questioned, object change is being assessed, determination is suspended, a safety concern exists, or revalidation is pending. Suspension prevents continued representation of the state as unrestricted while preserving the historical validation basis. Suspension Does Not Equal Invalidation VALIDOS™ establishes: Validation Suspended ≠ Invalidated Suspension means: Current applicability is temporarily unresolved. Invalidation means: The validation basis has been materially destroyed or determined no longer applicable. State Resumption A suspended state may resume where: the concern is resolved, the object remains equivalent, the original determination remains applicable, required controls are restored, or additional evidence supports resumption. Resumption must remain traceable. Invalidated State Invalidation occurs where the previous validation state can no longer legitimately remain active. Possible causes include: fundamental object change, invalid determination, invalid execution, compromised decisive evidence, critical source failure, discovered methodological defect, or new evidence conclusively contradicting the prior validation basis. Invalidation Scope Invalidation may apply to: complete object, specific version, one subsystem, one criterion domain, one environment, or one scope. VSGS therefore permits bounded invalidation where methodologically separable. Revalidation Required A Validation Object enters Revalidation Required where the existing validation basis cannot remain sufficient without new validation. Possible triggers include: material object change, validity expiration, significant scope expansion, changed operational environment, new risk profile, new critical evidence, regulatory requirement, accumulated drift, or unresolved Validation Suspension. Revalidation Required Is Not Invalidated The state: Revalidation Required means the previous validation basis no longer provides sufficient current assurance. It does not necessarily demonstrate that the object fails. Validation Conflicted A Validation Object may enter Validation Conflicted where multiple legitimate determinations or material findings create incompatible current validation implications. For example: different environments produce incompatible states, concurrent determinations conflict, or unresolved critical evidence prevents a single current state. Conflict must remain explicit until resolved, bounded, or converted into Partial Validation State. Partially Validated State A Validation Object may be Partially Validated where valid separation exists between: subsystems, populations, operating modes, jurisdictions, functions, environments, or criterion domains. A partial state should identify both: Validated Portion and: Unvalidated / Conditional / Negative Portion where applicable. State Multiplicity Complex Validation Objects may legitimately possess multiple concurrent state dimensions. For example: Performance State: Validated Safety State: Conditionally Validated Autonomy State: Validation Required VSGS permits multidimensional state representation where one global state would obscure material differences. State Hierarchy Validation State may be represented hierarchically. For example: Component State → Subsystem State → System State Higher-level state must remain traceable to the lower-level validation states supporting it. State Precedence Where several states apply simultaneously, governance may define precedence. For example: Validation Suspended may override an otherwise Validated state for current operational representation. Similarly: Validation Expired may prevent historical positive determination from being represented as currently active validation. Historical State and Current State VALIDOS™ distinguishes: Historical Validation State from: Current Validation State A system may historically have been: Validated while currently being: Revalidation Required Both facts remain true. The architecture must preserve both. State Continuity Validation State Continuity preserves the full lifecycle: State Assignment → State Activation → State Change → State Transition → Current State Historical states must not be overwritten when new states are assigned. State Record A formal Validation State Record may preserve: Validation State Identifier, Validation Object, object version, applicable Validation Determination, state classification, scope, Validation Depth, conditions, restrictions, limitations, effective point, validity period, expiration condition, state-change triggers, material change assessment, current status, transition history, revalidation requirement, and sufficient traceability. State Authority Where state assignment or transition requires formal authority, VSGS may govern: state issuer, state approval authority, delegated authority, state transition authority, suspension authority, invalidation authority, and reactivation authority. VSGS does not create legal authority where none exists. Automated Validation State Governance Some state transitions may be automated where rules are sufficiently explicit. For example: Validity Period Ends → Validation Expired or: Critical Configuration Change Detected → Revalidation Required Automation should remain traceable and governed. AI-Assisted Validation State Governance AI may assist with: change detection, state-condition monitoring, determination comparison, drift identification, revalidation trigger detection, and state-record maintenance. AI must not silently invent new state-transition logic outside the governed architecture. State Monitoring Validation State may require ongoing monitoring of conditions capable of affecting validity. Monitoring may include: object version, configuration, operating environment, incidents, performance drift, model drift, evidence changes, source changes, or expiration conditions. State monitoring does not itself constitute revalidation. It detects conditions requiring governance response. State Drift A Validation State may gradually lose applicability without one obvious material event. Examples include: accumulated model drift, changing population, slowly changing environment, dependency evolution, repeated small modifications, or cumulative evidence degradation. VSGS may govern Validation State Drift as a trigger for reassessment. State Confidence Where useful, implementations may represent confidence in the current state. However: State Confidence ≠ Validation State A state may be Validated while carrying moderate confidence within its legitimate scope. Confidence is supplementary and must not replace formal state classification. State Uncertainty Where current state applicability cannot be established with sufficient confidence, the object may require: Validation Suspended, Validation Conflicted, Revalidation Required, or another governed state. State uncertainty must not be hidden behind historical validation. State and Operational Reality The current Validation State should remain connected to the current operational reality of the Validation Object. Where the object materially diverges from the validated state, historical validation should not continue to create current- state confidence. State and Integrity Material integrity failures may affect Validation State. Where required, INTEGROS® may establish whether relevant objects, evidence, records, or systems retain sufficient integrity. VSGS consumes such information only insofar as it affects state applicability. State and Determination Reassessment If an Overall Validation Determination is: modified, suspended, withdrawn, or superseded, the applicable Validation State should be reassessed. Determination lifecycle changes and State lifecycle changes remain separate but connected. State Supersession A new valid state may supersede an earlier state. For example: Validated Version 3.0 may be superseded by: Conditionally Validated Version 4.0 The earlier state remains part of validation history. State Withdrawal A Validation State may be withdrawn where it was incorrectly assigned or where the underlying basis never legitimately supported it. Withdrawal should preserve historical accountability. Validation State Is Not Reliance Authorization This boundary is fundamental. VSGS answers: What validation condition does the Validation Object currently hold? It does not answer: Who may rely upon that state? A Validation Object may be: Validated while reliance is still prohibited for a specific use, jurisdiction, organization, or risk context. Therefore: Validated State ≠ Reliance Authorization Validation State Is Not Deployment Approval Likewise: Validation State ≠ Deployment Approval Deployment may require: regulatory approval, organizational authorization, risk acceptance, operational readiness, safety approval, or other independent governance. VALIDOS™ preserves validation as its own methodological domain. Governance Boundary Validation State Governance Standard begins when an applicable Validation Determination exists or when a Validation Object requires formal state classification. It ends when the current Validation State, its scope, conditions, validity, lifecycle transitions, state-change triggers, and revalidation implications have been sufficiently established and maintained. VSGS does not determine: operational reliance authorization, relying-party eligibility, reliance transfer, reliance conditions, reliance consequences, or the complete revalidation process. These responsibilities belong to the final VALIDOS™ Parent Standard. Minimum Governance Requirements A conforming implementation of VSGS should establish: 1. an identifiable Validation Object, 2. the applicable Validation Determination, 3. the current object version or state, 4. an explicit Validation State, 5. state scope, 6. Validation Depth, 7. state conditions, 8. state restrictions, 9. state limitations, 10. an effective point, 11. state validity or expiration logic, 12. material-change triggers, 13. state-change and transition rules, 14. suspension and invalidation conditions, 15. revalidation-required triggers, 16. historical state continuity, 17. a current Validation State Record, 18. and sufficient lifecycle traceability. Governance Outputs VSGS may produce: Validation State, Validation State Record, Validation State Identifier, Validation State Assignment, Validation State Scope Record, Validation State Depth Record, Validation State Condition Register, Validation State Restriction Record, Validation State Limitation Record, Validation State Effective Point, Validation State Validity Period, Validation State Expiration Condition, Validation State Monitoring Record, Material Change Record, Validation Change Materiality Assessment, Validation Equivalence Assessment, Validation State Change Trigger, Validation State Reassessment, Validation State Transition Record, Validation Suspension Record, Validation Resumption Record, Validation Invalidation Record, Validation Expiration Record, Revalidation Required Record, Validation Conflict State Record, Partial Validation State Record, Multidimensional Validation State Map, Validation State Hierarchy, Validation State Supersession Record, Validation State Withdrawal Record, Validation State History, and Validation State Continuity Reference. Operational Applications Validation State Governance Standard may be applied across: artificial intelligence, machine learning, autonomous systems, AI agents, software systems, digital infrastructure, datasets, predictions, simulations, scientific validation, medical systems, financial models, industrial systems, cybersecurity systems, critical infrastructure, digital identities, regulatory environments, public-sector systems, and any governed environment in which validation status must remain current over time. Relationship to Other OOF Architectures Validation State Governance Standard interoperates with: GOA™ OBIDENITY® INTEGROS® ORA™ AGA™ AIG® CLIA® MGIA™ ASGA™ RIS™ by providing the canonical validation-governance methodology through which validation conclusions are transformed into current, lifecycle-aware Validation States. GOA™ may establish authority governing state assignment, suspension, transition, and withdrawal. OBIDENITY® may preserve object identity, version continuity, provenance, and ownership relationships required for state continuity. INTEGROS® may establish integrity conditions affecting whether an existing Validation State remains applicable. ORA™ may identify changes in operational reality affecting current state validity. AGA™ may establish accountability for state assignment, monitoring, transition, suspension, and invalidation. RIS™ may influence the sensitivity of change triggers and revalidation requirements according to risk and consequence. AIG®, CLIA®, MGIA™, and ASGA™ may contribute domain-specific state-change signals for AI behavior, cognition, memory, and autonomous systems. VSGS does not replace these architectures. It governs specifically the current validation lifecycle condition of a Validation Object. Foundational Principle Validation is not a permanent property of an object; it is a governed state that must remain connected to the object, conditions, evidence, and reality that continue to justify it. Canonical Closing Statement Validation State Governance Standard establishes the lifecycle-state layer of VALIDOS™ — Validation Governance Architecture by transforming validation determinations into formal, current, bounded, traceable, and change-aware Validation States. Through governance of state assignment, scope, depth, conditions, limitations, validity periods, material change, equivalence, monitoring, suspension, invalidation, expiration, conflict, partial validation, revalidation triggers, state transitions, supersession, withdrawal, and historical continuity, VSGS ensures that validation cannot remain active merely because it was once established and that every current validation claim remains connected to the present condition of the Validation Object and the governed basis that continues to support it. Validation State Governance Standard Architecture: VALIDOS™ — Validation Governance Architecture Category: AI & Interpretation · Subcategory: Validation Governance Canonical Definition: Validation State Governance Standard (VSGS) defines the governance conditions under which Validation Objects are assigned, maintained, transitioned, restricted, suspended, invalidated, expired, superseded, and reclassified across formal Validation States based upon applicable Validation Determinations, object identity, object version, scope, conditions, lifecycle events, material change, temporal validity, unresolved limitations, and revalidation requirements. title: About Validation Source Reliability Standard
text: About Validation Source Reliability Standard About Validation Source Reliability Standard Governing Whether the Sources Behind Validation Evidence Can Be Relied Upon Evidence has an origin. Someone observed it. Something measured it. A system generated it. A repository stored it. A process transformed it. An organization supplied it. A model may have interpreted it. And every one of those relationships can affect validation. Validation Source Reliability Standard (VSRS) is the sixth Parent Standard of VALIDOS™ — Validation Governance Architecture, governing whether the sources behind Validation Evidence can be sufficiently identified, traced, assessed, bounded, and relied upon for the validation roles assigned to them. VSRS addresses one fundamental question: Can the source behind Validation Evidence be sufficiently relied upon for the role that evidence is expected to perform? Why Validation Source Reliability Standard Exists Validation may use evidence that appears convincing while the source conditions behind that evidence remain unclear. A source may be: unidentified, incorrectly attributed, dependent upon another source, operating outside its competence, financially interested in the result, methodologically dependent, based upon outdated information, separated from the original evidence by multiple intermediaries, or unable to demonstrate how the evidence was produced. None of these conditions automatically proves that the evidence is false. But each can materially affect how much validation confidence the evidence should support. VSRS exists to make those source conditions governable. Evidence Fitness Is Not Source Reliability VALIDOS™ deliberately separates two questions. Validation Evidence Fitness Standard asks: Is the evidence fit for the validation question? Validation Source Reliability Standard asks: Can the source behind that evidence be sufficiently relied upon? This separation is essential. Evidence may be highly relevant, applicable, well-covered, and adequate while originating from a source whose reliability remains uncertain. Likewise, an extremely reliable institution may provide evidence that is irrelevant to the Validation Criterion being examined. Therefore: Fit Evidence ≠ Reliable Source and: Reliable Source ≠ Fit Evidence Both conditions must be governed independently. Source Before Execution VALIDOS™ establishes the architectural progression: Validation Object → Validation Purpose & Scope → Validation Criteria → Validation Method → Validation Evidence Fitness → Validation Source Reliability → Validation Execution Before the architecture asks whether validation was correctly executed, it establishes: what is being validated, why it is being validated, against what criteria, through which methodology, whether the evidence is fit, and whether the sources behind that evidence are sufficiently reliable. This creates a stronger basis for execution governance. What Is a Validation Source? A Validation Source is not limited to a person or publication. It may include: an individual, organization, laboratory, institution, database, dataset origin, sensor, measuring instrument, AI model, operational system, software process, repository, document origin, monitoring system, external provider, or another entity capable of generating, recording, transmitting, transforming, interpreting, maintaining, or supplying Validation Evidence. The relevant question is not simply: Who supplied the evidence? It is: Which source relationships materially contributed to the evidence upon which validation depends? Source Identity Before Source Trust A source cannot be meaningfully assessed if its identity is unclear. VSRS therefore begins with source identification and attribution. Depending upon the validation context, it may be necessary to know: the organization, system, instrument, individual, model, repository, version, dataset origin, or another source representation. The required level of identity precision depends upon the validation role and consequence. Attribution Matters Evidence may be attributed directly to its origin. But evidence may also arrive through: reports, databases, publications, aggregators, intermediaries, AI-generated summaries, analytical systems, or derived datasets. VSRS distinguishes the entity presenting evidence from the entity that originally generated the underlying information. This prevents downstream presentation from being confused with upstream origin. Provenance Creates Context Validation becomes stronger when the pathway through which evidence reached the validation process can be reconstructed. That pathway may include: Origin → Generation → Recording → Transformation → Transmission → Aggregation → Storage → Retrieval → Validation Use Not every validation requires forensic reconstruction of every step. The required provenance depth should remain proportionate to the Validation Purpose, Depth, risk, consequence, and intended reliance. Source Lineage Reveals Hidden Dependence Ten apparently different sources may ultimately depend upon one original source. For example: multiple reports, multiple news articles, multiple databases, or multiple AI systems may all reproduce information derived from the same underlying dataset. Without lineage governance, these may appear to provide independent confirmation. VSRS makes the underlying dependence visible. Primary and Derived Sources VALIDOS™ distinguishes between primary and derived sources. A Primary Source originates the relevant observation, measurement, record, or event representation. A Derived Source obtains its evidentiary content through another source or transformation. Derived sources are not inherently weak. They may provide highly valuable: analysis, aggregation, interpretation, normalization, or contextualization. But their derivation must remain visible where it materially affects validation reliability. Capability Before Reputation Source reputation alone is not enough. A globally respected institution may be highly capable in one domain and inappropriate for another. Likewise, a small technical system may provide extremely reliable primary measurements within a narrow operational function. VSRS therefore asks: Is the source capable of performing the evidentiary role assigned to it? This shifts validation away from reputation-based trust toward role-specific reliability. Competence Where Judgment Matters Where evidence depends materially upon human or institutional judgment, competence may become important. Relevant considerations may include: expertise, qualification, experience, methodological understanding, domain knowledge, and demonstrated capability. VSRS does not create universal professional qualification rules. It governs whether the competence available is proportionate to the validation role being performed. Authority Is Not Reliability VALIDOS™ establishes an important distinction: Authority ≠ Reliability Authority may create a legitimate right to issue a decision, certification, opinion, or official record. Reliability concerns whether the source can be sufficiently relied upon for the particular evidentiary role. The two may overlap. They are not identical. Independence Matters Validation evidence may sometimes require independent sources. But independence is more complex than asking whether two organizations have different names. A source may be: organizationally independent, financially dependent, methodologically dependent, operationally independent, informationally dependent, analytically independent, or decisionally dependent. VSRS therefore treats independence as multidimensional. Multiple Sources Do Not Automatically Mean Independent Sources This distinction is particularly important. Suppose five reports support the same validation conclusion. If all five reports rely upon the same original dataset, they do not necessarily represent five independent evidentiary origins. VALIDOS™ therefore distinguishes: Source Count from: Source Independence and: Source Independence from: Source Diversity This prevents artificial corroboration. Conflict Does Not Automatically Mean Unreliable A conflict of interest is a governance condition, not an automatic verdict. A source may have a financial, organizational, reputational, contractual, competitive, or personal interest and still provide accurate evidence. But the conflict should be visible. VSRS therefore asks whether a conflict: exists, is material, can influence the evidentiary role, requires additional controls, requires corroboration, limits reliance, or materially affects Source Reliability. Incentives Matter Even Without Formal Conflict Sources operate within incentive structures. A source may be encouraged to: report favorable outcomes, minimize failures, emphasize particular metrics, omit uncertainty, select convenient evidence, or frame results strategically. VSRS allows these incentives to become part of source-reliability assessment where they materially affect validation. Intermediaries Create Additional Governance Conditions Evidence often does not travel directly from origin to validator. It may pass through systems that: translate, aggregate, filter, summarize, normalize, classify, anonymize, compress, or reinterpret it. Each material intermediary can change the evidentiary pathway. VSRS therefore governs the source chain rather than assuming that the final provider represents the complete origin. Transformation Can Change Meaning Evidence transformation may be legitimate and necessary. But transformation can also: remove detail, alter granularity, introduce assumptions, change statistical properties, hide uncertainty, or modify interpretation. VSRS therefore keeps material transformations visible. The question is not whether transformation occurred. The question is whether the transformation pathway remains sufficiently governable for validation reliance. Corroboration Must Be Real Corroboration can strengthen validation. But repeated information does not automatically create corroboration. VALIDOS™ establishes: Repetition ≠ Independent Corroboration True corroboration requires sufficient independence between the relevant evidentiary origins. VSRS therefore evaluates whether apparently converging sources possess hidden shared dependencies. Convergence Can Increase Confidence Where multiple sufficiently independent sources reach compatible evidentiary outcomes, confidence may increase. But convergence itself must remain governed. Several sources may converge because they share: the same dataset, the same methodology, the same upstream information, the same bias, the same model, or the same institutional assumptions. VSRS therefore asks not only: Do the sources agree? but: Why do the sources agree? Source Reliability Is Role-Specific A source should not simply receive a permanent label: Trusted or: Untrusted A source may be: Reliable for measurement Conditionally Reliable for interpretation and: Unreliable for conclusions outside its competence at the same time. VSRS therefore attaches reliability to the source-role relationship. Source Reliability Can Be Conditional A source may be reliable only under defined conditions. Examples include: a calibrated instrument within a specified range, an expert within a defined professional domain, a database within a defined period, a model within a specific version, a laboratory under defined procedures, or an organization within a specific jurisdiction. Conditional reliability must remain attached to subsequent validation use. Source Reliability Can Change Source reliability is not necessarily permanent. It may change because of: source modification, ownership change, system compromise, expired calibration, personnel change, newly discovered conflict, methodology change, altered incentives, new upstream dependencies, or newly discovered provenance information. VSRS therefore treats source reliability as a lifecycle condition. Reliability Can Expire Some Source Reliability Determinations should have a defined period of applicability. For example, reliability may depend upon: current calibration, active certification, current competence, current independence, a specific system version, or a particular organizational condition. Expiration does not automatically mean that the source becomes unreliable. It means that the previous reliability determination should no longer be assumed current. Source Reliability Is Not Truth This boundary is critical. VALIDOS™ establishes: Reliable Source ≠ True Claim A highly reliable source can be wrong. A historically unreliable source can occasionally provide correct information. VSRS does not transform source reputation into truth. It governs how much methodological reliance the source relationship can legitimately support within validation. Source Reliability Is Not Evidence Fitness Likewise: Reliable Source ≠ Fit Evidence A highly reliable source may provide evidence irrelevant to the current validation. And: Fit Evidence ≠ Reliable Source Highly relevant evidence may originate from an uncertain source. This separation is one of the structural strengths of VALIDOS™. Source Reliability Is Not Validation Even: Fit Evidence + Reliable Source does not mean: Validation Object Valid Those conditions merely establish a stronger evidentiary basis upon which subsequent Validation Execution and Validation Determination can operate. VALIDOS™ therefore prevents premature validity conclusions at every stage. Position Within VALIDOS™ Validation Source Reliability Standard is the sixth Parent Standard of VALIDOS™ — Validation Governance Architecture. Its architectural position is: Validation Object → Validation Purpose & Scope → Validation Criteria → Validation Method → Validation Evidence Fitness → Validation Source Reliability → Validation Execution → Validation Determination → Validation State → Validation Reliance & Revalidation The architecture has now progressed from defining the validation problem to establishing both: what evidence is fit and: whether the sources behind that evidence can be relied upon. Relationship to Other OOF® Architectures VSRS operates alongside complementary OOF® architectures. OBIDENITY® may establish origin, identity, ownership, provenance, transfer, and continuity relationships. INTEGROS® may establish integrity conditions affecting sources and evidentiary pathways. GOA™ may establish governance authority and structural responsibilities. AGA™ may establish accountability relationships concerning evidence generation, transformation, review, and use. ORA™ may establish whether source information corresponds to operational reality. AIG®, CLIA®, MGIA™, and ASGA™ may create specialized source conditions for AI behavior, cognition, memory, and autonomous systems. RIS™ may influence the required strength of source assurance according to risk and consequence. VSRS does not duplicate these architectures. It consumes relevant governed information and answers a narrower validation-specific question: What does this information mean for the reliability of this source in this validation role? Why It Matters Modern validation increasingly depends upon complex evidence chains. An AI validation may involve: Sensor → Dataset → Data Processor → Model → Analytical Tool → Human Evaluator → Validation Record A scientific validation may involve: Experiment → Instrument → Researcher → Statistical Processing → Publication → Secondary Analysis An operational validation may involve: Event → System Log → Aggregator → Dashboard → Analyst → Validation Decision At every transition, source relationships matter. VSRS provides a methodology for making those relationships visible and governable. From Source Trust to Source Governance Traditional validation may ask: Do we trust this source? VALIDOS™ replaces this with a stronger set of questions: Who or what is the source? What role does it perform? Where did its information originate? What transformations occurred? Is it capable of performing this role? Is it independent where independence matters? What dependencies exist? What conflicts or incentives exist? What are the boundaries of its reliability? Can the source relationship be reconstructed? This transforms source trust from an intuitive judgment into a governable methodological structure. Foundational Principle Evidence cannot become more trustworthy merely because its source remains unquestioned. Canonical Closing Statement Validation Source Reliability Standard establishes the source-qualification layer of VALIDOS™ — Validation Governance Architecture. By separating source reliability from evidence fitness, truth, authority, and final validity, and by governing source identity, attribution, provenance, lineage, capability, competence, independence, dependence, conflicts, incentives, intermediaries, transformations, corroboration, convergence, limitations, uncertainty, change, expiration, and traceability, VSRS transforms source trust from an assumption into a governable validation condition. title: Validation Source Capability & Competence Module (VSCCM)
text: Validation Source Capability & Competence Module (VSCCM) Validation Source Capability & Competence Module (VSCCM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VALIDOS™ — Validation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Validation Source Reliability Standard (VSRS) Operational Layer: Validation Source Reliability Governance Layer Category: AI & Interpretation Subcategory: Validation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Validation Source Capability & Competence Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 9 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS® · ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Validation Source Capability & Competence Canonical Definition Validation Source Capability & Competence Module (VSCCM) defines the governance framework for determining whether an identified Validation Source possesses the technical, operational, methodological, informational, professional, analytical, observational, measurement, or domain-specific capability and competence necessary to perform the evidentiary role assigned to it within a governed validation process. It establishes the conditions under which an identifiable and traceable source may be recognized as capable and sufficiently competent for a specific validation-source role. Operational Role VSCCM serves as the third internal governance space of the Validation Source Reliability Standard. The preceding modules establish: VSIAM — Who or what is the source, and can the evidence be attributed to it? VSPLM — Where did the evidence originate, how did it reach validation, and upon which upstream sources does it depend? VSCCM asks: Is the source actually capable and sufficiently competent to perform the evidentiary role assigned to it? The governed progression is: Identified Source → Defined Source Role → Capability Requirements → Capability Assessment → Competence Requirements → Competence Assessment → Role Fitness Determination VSCCM does not determine overall Source Reliability. It establishes whether the source possesses the functional capability and competence required for its assigned role. Module Operational Space VSCCM governs: validation-source capability, source competence, role capability, technical capability, measurement capability, observational capability, operational capability, analytical capability, methodological capability, informational capability, professional competence, domain competence, system capability, instrument capability, capability boundaries, competence boundaries, capability evidence, competence evidence, capability limitations, competence limitations, capability uncertainty, competence uncertainty, capability degradation, competence degradation, capability change, competence change, and capability-and-competence traceability. Module Function VSCCM applies after source identity, attribution, provenance, and material lineage have been sufficiently established. Its function is to prevent: source reputation being mistaken for functional capability, institutional authority being mistaken for technical competence, professional qualification being assumed relevant to every domain, a measuring instrument being used outside its validated range, an AI model being treated as competent outside its demonstrated capabilities, access to information being mistaken for ability to interpret it, operational experience being mistaken for methodological expertise, historical competence being assumed current, capability in one role being transferred automatically to another, and source confidence being mistaken for source competence. Capability and Competence Are Related but Distinct VALIDOS™ distinguishes: Capability from: Competence Capability asks: Can the source technically, operationally, informationally, or functionally perform the evidentiary task? Competence asks: Does the source possess sufficient knowledge, expertise, methodological understanding, qualification, or demonstrated proficiency to perform the role appropriately? A source may possess one without fully possessing the other. Capability Is Role-Specific Capability is not a universal property. A source may be highly capable in one role and incapable in another. For example: A sensor may be highly capable of measuring temperature. It may have no capability to determine structural integrity. A financial analyst may be highly competent in market analysis. That does not establish medical competence. An AI model may perform strongly in document classification. That does not establish capability for autonomous safety decisions. VALIDOS™ therefore establishes: Capability must be assessed against the exact evidentiary role assigned to the source. Source Role Requirements Before capability can be assessed, the source role must be sufficiently defined. Possible roles may include: measurement, observation, recording, analysis, interpretation, classification, aggregation, transformation, expert judgment, monitoring, data provision, operational reporting, or another evidentiary function. Each role may create different capability and competence requirements. Technical Capability Technical capability concerns whether a source possesses the technical means necessary to perform its assigned role. Relevant considerations may include: hardware capability, software capability, system functionality, computational capability, instrument specification, measurement range, resolution, detection limits, interoperability, or technical operating conditions. Technical capability should be assessed relative to the validation requirement rather than assumed from system availability. Measurement Capability Where a source generates measurements, VSCCM examines whether it is capable of measuring the relevant property with sufficient: range, sensitivity, precision, resolution, repeatability, stability, and operational suitability. The Evidence Adequacy Standard governs whether the resulting evidence is adequate. VSCCM governs whether the source itself is capable of producing the type of measurement required. Observational Capability Some sources generate evidence through observation rather than direct measurement. Observational capability may depend upon: access, visibility, detection ability, observation conditions, temporal presence, system coverage, or another factor affecting what the source could actually observe. A source cannot reliably report conditions it had no meaningful capability to observe. Operational Capability A source may need sufficient operational access or operational functionality. For example: A monitoring system may be technically sophisticated but unable to observe a subsystem outside its telemetry coverage. An employee may understand an operation but lack access to the relevant event. An external auditor may possess expertise but not direct operational visibility. VSCCM distinguishes theoretical capability from actual operational capability. Informational Capability A source may possess competence but lack access to the information necessary to perform the assigned role. Informational capability asks whether the source had sufficient access to: relevant data, records, system states, documentation, events, or other required information. This prevents expertise from compensating for absence of information. Analytical Capability Where a source performs analysis, VSCCM evaluates whether it possesses sufficient capability to execute the required analytical function. This may concern: statistical analysis, computational analysis, causal analysis, comparative analysis, risk analysis, pattern recognition, model evaluation, or another defined analytical task. The correctness of the Validation Method remains governed separately. VSCCM determines whether the source can legitimately perform the analytical role assigned to it. Methodological Capability A source may possess domain knowledge while lacking the methodological capability required by a specific validation process. Methodological capability may concern: experimental design, statistical reasoning, validation methodology, evidence interpretation, uncertainty analysis, sampling, simulation, or another relevant methodological function. VSCCM therefore prevents domain expertise from automatically implying methodological competence. Professional Competence Where professional judgment materially contributes to Validation Evidence, VSCCM may assess: qualifications, certifications, professional standing, relevant experience, demonstrated proficiency, specialized training, or equivalent competence indicators. Formal credentials may support competence. They do not automatically establish competence for every assigned role. Domain Competence Domain competence concerns whether the source possesses sufficient understanding of the subject matter relevant to the evidentiary role. Domains may include: medicine, finance, engineering, cybersecurity, law, industrial operations, artificial intelligence, infrastructure, or another specialized field. Competence should remain bounded to the domain actually demonstrated. Experience and Competence Experience can strengthen competence. However: Experience ≠ Automatic Competence Long experience with an outdated methodology may not establish current competence. Likewise, limited formal experience may coexist with strong demonstrated capability. VSCCM therefore allows multiple forms of competence evidence rather than relying upon one indicator. Certification and Competence Certification may provide evidence of competence within its defined scope. VALIDOS™ establishes: Certification ≠ Universal Competence A certification may be: scope-limited, time-limited, jurisdiction-limited, version-specific, role-specific, or dependent upon continued conditions. VSCCM therefore examines what the certification actually demonstrates. Authority and Competence Authority may permit a source to act. Competence determines whether the source can perform the assigned evidentiary role appropriately. Therefore: Authority to Act ≠ Competence to Validate An institution may possess legal authority while relying upon specialized experts or technical systems for evidentiary functions. VSCCM preserves this distinction. AI Source Capability Where an AI model or AI system acts as a Validation Source, capability assessment may include: model function, model version, demonstrated task performance, context-window limitations, modality limitations, tool access, information access, known failure modes, uncertainty behavior, and operating constraints. Model scale, popularity, or general benchmark performance does not automatically establish capability for the specific validation role. Autonomous Source Capability Where an autonomous system generates Validation Evidence, capability assessment may additionally consider: sensor access, decision boundaries, operating permissions, environmental awareness, state visibility, system dependencies, and operational constraints. Autonomy does not establish evidentiary competence by itself. Instrument Capability Measurement instruments may possess defined operating boundaries. These may include: calibration range, environmental tolerance, sensitivity, measurement uncertainty, operating temperature, sampling frequency, or another technical constraint. Evidence generated outside those boundaries may require qualification. Capability Boundary A Capability Boundary defines the conditions within which a source can legitimately perform its evidentiary role. The boundary may concern: task type, domain, measurement range, environment, population, system version, information access, operating state, or another relevant condition. Capability must not silently extend beyond demonstrated boundaries. Competence Boundary A Competence Boundary defines the scope within which demonstrated knowledge, expertise, qualification, or proficiency remains relevant. For example: A specialist may possess deep competence within one medical discipline but not another. An AI model may demonstrate competence on one task family but not on a materially different task. Competence should therefore remain explicitly bounded. Capability Evidence Capability claims should themselves possess supporting evidence where material. Capability evidence may include: technical specifications, calibration records, performance tests, proficiency results, operational history, benchmark results, certification, controlled demonstrations, or other appropriate evidence. VSCCM does not require one universal evidence type. The evidence should correspond to the capability claim being made. Competence Evidence Competence evidence may include: qualifications, certifications, training records, demonstrated performance, relevant experience, professional assessments, peer review, proficiency testing, or another defensible competence indicator. The strength required should remain proportionate to the validation role. Self-Declared Capability A source may claim its own capability or competence. Self-declaration may provide information. It does not automatically establish the claim. Where validation consequence is significant, independent or externally verifiable capability evidence may be required. Capability Limitation A source may be capable overall while possessing known limitations. Examples include: reduced precision at boundary conditions, limited language coverage, limited population representation, inability to observe certain system states, limited historical access, or reduced performance under degraded conditions. Limitations must remain visible in subsequent Source Reliability governance. Competence Limitation Competence may also be limited. Examples include: narrow specialization, outdated training, insufficient experience with a new system, lack of methodological expertise, or incomplete understanding of a relevant domain. A limitation does not automatically make the source unusable. It constrains the role for which competence can legitimately be claimed. Capability Uncertainty Where available information is insufficient to establish capability, VSCCM preserves: Capability Undetermined rather than assuming capability from reputation, authority, or availability. Competence Uncertainty Where competence cannot be sufficiently established, VSCCM preserves: Competence Undetermined This may require: additional evidence, independent assessment, restricted source role, corroboration, or another governance response. Capability Status VSCCM may establish: Capability Established The source possesses sufficient capability for the defined evidentiary role. Capability Conditionally Established Capability exists only within specified boundaries or conditions. Capability Undetermined Available information is insufficient to determine capability. Capability Insufficient The source does not possess sufficient capability for the proposed role. Competence Status VSCCM may establish: Competence Established The source possesses sufficient competence for the assigned evidentiary role. Competence Conditionally Established Competence is sufficient only within defined conditions or boundaries. Competence Undetermined Available information is insufficient to establish competence. Competence Insufficient The source does not possess sufficient competence for the assigned role. Role Fitness Capability and competence are integrated into a Source Role Fitness assessment. Possible outcomes may include: Role Fit Conditionally Role Fit Role Fitness Undetermined Role Unfit Role Fitness remains an input into overall Source Reliability Determination. It is not itself a Source Reliability status. Capability Degradation Capability may degrade because of: equipment aging, calibration loss, software degradation, infrastructure failure, reduced information access, model drift, system modification, environmental change, or another material condition. Historical capability should not automatically be treated as permanent. Competence Degradation Competence may degrade because of: outdated knowledge, expired qualifications, loss of practice, domain evolution, methodology change, or changed role requirements. Competence may therefore require periodic reassessment. Capability Change Capability may improve or decline because of: system upgrade, model update, new tools, additional access, new sensors, improved infrastructure, changed configuration, or altered operating conditions. Material changes must remain traceable. Competence Change Competence may change through: training, certification, experience, role change, specialization, methodological development, or loss of required qualification. VSCCM preserves the temporal relationship between competence and the evidence produced. Capability at Time of Evidence Generation A critical rule is: Current capability does not automatically prove historical capability. The relevant question may be whether the source possessed sufficient capability when the evidence was generated. Likewise: Historical capability does not automatically establish current capability. VSCCM therefore keeps capability temporally situated. Competence at Time of Contribution Where competence materially affects evidence, the relevant competence state is the one existing when the source performed the evidentiary role. Subsequent qualification cannot automatically repair an earlier competence deficiency. Capability and Evidence Adequacy VSCCM maintains a strict boundary with VEFS. VEFS asks: Is the resulting evidence adequate? VSCCM asks: Was the source capable and competent to perform the role that produced or handled that evidence? A capable source may produce inadequate evidence. An apparently adequate evidence item may have been produced by a source whose capability cannot be established. Both conditions require separate governance. Capability and Source Reliability Capability is necessary for many source roles. But: Capability ≠ Source Reliability A technically capable source may still be: conflicted, dependent, manipulated, compromised, or otherwise unreliable. VSCCM therefore provides one component of Source Reliability governance. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Establish Source Role Identify the exact evidentiary function performed by the source. 2. Establish Capability Requirements Determine the technical, operational, informational, analytical, methodological, or other capabilities required for that role. 3. Assess Source Capability Evaluate whether the source possesses the required capability within the relevant conditions. 4. Establish Competence Requirements Where judgment or expertise matters, identify the knowledge, qualification, experience, or proficiency required. 5. Assess Source Competence Evaluate the available competence evidence. 6. Establish Boundaries and Limitations Define material: capability boundaries, competence boundaries, limitations, conditions, and uncertainty. 7. Establish Capability & Competence Status Classify the relevant source conditions. 8. Determine Source Role Fitness Determine whether the source is: Role Fit, Conditionally Role Fit, Role Fitness Undetermined, or Role Unfit. 9. Preserve Lifecycle Traceability Maintain: Validation Source reference, Source Role, capability requirements, capability evidence, Capability Status, competence requirements, competence evidence, Competence Status, capability boundaries, competence boundaries, limitations, uncertainty, Role Fitness, evidence-generation time, change history, reassessment triggers, and sufficient lifecycle traceability. Capability & Competence Outputs VSCCM may produce: Source Capability Profile, Source Capability Assessment, Source Competence Profile, Source Competence Assessment, Technical Capability Record, Measurement Capability Record, Observational Capability Record, Operational Capability Record, Informational Capability Record, Analytical Capability Record, Methodological Capability Record, Capability Boundary, Competence Boundary, Capability Limitation Record, Competence Limitation Record, Capability Status, Competence Status, Source Role Fitness Determination, Capability Change Record, Competence Change Record, and Capability & Competence Reassessment Trigger. Use Case 1 — Industrial Sensor Scenario A validation relies upon measurements from an industrial sensor. Application VSCCM determines that the sensor is calibrated and technically capable within a defined measurement range. Some measurements were generated beyond that range. Result The sensor may remain Role Fit within its established Capability Boundary while measurements outside that boundary cannot derive source-capability confidence from the same determination. Use Case 2 — AI Validation Source Scenario An AI model is used to classify technical incident reports during validation. Application VSCCM evaluates the specific model version, demonstrated classification performance, domain limitations, language coverage, information access, and known failure conditions. Result Strong general model performance is not treated as universal competence. The AI source receives a role-specific capability determination. Use Case 3 — Expert Assessment Scenario A highly experienced engineer provides an expert interpretation of a medical-device software failure. Application VSCCM distinguishes engineering competence from the specialized medical and clinical competence potentially required for parts of the assessment. Result The expert may be Role Fit for technical failure analysis while additional expertise is required for clinical conclusions. Architectural Position Validation Source Capability & Competence is the third internal governance space of the Validation Source Reliability Standard (VSRS). The progression now becomes: Source Identity & Attribution → Source Provenance & Lineage → Source Capability & Competence VSIAM establishes: Who or what is the source? VSPLM establishes: Where did its evidence originate and upon what does it depend? VSCCM establishes: Can the source actually perform the evidentiary role assigned to it? The next governance stage can then examine: Is the source sufficiently independent, and what conflicts, incentives, or dependencies may affect its evidentiary role? The VSRS progression therefore continues: Identity & Attribution → Provenance & Lineage → Capability & Competence → Independence & Conflict → Source Reliability Determination Foundational Principle A source should not be trusted to perform an evidentiary role merely because it exists, is authoritative, or appears credible; it must be capable and sufficiently competent for that role. Canonical Closing Statement Validation Source Capability & Competence Module establishes the functional qualification layer of source reliability governance within VALIDOS™ by determining whether Validation Sources possess the technical, operational, informational, analytical, methodological, professional, and domain-specific capability and competence required for their assigned evidentiary roles. By governing role requirements, demonstrated capability, competence evidence, boundaries, limitations, uncertainty, degradation, change, temporal fitness, and Source Role Fitness, VSCCM prevents reputation, authority, access, certification, or confidence from substituting for demonstrated ability to perform the evidentiary function upon which validation depends.
