title: Validation Source Reliability Determination Module (VSRDM)
text: Validation Source Reliability Determination Module (VSRDM) Validation Source Reliability Determination Module (VSRDM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VALIDOS™ — Validation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Validation Source Reliability Standard (VSRS) Operational Layer: Validation Source Reliability Governance Layer Category: AI & Interpretation Subcategory: Validation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Validation Source Reliability Determination Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 9 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS® · ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Validation Source Reliability Determination Canonical Definition Validation Source Reliability Determination Module (VSRDM) defines the governance framework for integrating source identity, attribution, provenance, lineage, capability, competence, independence, conflicts, incentives, dependencies, transformations, limitations, uncertainty, corroboration, and source-role requirements into a formal determination of whether a Validation Source can be sufficiently relied upon for its assigned role within a governed validation process. It establishes the final source-reliability governance gate between Source Qualification and subsequent Validation Execution Governance within VALIDOS™. Operational Role VSRDM serves as the fifth and final internal governance space of the Validation Source Reliability Standard. The preceding modules establish: VSIAM — Validation Source Identity & Attribution VSPLM — Validation Source Provenance & Lineage VSCCM — Validation Source Capability & Competence VSICM — Validation Source Independence & Conflict VSRDM asks: Considering the complete governed source relationship, can this source be sufficiently relied upon for the validation role assigned to it? The governed progression is: Identified Source → Traceable Source → Capable & Competent Source → Independence & Conflict Assessment → Integrated Reliability Assessment → Source Reliability Determination VSRDM does not determine whether Validation Evidence is fit. It does not determine whether the Validation Object is valid. It determines whether the complete source relationship supporting Validation Evidence is sufficiently reliable for its assigned validation role. Module Operational Space VSRDM governs: integrated source reliability, source-reliability determination, source-reliability status, source-role reliability, reliability materiality, provenance reliability, capability contribution, competence contribution, independence contribution, conflict contribution, dependency contribution, transformation contribution, corroboration contribution, reliability limitations, reliability uncertainty, reliability conditions, reliability restrictions, source reliability readiness, source reliability expiration, source reliability reassessment, source reliability suspension, source reliability withdrawal, reliability continuity, and source-reliability traceability. Module Function VSRDM applies after the material source conditions have been assessed through the preceding VSRS modules. Its function is to prevent: source reliability being reduced to reputation, perfect source identity being mistaken for reliability, strong competence overriding severe conflicts automatically, independence being treated as sufficient without capability, multiple source strengths being blindly averaged, unresolved provenance gaps disappearing during final assessment, conditional source relationships being represented as unconditional trust, corroboration being counted without accounting for shared lineage, source uncertainty being converted into confidence, and qualified sources being treated as globally reliable beyond the role actually assessed. Source Reliability as an Integrated Condition VALIDOS™ treats Source Reliability as an integrated governance condition. Reliability cannot be established from one characteristic alone. VSRDM considers the complete source structure across: Identity & Attribution Provenance & Lineage Capability & Competence Independence & Conflict together with material: Dependencies Transformations Corroboration Limitations Uncertainty and: Assigned Source Role A source may perform strongly across several dimensions while remaining unreliable for one critical evidentiary role because of a material weakness elsewhere. Reliability Integration Principle VSRDM establishes: Source reliability should not be determined through blind averaging. For example: Strong competence cannot automatically neutralize an uncontrolled conflict. Perfect independence cannot compensate for lack of capability. Clear source identity cannot compensate for unknown provenance where provenance is critical. Multiple favorable reports cannot compensate for one shared compromised upstream source. Reliability determination must therefore remain materiality-sensitive. Source Reliability Inputs VSRDM may consume governed outputs including: Source Identity Records, Evidence Attribution Records, Provenance Records, Source Lineage Maps, Provenance Gap Records, Source Capability Assessments, Source Competence Assessments, Source Role Fitness Determinations, Source Independence Assessments, Conflict-of-Interest Records, Dependency Maps, Source Incentive Records, Corroboration Independence Assessments, transformation records, limitations, uncertainty, Validation Purpose, Validation Scope, Validation Depth, Validation Criteria, and assigned Source Role. These inputs form the basis of the integrated Source Reliability Determination. Source Role Reliability Reliability is always assessed relative to a specific source role. A source may therefore be: Reliable as a measurement source while: Conditionally Reliable as an interpreter and: Unreliable as an independent assurance source at the same time. VALIDOS™ establishes: Source Reliability is role-specific, not universal. Reliability Materiality Not every source weakness has equal significance. VSRDM may distinguish conditions that are: immaterial, minor, material, critical, or validation-blocking. Materiality may depend upon: the source role, evidence criticality, Validation Criterion affected, Validation Depth, intended reliance, consequence of error, source substitutability, and availability of independent corroboration. A critical source weakness must not disappear because the overall source profile is otherwise strong. Critical Source Role Certain source roles may be critical to validation. Examples may include: sole measurement source, primary evidence origin, only available expert source, critical benchmark provider, sole operational record system, or independent assurance source. Where a critical source is materially unreliable, downstream validation may require: replacement, additional corroboration, reduced scope, restricted reliance, or further governance action. Provenance Reliability Contribution Provenance and lineage affect reliability by revealing: origin clarity, upstream dependencies, transformation history, shared-source concentration, hidden intermediaries, or provenance gaps. A source may be otherwise competent and independent while still carrying substantial reliability uncertainty because its evidentiary origin cannot be sufficiently reconstructed. Capability & Competence Contribution Capability and competence contribute to reliability only within the role and boundary in which they were established. A source should not receive reliability credit beyond: its technical capability, operating range, professional competence, domain competence, informational access, or demonstrated task fitness. Independence Contribution Independence may strengthen source reliability where the source is expected to provide unbiased or independent evidence. However: Independent ≠ Automatically Reliable Independence is one reliability dimension. Its significance depends upon the source role. Conflict Contribution A conflict does not automatically produce Source Unreliable status. VSRDM evaluates: conflict type, materiality, transparency, controls, residual conflict, available corroboration, and the role of the source. A controlled minor conflict may coexist with strong reliability. An uncontrolled material conflict in a sole critical source may materially constrain reliability. Dependency Contribution A source may depend upon: external data, common methods, shared infrastructure, upstream sources, analytical tools, or other systems. VSRDM evaluates whether these dependencies materially weaken source reliability or reduce the independence of corroboration. Transformation Contribution Evidence transformations may create reliability conditions. Where a source: aggregates, translates, normalizes, filters, summarizes, classifies, or analytically transforms evidence, VSRDM considers whether the transformation pathway is sufficiently governed for the assigned role. Corroboration Contribution Corroboration may strengthen source reliability confidence where genuinely independent sources support compatible conclusions. However: Corroboration Strength = Agreement × Independence × Lineage Diversity conceptually, not merely source count. VSRDM therefore consumes the independence and lineage findings established earlier rather than counting sources mechanically. Reliability Limitation A source may be reliable while carrying limitations. Examples include: reliable only within one measurement range, reliable only for one population, reliable only for raw data generation, reliable only under current calibration, reliable only within one system version, or reliable only with independent corroboration. Limitations remain part of the Reliability Determination. Reliability Condition A reliability condition specifies what must remain true for the Source Reliability status to remain applicable. Examples include: continued calibration, unchanged model version, continued independence, defined contractual controls, preserved information access, ongoing certification, or continued availability of an independent corroborating source. Conditions must remain visible throughout subsequent validation governance. Reliability Restriction A source may be restricted to a limited validation role. For example: May support evidence generation but not independent assurance. or: May support contextual interpretation but not final technical determination. Role restriction allows useful sources to remain within validation without assigning them authority or confidence beyond their legitimate function. Reliability Uncertainty Where material source conditions remain unresolved, VSRDM preserves uncertainty. Sources may therefore receive: Source Reliability Undetermined rather than being forced into binary trusted/untrusted classifications. Uncertainty may arise from: incomplete provenance, uncertain source identity, competence ambiguity, hidden dependencies, unresolved conflicts, or insufficient independence evidence. Source Reliability Status VSRDM may establish the following canonical source-reliability states: Source Reliable The source is sufficiently identifiable, traceable, capable, competent, appropriately independent, conflict-governed, and reliable for the defined source role. Source Conditionally Reliable The source may perform the assigned validation role only under explicit conditions, limitations, restrictions, corroboration requirements, or other controls. Source Reliability Undetermined Available information is insufficient to establish a defensible Source Reliability Determination. Source Reliability Insufficient Material source-reliability requirements remain unresolved or inadequately supported. Source Unreliable The source cannot legitimately perform the proposed validation role. These statuses apply to the source-role relationship. They do not represent Evidence Fitness or the Validation State of the Validation Object. Reliable Does Not Mean Correct VALIDOS™ establishes: Source Reliable ≠ Every Source Output Correct A reliable source may still make an error. Reliability means that the source relationship is sufficiently trustworthy for the role assigned within validation. The actual evidentiary content must still be governed through the wider validation process. Unreliable Does Not Mean False Likewise: Source Unreliable ≠ Evidence Automatically False Evidence from an unreliable source may occasionally be correct. The reliability status concerns how much governed confidence the source relationship can support. Independent evidence may later confirm the same underlying condition. Source Reliability and Evidence Fitness VSRDM preserves the separation: Evidence Fitness → Is the evidence fit? Source Reliability → Can the source behind it be relied upon? A robust validation may require both. Possible combinations include: Evidence Fit + Source Reliable Evidence Fit + Source Conditionally Reliable Evidence Fit + Source Reliability Undetermined Evidence Unfit + Source Reliable and other combinations. No single combination automatically produces the final Validation Determination. Reliability-Qualified Evidence Basis Once source reliability has been established, the evidence basis can become a Reliability-Qualified Evidence Basis. This does not mean that evidence has become true or that the Validation Object has passed validation. It means that the evidentiary basis now carries both: Evidence Fitness information and: Source Reliability information necessary for subsequent validation execution. Source Reliability Readiness A source relationship may be sufficiently ready for subsequent validation governance when: source identity is established, attribution is sufficient, relevant provenance is available, critical lineage dependencies are understood, capability and competence are adequate, independence requirements are addressed, conflicts are governed, limitations are explicit, and an appropriate Source Reliability status exists. Conditional Progression A Conditionally Reliable source may progress only where the relevant conditions can remain visible and enforceable. Examples include: independent corroboration required, restricted source role, specific version only, use only within defined operating conditions, disclosure required, or enhanced oversight required. These conditions must not disappear during Validation Execution. Source Reliability Expiration A Reliability Determination may expire or require reassessment because of: elapsed time, calibration expiration, qualification expiration, model update, system change, ownership change, organizational restructuring, new conflict, new upstream dependency, provenance correction, competence change, or changed Validation Scope. Expiration means the previous determination can no longer be assumed current. Source Reliability Reassessment Possible reassessment outcomes include: Reliability Maintained Reliability Modified Conditional Reliability Additional Source Qualification Required Reliability Suspended Reliability Withdrawn This prevents historical source trust from persisting after material source conditions have changed. Reliability Suspension A source may require temporary suspension where material concerns arise but cannot yet be fully resolved. Examples include: suspected compromise, unresolved calibration issue, disputed provenance, newly discovered conflict, or pending competence review. Suspension preserves uncertainty without prematurely issuing a final Unreliable determination. Reliability Withdrawal Reliability may be withdrawn where the basis of the previous determination no longer exists. Possible triggers include: source manipulation, proven provenance fraud, critical capability failure, uncontrolled conflict, compromised system, materially false attribution, or another critical reliability failure. Withdrawal must remain traceable. Reliability Continuity Source Reliability information should remain attached to the evidence throughout: Validation Execution → Validation Determination → Validation State → Reliance & Revalidation This preserves the ability to determine which sources supported a later validation result and what reliability conditions applied at the time. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Consolidate Source Reliability Inputs Collect governed outputs from: Source Identity & Attribution, Source Provenance & Lineage, Source Capability & Competence, and Source Independence & Conflict. 2. Identify Material Reliability Conditions Identify: limitations, uncertainties, dependencies, transformations, conflicts, independence conditions, corroboration requirements, and role restrictions. 3. Assess Materiality Determine which conditions are: immaterial, material, critical, or validation-blocking. 4. Assess Role-Specific Reliability Evaluate the source specifically against the evidentiary role it is expected to perform. 5. Establish Reliability Status Classify the source as: Source Reliable, Source Conditionally Reliable, Source Reliability Undetermined, Source Reliability Insufficient, or Source Unreliable. 6. Establish Conditions, Limitations, and Restrictions Define the boundaries within which the Source Reliability status may legitimately apply. 7. Establish Reassessment Triggers Identify material events requiring future review. 8. Create Source Reliability Record Preserve: Validation Source reference, source identity, source role, attribution status, provenance status, lineage structure, capability status, competence status, independence status, conflict status, dependencies, transformations, corroboration information, limitations, uncertainty, restrictions, reliability status, determination basis, effective period, reassessment triggers, version, changes, and sufficient lifecycle traceability. Source Reliability Governance Flow VSRDM completes the VSRS internal progression: Source Identity & Attribution → Source Provenance & Lineage → Source Capability & Competence → Source Independence & Conflict → Source Reliability Determination This transforms an evidentiary source from an assumed origin into a formally governed reliability relationship. Governance Outputs VSRDM may produce: Source Reliability Determination, Source Reliability Record, Source Reliability Status, Reliability-Qualified Evidence Basis, Source Role Reliability Profile, Source Reliability Condition Record, Source Reliability Limitation Record, Source Reliability Restriction Record, Source Reliability Uncertainty Record, Source Reliability Reassessment Trigger, Source Reliability Expiration Condition, Source Reliability Suspension Record, Source Reliability Withdrawal Record, Source Reliability Change Record, and Source Reliability Continuity Reference. Use Case 1 — External AI Safety Assessment Scenario An external consultancy performs an AI safety assessment. The consultancy is technically competent, but the work is funded by the AI vendor and uses several datasets supplied by that vendor. Application VSRDM integrates: established source identity, clear provenance, strong competence, partial informational dependence, financial conflict, and available independent corroboration. Result The consultancy may receive: Source Conditionally Reliable for defined assessment roles, with funding and information dependencies preserved as explicit conditions rather than being ignored or treated as automatic disqualification. Use Case 2 — Industrial Measurement Source Scenario A calibrated industrial sensor provides critical measurements for validation. The sensor is well identified, directly attributable, and technically capable. A recent maintenance event creates uncertainty about calibration continuity. Application VSRDM integrates the otherwise strong reliability profile with the unresolved calibration condition. Result The source may receive: Source Reliability Undetermined or: Source Conditionally Reliable until the calibration condition is resolved. Use Case 3 — Internet Claim Verification Scenario Dozens of online sources repeat the same factual claim. Application VSRDM consumes lineage analysis showing that most sources derive from one original report. Several additional sources rely upon one shared secondary dataset. Result The apparent number of sources does not produce artificial reliability confidence. The actual source structure is assessed according to origin, capability, independence, shared dependencies, and corroboration quality. Architectural Position Validation Source Reliability Determination is the fifth and final internal governance space of the Validation Source Reliability Standard (VSRS). The complete VSRS progression is: Validation Source Identity & Attribution → Validation Source Provenance & Lineage → Validation Source Capability & Competence → Validation Source Independence & Conflict → Validation Source Reliability Determination Together, these five governed spaces transform source trust from an assumption into a structured source-reliability determination. The VALIDOS™ lifecycle can now progress from: Qualified Validation Evidence to: Reliability-Qualified Validation Evidence and then to the next governance question: Was the approved validation process actually executed as governed? Foundational Principle A source becomes reliable for validation only when the complete source relationship supports the role it is expected to perform. Canonical Closing Statement Validation Source Reliability Determination Module completes source-reliability governance within VALIDOS™ by integrating identity, attribution, provenance, lineage, capability, competence, independence, conflicts, incentives, dependencies, transformations, corroboration, limitations, uncertainty, conditions, restrictions, change, and traceability into a formal role-specific Source Reliability Determination. VSRDM ensures that validation confidence is never derived from source reputation, authority, popularity, repetition, or apparent independence alone, but from a reconstructable and governable source relationship capable of legitimately supporting the evidentiary role upon which validation depends. title: Validation Source Reliability Standard
text: Validation Source Reliability Standard Validation Source Reliability Standard Standard ID: VSRS OriginID: OOF-OID-AI-VALIDOS-VSRS-2026-08-09-0006 Architecture: VALIDOS™ — Validation Governance Architecture Category: AI & Interpretation Subcategory: Validation Governance Type: Parent Standard Governed Space: Validation Source Reliability Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 9 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS® · ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Canonical Definition Validation Source Reliability Standard (VSRS) defines the governance conditions under which sources providing, generating, transmitting, recording, transforming, interpreting, or maintaining Validation Evidence are identified, attributable, provenance-aware, independence-assessed, integrity-aware, competence-aware, conflict-aware, and sufficiently reliable for their assigned role within a governed validation process. Canonical Definition Extension Evidence does not exist independently of origin. It is generated, observed, recorded, measured, transmitted, transformed, interpreted, stored, or supplied by one or more sources. A piece of evidence may be highly relevant, applicable, comprehensive, and adequate while the reliability of the source behind that evidence remains uncertain. VALIDOS™ therefore separates: Evidence Fitness from: Source Reliability Validation Source Reliability Standard governs the second question. It establishes the conditions necessary to determine: where Validation Evidence originated, which source produced or supplied it, whether the source can be sufficiently identified, whether attribution can be established, whether provenance is sufficiently reconstructable, whether the source possesses the required competence or capability, whether relevant independence exists, whether conflicts of interest are visible, whether the evidence passed through intermediaries, whether material transformations occurred, whether source integrity conditions are known, whether corroboration is required, whether source reliability has materially changed, and whether the source can legitimately support the evidentiary role assigned to it. VSRS does not determine whether evidence is relevant or adequate. It does not determine whether the Validation Object is valid. It determines whether the source relationship behind Validation Evidence is sufficiently reliable for governed validation use. Core Question Can the source behind Validation Evidence be sufficiently identified, traced, assessed, and relied upon for the validation role assigned to it? Purpose The purpose of Validation Source Reliability Standard is to prevent validation confidence from being derived from evidence whose source basis is unknown, insufficiently attributable, materially conflicted, methodologically incapable, excessively dependent, provenance-deficient, or otherwise unreliable. The standard prevents validation from silently treating: anonymous origin as established origin, publication as reliability, institutional authority as universal competence, repetition as independence, multiple intermediaries as multiple independent sources, source popularity as methodological credibility, source confidence as evidence quality, and source reputation as permanent reliability. VSRS creates a governed source-reliability layer between qualified evidence and subsequent validation execution. Governance Objective VSRS establishes a governed Validation Source Reliability Framework capable of determining whether sources behind Validation Evidence possess sufficient reliability for their assigned validation roles. The standard seeks to ensure that: source identity is sufficiently established, source attribution is traceable, provenance is reconstructable, source roles are explicit, material intermediaries are visible, material transformations are traceable, competence is proportionate to the source role, independence is assessed where required, conflicts of interest remain visible, source dependencies are identifiable, corroboration requirements can be established, source reliability conditions remain bounded, reliability change can be detected, and source reliability can be formally determined. Operational Role Validation Source Reliability Standard serves as the source-qualification stage of the VALIDOS™ validation lifecycle. The preceding architecture establishes: Validation Object → Validation Purpose & Scope → Validation Criteria → Validation Method → Validation Evidence Fitness VSRS then asks: Can the sources underlying that qualified evidence basis be sufficiently relied upon? Its structural progression is: Qualified Validation Evidence → Source Identification → Source Provenance → Source Capability → Independence & Conflict Assessment → Source Reliability Determination → Reliability-Qualified Evidence Basis The resulting source-qualified evidence basis can then progress into Validation Execution governance. Governance Scope Validation Source Reliability Standard governs: validation-source identification, source attribution, source origin, source provenance, source lineage, source roles, source capability, source competence, source authority where relevant, source independence, source dependence, conflicts of interest, source incentives, source intermediaries, evidence transformations, source integrity conditions, source corroboration, source convergence, source reliability limitations, source reliability uncertainty, source reliability status, source reliability change, source reliability expiration, source reliability reassessment, and source-reliability traceability. Validation Source For the purposes of VALIDOS™, a Validation Source is any identifiable entity, system, process, instrument, repository, person, organization, model, sensor, database, document origin, operational environment, or other origin capable of materially contributing Validation Evidence. A source may: generate evidence, observe evidence, record evidence, measure evidence, transform evidence, transmit evidence, interpret evidence, aggregate evidence, preserve evidence, or provide evidence. Different source roles may require different reliability conditions. Source Identity Source reliability cannot be meaningfully governed where the relevant source cannot be sufficiently distinguished. Source identity may require identification of: source entity, source instance, system, instrument, organization, individual, repository, model, dataset origin, version, or another relevant source representation. The required identity precision should correspond to the validation role and consequence. Source Attribution VSRS governs whether Validation Evidence can be sufficiently attributed to the source claimed to have generated, observed, recorded, transmitted, or supplied it. Attribution may be: Direct Derived Intermediated Aggregated Uncertain or: Unattributed Attribution status must remain visible where it materially affects source reliability. Source Provenance Provenance establishes the history through which evidence reached the validation process. The governed progression may include: Origin → Generation → Recording → Transformation → Transmission → Aggregation → Storage → Retrieval → Validation Use Not every validation requires complete reconstruction of every technical event. The required provenance depth must be proportionate to the evidentiary role, Validation Depth, and consequence of reliance. Source Lineage Evidence may derive from multiple upstream sources. A final report, dataset, benchmark, or analytical output may represent a downstream source while depending upon: primary observations, external datasets, prior studies, other models, third-party measurements, or aggregated records. VSRS requires material upstream dependencies to remain visible where they affect reliability. Primary and Derived Sources VALIDOS™ distinguishes between: Primary Source and: Derived Source A Primary Source originates the relevant observation, measurement, record, or event representation. A Derived Source obtains its evidentiary content through another source or transformation. Derived evidence is not automatically less reliable. However, derivation creates additional lineage and transformation conditions that may require governance. Source Capability A source must be capable of performing the evidentiary role assigned to it. Capability may concern: measurement capability, observation capability, technical capability, analytical capability, domain capability, operational access, data access, or another relevant function. A source may be highly reputable while lacking capability for a particular evidentiary role. Source Competence Where human, institutional, professional, or analytical judgment contributes materially to Validation Evidence, competence may require assessment. Relevant considerations may include: expertise, qualification, experience, methodological understanding, domain knowledge, or demonstrated capability. VSRS does not establish universal professional qualification requirements. It governs whether competence is sufficient for the role assigned within validation. Source Authority and Source Reliability Authority may be relevant but is not equivalent to reliability. VALIDOS™ establishes: Source Authority ≠ Source Reliability An authoritative institution may be highly reliable within its governed domain while remaining unsuitable for conclusions outside its competence or evidentiary role. Likewise, a non-authoritative source may provide highly reliable primary evidence. VSRS therefore evaluates reliability according to function rather than title alone. Source Independence Some validation roles require independent evidence. Independence may concern separation from: the Validation Object creator, system operator, financial beneficiary, decision authority, evidence generator, prior evaluator, or another materially interested party. Independence requirements should be proportionate to Validation Purpose, Depth, and consequence. Independence Is Not Binary A source may possess different forms and degrees of independence. Possible dimensions include: organizational independence, financial independence, methodological independence, operational independence, informational independence, analytical independence, and decision independence. A source should not be classified as simply "independent" without regard to the independence dimension relevant to the validation role. Source Dependence Multiple sources may appear independent while relying upon the same upstream origin. For example: ten publications may all repeat information from one original dataset. Counting them as ten independent sources would create false corroboration. VSRS therefore governs source dependence and shared lineage. Conflict of Interest A conflict of interest does not automatically make a source unreliable. It creates a governance condition. Material conflicts may include: financial interest, organizational interest, reputational interest, operational ownership, contractual dependence, competitive interest, personal interest, or another incentive capable of affecting evidentiary behavior. Conflicts should be identified, assessed, and incorporated into the Source Reliability Determination. Source Incentives Source reliability may be affected by incentives even where no formal conflict exists. Incentives may encourage: selective reporting, favorable interpretation, omission, exaggeration, under-reporting, or evidentiary framing. VSRS therefore permits incentive analysis where material to validation reliability. Source Intermediaries Evidence may pass through intermediaries before reaching validation. Intermediaries may: transmit, translate, aggregate, reformat, summarize, filter, classify, or transform evidence. Each material intermediary may create additional provenance and reliability conditions. Evidence Transformation Transformation can change evidentiary meaning. Examples include: aggregation, normalization, translation, compression, filtering, statistical processing, model interpretation, summarization, anonymization, or format conversion. VSRS governs whether material transformations are sufficiently identifiable and traceable. It does not determine whether the resulting evidence is adequate; that remains within VEFS. Source Integrity Conditions VSRS may consume relevant integrity information concerning whether a source, record, system, instrument, or evidentiary pathway has remained protected against material alteration, corruption, substitution, or loss. Where integrity governance is required, INTEGROS® may provide complementary integrity conditions. VSRS uses such information only insofar as it affects source reliability within validation. Source Corroboration Some source roles may require corroboration. Corroboration asks whether materially independent sources support compatible evidentiary conclusions. VSRS distinguishes genuine corroboration from repetition. Repeated information from one upstream source does not constitute independent corroboration. Source Convergence Where multiple sufficiently independent sources converge upon compatible evidence, source reliability confidence may increase. However, convergence must not automatically override: shared bias, shared methodology, shared datasets, shared incentives, or common upstream dependencies. VSRS therefore requires convergence to remain lineage-aware. Source Reliability Limitations A source may be reliable within defined boundaries. For example: reliable for raw measurement but not interpretation, reliable for one jurisdiction but not another, reliable for one operating environment, reliable for one data type, or reliable only within a defined period. Source Reliability Determinations must preserve these boundaries. Source Reliability Uncertainty Where source identity, provenance, capability, independence, or another material condition cannot be sufficiently established, VSRS preserves uncertainty. Possible outcomes should not be forced into a binary trusted/untrusted classification. Uncertainty itself is a governed source condition. Source Reliability Status VSRS may establish conditions such as: Source Reliable The source is sufficiently reliable for the defined validation role. Source Conditionally Reliable The source may support validation only within explicit conditions, limitations, or restrictions. Source Reliability Undetermined Available information is insufficient to establish a defensible reliability determination. Source Reliability Insufficient Material source-reliability requirements remain unresolved. Source Unreliable The source cannot legitimately perform the proposed validation role. These states apply to the source-role relationship. They do not represent Evidence Fitness or the Validation State of the Validation Object. Source Reliability Is Role-Specific VALIDOS™ establishes: A source is not universally reliable or unreliable. The same source may be: Reliable for direct measurement, Conditionally Reliable for interpretation, and: Unreliable for conclusions outside its capability. Reliability must therefore remain connected to the exact evidentiary role assigned to the source. Source Reliability and Evidence Fitness VALIDOS™ maintains the architectural separation: Evidence Fitness asks: Is the evidence fit for the validation question? Source Reliability asks: Can the source behind that evidence be sufficiently relied upon for its assigned role? Neither condition substitutes for the other. Possible combinations include: Fit Evidence + Reliable Source Fit Evidence + Unreliable Source Unfit Evidence + Reliable Source Unfit Evidence + Unreliable Source Only by governing both dimensions can VALIDOS™ distinguish evidentiary quality from source trustworthiness. Source Reliability and Truth A reliable source does not automatically make every statement true. VALIDOS™ establishes: Reliable Source ≠ True Claim Source reliability concerns the credibility of the source relationship within validation. Truth-oriented assessment remains a separate methodological question. Source Reliability and Execution VSRS does not determine whether the approved validation methodology was correctly executed. A reliable source can still be used incorrectly. An unreliable source can also be correctly processed while producing a weak validation basis. Execution governance therefore remains a subsequent independent VALIDOS™ responsibility. Source Reliability Change Source reliability may change because of: source modification, ownership change, capability change, newly discovered conflicts, provenance discovery, compromised systems, altered incentives, new upstream dependencies, changed methodology, or new reliability evidence. Material change may require reassessment. Source Reliability Expiration A Source Reliability Determination may be time-bounded. Expiration may be appropriate where reliability depends upon: certification periods, calibration, organizational conditions, system versions, personnel qualifications, current independence, or another time-sensitive condition. Expiration does not mean the source becomes unreliable automatically. It means the previous determination can no longer be assumed current without reassessment. Source Reliability Traceability Source Reliability should remain traceable to: Validation Evidence, source identity, source role, provenance, lineage, capability, competence where applicable, independence, dependencies, conflicts, transformations, corroboration, limitations, uncertainty, reliability status, and subsequent validation use. This creates reconstructable source governance across the VALIDOS™ lifecycle. Governance Boundary Validation Source Reliability Standard begins when qualified Validation Evidence possesses identifiable or potentially identifiable sources requiring reliability assessment. It ends when the material source relationships behind the evidence basis have been sufficiently identified, traced, assessed, bounded, and assigned a Source Reliability status for their intended validation roles. VSRS does not determine: Validation Object identity, Validation Purpose or Scope, Validation Criteria, Validation Method suitability, Evidence Relevance, Evidence Applicability, Evidence Coverage, Evidence Adequacy, Validation Execution conformity, final Validation Determination, Validation State, reliance authorization, or revalidation requirements. These responsibilities belong to other VALIDOS™ Parent Standards. Minimum Governance Requirements A conforming implementation of VSRS should establish: 1. identifiable validation-source relationships, 2. sufficient source attribution, 3. relevant source provenance and lineage, 4. material source roles, 5. source capability for the assigned role, 6. competence where materially required, 7. independence assessment where applicable, 8. source-dependence visibility, 9. material conflict-of-interest visibility, 10. material intermediary and transformation visibility, 11. corroboration conditions where required, 12. source-reliability limitations and uncertainty, 13. a Source Reliability Determination, 14. and sufficient lifecycle traceability. Governance Outputs VSRS may produce: Validation Source Register, Source Identity Record, Source Attribution Record, Source Provenance Record, Source Lineage Map, Source Role Record, Source Capability Assessment, Source Competence Assessment, Source Independence Assessment, Source Dependence Map, Conflict-of-Interest Record, Source Incentive Record, Evidence Transformation Record, Source Corroboration Assessment, Source Reliability Limitation Record, Source Reliability Determination, Source Reliability Change Record, Source Reliability Reassessment Trigger, and Reliability-Qualified Evidence Basis. Operational Applications Validation Source Reliability Standard may be applied across: artificial intelligence, machine learning, autonomous systems, scientific evidence, datasets, benchmark results, AI-generated information, predictions, simulations, expert assessments, sensor systems, operational records, enterprise analytics, financial services, healthcare, industrial operations, regulatory compliance, critical infrastructure, digital assets, digital identities, public-sector decision systems, and any governed environment requiring source-aware validation. Relationship to Other OOF Architectures Validation Source Reliability Standard interoperates with: GOA™ OBIDENITY® INTEGROS® ORA™ AGA™ AIG® CLIA® MGIA™ ASGA™ RIS™ by providing the canonical validation-governance methodology for assessing whether sources underlying Validation Evidence can be sufficiently relied upon for their assigned validation roles. OBIDENITY® may provide complementary origin, identity, ownership, provenance, and continuity information. INTEGROS® may provide complementary integrity conditions. AGA™ may provide complementary accountability relationships. ORA™ may provide complementary operational-reality information. VSRS does not duplicate these architectures. It consumes relevant governed information where necessary and determines what that information means specifically for source reliability within validation. Foundational Principle Evidence cannot become more trustworthy merely because its source remains unquestioned. Canonical Closing Statement Validation Source Reliability Standard establishes the source-qualification layer of VALIDOS™ — Validation Governance Architecture. By governing source identity, attribution, provenance, lineage, capability, competence, independence, dependence, conflicts, incentives, intermediaries, transformations, corroboration, convergence, limitations, uncertainty, change, expiration, and traceability, VSRS ensures that validation does not rely upon evidence without also governing the reliability of the sources and source relationships from which that evidence derives. Validation Source Reliability Standard Architecture: VALIDOS™ — Validation Governance Architecture Category: AI & Interpretation · Subcategory: Validation Governance Canonical Definition: Validation Source Reliability Standard (VSRS) defines the governance conditions under which sources providing, generating, transmitting, recording, transforming, interpreting, or maintaining Validation Evidence are identified, attributable, provenance-aware, independence-assessed, integrity-aware, competence-aware, conflict-aware, and sufficiently reliable for their assigned role within a governed validation process. title: VALIDOS® Complete Standards & Modules Index
text: VALIDOS® Complete Standards & Modules Index VALIDOS® Complete Standards & Modules Index Validation Governance Architecture — Validation Governance Layer Official Validation Governance Architecture Map for AI Systems, Autonomous Systems, Digital Assets, Organizations, Critical Infrastructure, Decision Systems, Scientific Claims, Operational Processes, and Future Validation Environments This document serves as the official OOF® validation governance architecture map and structural index used for validation governance design, validation governance navigation, validation governance classification, validation diagnostics, validation architecture development, validation governance assessment, validation lifecycle governance, validation reliance governance, revalidation governance, and validation interoperability across AI systems, autonomous systems, organizations, digital assets, critical infrastructure, decision environments, scientific and technical systems, operational processes, and future validation environments. VALIDOS® consists of 10 Parent Standards and 50 Core Modules. Additional standards and modules may be added when new governable validation spaces are identified. However, the standards and modules listed below form the core structural backbone of VALIDOS®. 1. Validation Object Standard (VOBS) Governed Space: Validation Object Core Question: What exactly is being validated, how must the Validation Object be identified and bounded, and how can its version, relationships, and fitness for validation remain governed throughout the validation lifecycle? Modules: VOIM — Validation Object Identification Module VOBM — Validation Object Boundary Module VOVM — Validation Object Version Module VORM — Validation Object Relationship Module VOFM — Validation Object Fitness Module 2. Validation Purpose & Scope Standard (VPSS) Governed Space: Validation Purpose & Scope Core Question: Why is validation being performed, what must it cover, at what Validation Depth must it operate, where is it applicable, and which limitations must remain explicitly governed? Modules: VPIM — Validation Purpose Identification Module VSCDM — Validation Scope Definition Module VDCM — Validation Depth Calibration Module VAMM — Validation Applicability Mapping Module VLGM — Validation Limitation Governance Module 3. Validation Criteria Standard (VCRS) Governed Space: Validation Criteria Core Question: Against which explicit, applicable, sufficiently formulated, threshold-bounded, and internally coherent criteria must the Validation Object be evaluated? Modules: VRDM — Validation Requirement Derivation Module VCFM — Validation Criterion Formulation Module VTCM — Validation Threshold Calibration Module VARCM — Validation Acceptance & Rejection Conditions Module VCCM — Validation Criteria Coherence Module 4. Validation Method Standard (VMTS) Governed Space: Validation Method Core Question: Which validation method or combination of methods is eligible and suitable for the Validation Object, purpose, scope, criteria, consequence, and required Validation Depth, and when is that method ready for governed execution? Modules: VMEM — Validation Method Eligibility Module VMSM — Validation Method Suitability Module VMCM — Validation Method Configuration Module VMIM — Validation Method Integration Module VMRM — Validation Method Readiness Module 5. Validation Evidence Fitness Standard (VEFS) Governed Space: Validation Evidence Fitness Core Question: Is the available validation evidence sufficiently relevant, applicable, comprehensive, adequate, and fit to support the intended validation determination? Modules: VERM — Validation Evidence Relevance Module VEAM — Validation Evidence Applicability Module VECM — Validation Evidence Coverage Module VEADM — Validation Evidence Adequacy Module VEFDM — Validation Evidence Fitness Determination Module 6. Validation Source Reliability Standard (VSRS) Governed Space: Validation Source Reliability Core Question: Are the sources producing or supporting validation evidence sufficiently identifiable, attributable, provenance-grounded, capable, independent where necessary, and reliable for the intended validation purpose? Modules: VSIAM — Validation Source Identity & Attribution Module VSPLM — Validation Source Provenance & Lineage Module VSCCM — Validation Source Capability & Competence Module VSICM — Validation Source Independence & Conflict Module VSRDM — Validation Source Reliability Determination Module 7. Validation Execution Standard (VEXS) Governed Space: Validation Execution Core Question: How must an authorized and ready validation method be instantiated, controlled, observed, traced, protected against unmanaged deviations and exceptions, and completed in conformity with its governed validation basis? Modules: VEBAM — Validation Execution Basis & Authorization Module VEICM — Validation Execution Instantiation & Control Module VEOTM — Validation Execution Observation & Traceability Module VEDEGM — Validation Execution Deviation & Exception Governance Module VECCM — Validation Execution Completeness & Conformity Module 8. Validation Determination Standard (VDTS) Governed Space: Validation Determination Core Question: What determination does the complete governed validation record legitimately support, how must individual criterion results be qualified and integrated, and how must conflict, uncertainty, partial satisfaction, and negative findings remain reflected in the overall determination? Modules: VDBRQM — Validation Determination Basis & Result Qualification Module VCDM — Validation Criterion Determination Module VDCUGM — Validation Determination Conflict & Uncertainty Governance Module VCCIM — Validation Cross-Criterion Integration Module OVDM — Overall Validation Determination Module 9. Validation State Governance Standard (VSGS) Governed Space: Validation State Governance Core Question: What Validation State may legitimately be assigned to the Validation Object, under which conditions does that state apply, how must material change affect it, and how must transitions, revalidation triggers, and lifecycle continuity remain governed? Validation Reliance & Revalidation Standard (VRRS) Governed Space: Validation Reliance & Revalidation Core Question: Who or what may legitimately rely upon the current Validation State, for which purpose, scope, conditions, authorization, consequence, and duration, and how must changed validation reality trigger bounded revalidation, renewal, restriction, suspension, or withdrawal of reliance? Architectural Position VALIDOS® governs the complete validation governance lifecycle. The architecture progresses: Validation Object → Validation Purpose & Scope → Validation Criteria → Validation Method → Validation Evidence Fitness → Validation Source Reliability → Validation Execution → Validation Determination → Validation State → Validation Reliance & Revalidation Together these standards govern what is being validated, why and within which boundaries validation occurs, against which governed criteria the Validation Object is evaluated, which methods may legitimately perform that validation, what evidence is fit for the intended validation purpose, whether the sources supporting that evidence are sufficiently reliable, how validation is operationally executed, what determination the complete governed validation record supports, what Validation State may consequently exist, who or what may legitimately rely upon that state, and when changed validation reality requires revalidation. VALIDOS® therefore does not terminate when a Validation Determination is issued or a Validation State is assigned. Its lifecycle becomes recursive when a Validation State enters operational reliance: Validation Object → Purpose & Scope → Criteria → Method → Evidence Fitness → Source Reliability → Execution → Determination → Validation State → Reliance → Monitoring → Material Change → Revalidation Trigger → Revalidation Scope & Delta → Validation Reuse → Revalidation Execution → New Determination → New Validation State → Renewed, Restricted, Suspended, or Withdrawn Reliance This recursive structure allows validation governance to remain responsive to changes in the Validation Object, validation purpose, scope, criteria, methods, evidence, sources, execution conditions, operational reality, dependencies, Validation State conditions, and intended reliance throughout the complete operational lifecycle. Cross-Architecture Boundary VALIDOS® ↔ GOA® GOA® governs the architecture and constitutional conditions of governance itself. VALIDOS® governs the methodological lifecycle through which Validation Objects acquire, maintain, change, or lose governed validation status. VALIDOS® ↔ ORA® ORA® governs what is actually occurring in Operational Reality. VALIDOS® governs whether a defined Validation Object can legitimately support a validation determination under governed validation conditions. VALIDOS® ↔ OBIDENITY® OBIDENITY® governs origin, identity, ownership, authority, permission, provenance, transfer, and continuity. VALIDOS® governs validation-specific use of identified Validation Objects, sources, actors, evidence references, and governed validation records. VALIDOS® ↔ INTEGROS® INTEGROS® governs integrity across governed objects, information, states, processes, and records. VALIDOS® governs whether the complete validation basis legitimately supports a Validation Determination, Validation State, and bounded reliance. VALIDOS® ↔ ADIT® ADIT® governs evidential observation, preservation, verification, traceability, and auditability of what occurred. VALIDOS® governs the fitness and governed use of evidence within the validation lifecycle and the determination that the complete validation basis may support. VALIDOS® ↔ AGA® AGA® governs authority, responsibility, accountability, attribution, escalation, and decision relationships. VALIDOS® governs validation methodology, execution, determination, state, reliance, and revalidation conditions without absorbing general accountability governance. VALIDOS® ↔ SIMULOS® SIMULOS® governs the methodological conditions under which simulation and simulation-derived outputs acquire bounded meaning and evidential relevance. VALIDOS® governs whether simulation-derived evidence, together with the complete validation basis, sufficiently supports a Validation Determination and intended reliance. VALIDOS® ↔ AIG® / ASGA® AIG® and ASGA® govern the behavior, authority, autonomy, constraints, permissions, and operation of actual AI and autonomous systems. VALIDOS® may validate those systems, their states, claims, capabilities, outputs, or operational conditions without assuming governance of their actual behavior or autonomous authority. VALIDOS® ↔ CLIA® / MGIA® CLIA® and MGIA® govern cognition and memory where reasoning, interpretation, retained information, or historical continuity materially influence governed systems. VALIDOS® governs the validation lifecycle in which such cognition or memory may constitute part of the Validation Object, method, evidence, execution context, or reliance basis. VALIDOS® governs the methodological conditions under which a Validation Object is identified and bounded, validation purpose and scope are established, criteria and methods are governed, evidence fitness and source reliability are determined, validation is operationally executed, a defensible determination is formed, a bounded Validation State is assigned, reliance remains controlled, and material change triggers proportionate revalidation throughout the complete validation lifecycle.
